#6817. Dutch Apple Snacking Cake

Every autumn the siren song of baking calls bakers home until the volume becomes too much to bear. And at that moment, the only thing that can silence it is a warm-spiced apple cake—the kind that hugs you closer than a knit sweater. This recipe, which keeps things simple, relies on the winning combination of cinnamon and apples to perfume a vanilla cake with pockets of tender fruit. A blanket of cinnamon streusel crowns the cake, giving it a contrasting crunch and a coffee-cake-like character. Feel free to stash the cake on your counter, slicing it throughout the week, enjoying its plush interior as it magically gets better with time.

More cozy bakes this way: Caramel Apple Snacking Cake; Chocolate Olive Oil Cake; and Lemon Poppy Seed Loaf.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly coat an 8x8" metal baking pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line with parchment paper, leaving overhang on all sides. Lightly coat parchment with nonstick spray. Place 1¼ cups (156 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (packed; 200 g) light brown sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1½ tsp. ground cinnamon, ½ tsp. baking powder, and ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, melted, in a large bowl and mix with your hands, squeezing together as needed, until marble-size clumps form. Set streusel aside.

Toss 1 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 2 large), peeled, cored, thinly sliced, slices halved crosswise, and 2 Tbsp. (16 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl to coat.

Whisk 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1½ tsp. baking powder, ¼ tsp. baking soda, and remaining 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl to combine. Add ½ cup (1 stick) chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until no visible pieces remain. (Mixture should look like lightly moistened sand. Don’t worry about overworking it.) Add 2 large eggs, ⅔ cup buttermilk, 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil, and 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract and stir until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Mix in about two thirds of apples.

Scrape batter into prepared pan and spread into an even layer; smooth surface. Scatter reserved streusel and remaining apples over, letting them organically intermix. Bake cake until a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 65–75 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan. Using parchment overhang, lift cake out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Dust with powdered sugar and cut into 12 pieces if serving immediately.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 5 days ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6815. Bob Haircuts Are Everywhere—9 Signs It Is (or Isn’t) Right for You

Time to think long and hard about your hair type, style, and concerns.

If you can count on one thing, it’s that the bob haircut will be a forever trend. It’s evolved past trend status at this point, with a new style emerging every few weeks whenever the latest celebrity cuts theirs (most recently, it was Billie Eilish and Ariana Grande). There’s the clavi cut, the boyfriend bob, the shaggy bob, the elongated bob—the list goes on. But is the haircut actually right for you?

At Cosmo, we refuse to believe anyone “can’t pull off” a bob, or any haircut really. “The bob is a great style because it’s highly adaptable to most face shapes,” says hairstylist Anne Veck. “You can tailor it perfectly by playing with the length or deciding on a dramatic micro fringe or a soft, side sweep.” In other words, there’s a bob for everyone.

But cutting a bob isn’t just getting a new haircut—it’s a full-on lifestyle shift. As a proud bob-haver myself, I ran through all the considerations before chopping my hair to its shortest length ever a few months ago—and ya know what, I have zero regrets, but definitely lots to think about. So… how do you know if you’re actually ready for one? Let’s get into it.

Texture plays a huge part in the type of bob that will suit you. For instance, thinner hair will look great with a blunt cut, while thick hair looks best with a graduated style to take some of the weight out of the hair. But if you have medium-thickness, straight or wavy hair, a bob is a no-brainer, since almost any cut will work with little daily styling for that effortless, cool-girl vibe.

All this to say, bobs often work well on curly hair too, especially if you go to a hairstylist who is well-versed in curly hair. They might have to cut more layers to take off some weight if your hair is very coarse, or they could opt for a dry, blunt cut to achieve more thickness if your curls are fine.

No matter your hair thickness, texture, or density, bobs require a lot more upkeep than longer styles. Bob maintenance is nothing to sniff at when you have to make sure you have a trim in the diary every few months. And if your hair grows quicker than normal, then it might need to be more frequent than that. Can you afford this kind of upkeep? It’s definitely something to factor into your beauty budget at least quarterly if you do have the snip.

Keep this in mind if you have very damaged hair, too. Bobs can require some heat styling, so if your strands are fighting for their life from color or chemical damage already, all that heat styling could cause some unnecessary breakage.

Bobs are a statement style, and if you go from really long to really short, you will get comments and questions about your new look. As someone who thrives on people complimenting my hair, I loved this, but if you don't, you might want to do a gradual cut, rather than a big chop to stop the inevitable attention your new look will bring.

Bobs are an excellent way to do some gentle facial contouring without booking in with an aesthetics clinic. Working with your stylist, you can cut and layer your bob to emphasize the contours of your face. Styles like the bottleneck bob are built to flatter when gently waved and suit everyone.

Something I didn’t think about enough was the constant styling I would be doing after working out, as it’s harder to hide hair that needs a wash when your hair is shorter. Also, you need to think about how long your hair needs to be to be tied back. It sounds small, but dozens of hair ties later, you will be cursing the day you sat in that salon.

If your hair is highly porous (curly-haired gals and bleached peeps, I’m talking to you), it’s not impossible to have a bob; it’ll just take a few more products to keep it looking fresh when it’s sticky and humid outside. I mean, I live in drizzly London and have a bob, so it is doable, but there have been weeks where I have to wear my hair in a low bun for the majority of the days to keep my strands tucked away from the elements.

Low maintenance? We don’t know her here in bob-land. Yes, it’s less laborious to style than, say, bangs, but any bob (no matter your hair texture) will require at least a few minutes each morning to zhuzh, so you have to factor this into your getting-ready time.

Regardless of the type of bob you cut, be warned that there can be some awkward moments in the growth phase. When your bob starts skimming your shoulders, the hair can flip in and out in a way that some might find a bit wonky, tbh. If you’re not committed to having this length for a while, then you might be setting yourself up for a few months with an awkward length.

Your curls are likely to spring up and look much shorter than they’re actually cut. For some, this look is super cute and accentuates your facial features. But if you’re not ready to go extra short, bring this up to your stylist; they might recommend opting first for a lob length.

Anne Veck is a hairstylist and hair educator based in the UK

#6811. Cottage Cheese Meatballs

Adding cottage cheese to a meatball might sound like an attempt to cram extra protein into a recipe, but it’s not the only valid reason. Something magical happens with the addition of cottage cheese: It practically disappears in the baking process, lending the meatballs juiciness and a subtle savory-salty flavor. As a bonus, the cottage cheese helps to stretch the recipe and you’ll end up with almost twice as many meatballs from one pound of ground beef.

Think of this recipe as a bit of a blank canvas, allowing you to use the meatballs however you please. You can bake them and pop them in your mouth as is, drop them into simmering tomato sauce, or stuff them between slices of bread for a hearty sandwich. They, like most meatballs, are also very meal-prep-friendly and take to freezing well.

More great cottage cheese recipes this way: Cottage Cheese Lasagna; Cottage Cheese Caramelized Onion Dip; and Roasted Honeynut Squash With Cottage Cheese and Chili Crisp.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Mix together 1 large egg, 4 garlic cloves, finely chopped, one 16-oz. container cottage cheese, 1 lb. ground beef, 1 cup Italian breadcrumbs, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper in a large bowl to combine. Scoop out into 2-Tbsp. (heaping) portions and roll into smooth balls between your hands (you should have about 30).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large nonstick skillet over high heat. Working in batches and adding more oil between batches as needed, cook meatballs in a single layer, turning halfway through, until browned on 2 sides, about 3 minutes per batch. Transfer to a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet and bake in oven until cooked through, 12–14 minutes.

Do Ahead: Meatballs can be made 3 days ahead. Let cool; transfer to an airtight container and chill, or freeze up to 1 month.

#6810. Skyler Gisondo on His New Fashion Campaign—and Dressing Like Harrison Ford in the ’90s

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

The Primetime star is gearing up in Bonobos and getting ready for a very big 2027.

Skyler Gisondo is remarkably easy to talk to. If you’ve seen him on one of your various screens—whether as Decoy Dan from Primetime, Jimmy Olsen from Superman, or maybe just that meme of him from a decade-old red-carpet photo—you probably assumed as much. It’s the big smile, the friendly eyes, the freckles, the general sense of wholesomeness. But I can confirm it, because even though I know we’ve got a relatively brief window of time to discuss his new campaign with men’s fashion brand Bonobos over Zoom, we spend the first few minutes of our chat just … shooting the shit. It feels like catching up with a buddy you haven’t seen in a while. Relaxed. Natural.

Thankfully, the vibe continues as we start digging into matters of style. Gisondo tells me he’s always been interested in dressing well but hasn’t always known where to start. “I would see a cool dude walking down the street or something, and think, ‘Man, I want to look like that guy.’ But I never knew how. I always felt lost,” he says. He describes his 20s as a decade of “desperately trying on shoes that didn’t fit or something.”

He turned 30 recently, though, and “I really feel like over the last couple of years, I’ve homed in on my sense of style, what I feel good and confident in.” A very good time, then, to star in a fashion campaign—especially considering this seems like a breakout moment for the actor. He’s been working consistently since he was a kid, but his performance in Primetime as a young actor who gradually realizes just how toxic the entertainment industry can be has clearly launched him to another level. And he still has his upcoming role in Focker-in-Law this November and a couple more appearances as Jimmy Olsen (in Man of Tomorrow on the big screen and The People v. Gorilla Grodd on television) on the docket for 2027.

Over the course of our conversation, we touch on everything from dressing like a cowboy (a mistake) to using Harrison Ford in the ’90s as your style North Star (a very good idea). We also chat about the stuff he’s stolen from sets for his own wardrobe, the psychological validation of joining the Shrek franchise, and why, after Primetime, we can expect more creative big swings in the future. Read on for a few highlights.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

“It’s ultimately about your own confidence. I feel like the sweet spot for fashion is when what you look like reflects how you feel inside—when you get to this equilibrium and it allows you to be a more fully realized version of yourself. We all grow and our sense of fashion evolves with us but ultimately like I feel like there should be some current that runs through all of it. The stuff I’m drawn to is the more timeless, classic stuff. I look at Harrison Ford in the ’90s and I’m just like, it doesn’t get cooler, you know?”

“For a while, for whatever reason, me and every actor I know were like trying to look like a cowboy. And it just hit me one day: ‘None of us have ever worked a day in our lives on a cattle ranch, man.’ I don’t even know how to use a hammer! Like, what are we doing? Can we just be ourselves?”

“I’m pretty active. I surf and hike a lot when I’m at home. And I love walking; if I have an hour or two between meetings, I’ll just walk a few miles and take calls. I want something comfortable and functional, and I find a lot of vintage workwear just hits that and fits me well. And the story is so compelling to me. The idea of ‘Who’s worn this? What were they getting up to?’ ”

“What drew me to the campaign and to the clothes is that there’s a kind of timelessness to that style. My mom thought I looked amazing in the photos. My girlfriend too. My grandma and my sisters thought I looked great. It’s this very accessible and sort of classically cool thing they have going on. And I felt like me. I felt confident—so much so that I stole several items from the set.”

“With shows and movies, the fear is that it’s a one-of-one item that you might need back for another season. But that’s when you hit them with the ‘pretty, pretty please?’ You say, ‘I swear to God, I’ll guard it with my life.’ And they say, ‘Okay, but you can’t tell anybody.’ With a campaign, it’s probably easier because they’re excited for you to have it and represent. But probably 80 percent of my closet is basically just clothes stolen from characters and sets. It’s fun because you get to try on a bunch of versions of yourself and learn what you like.

“For instance, with Jimmy Olsen in the first Superman movie, they did a fantastic job with this retro-future thing. And then in The People v. Gorilla Grodd, they went a little more vintage-y in a way that felt more like me, Skyler, personally. I tried to steal almost the entire closet.”

“Well, right now I’m doing press for Primetime and Focker-in-Law. I’m doing another movie for A24 called Goblin that I’m not sure how much I can say about; I really don’t want to get fired. But I’m so excited. It’s the most insane script I think I have ever read, and it’s definitely a big swing. We have Man of Tomorrow coming out in the summer, and then Shrek 5. The number of texts I got when I got Shrek … ‘You made it, man! Oh my God! I had no idea you made it!’ I was like, ‘Thank you. Yeah, baby! Shrek 5!’

“But ultimately, it’s a very exciting moment because it’s the first time I have people asking, ‘What do you want to do?’ And I’m like, ‘Damn! I never really thought about that!’ I feel like Primetime lit a fire under me in a real way. And even though I’ve kind of been doing this my whole life, I feel a sense of drive that I’ve never felt really in this way before. So, yeah, man, I’m excited.”

#6807. Salt Bread (Shio Pan)

Welcome to the Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep into why it works. This month we welcome deputy food editor Hana Asbrink to be our guest baker. Come bake and learn with us—and don’t forget to join the Bake Club group chat over on Substack.

The version of this recipe that appeared in our November 2026 print issue has the incorrect bake time listed. The recipe that follows features the correct total bake times of 15–18 minutes (please see step 8).

Salt bread is a wondrous buttery roll known as shio pan in Japanese or sogeum ppang in Korean. It originated in Japan in 2014 and quickly became popularized in Korea soon thereafter, taking off in the post-Covid era around 2021. It’s formed by rolling each ball of dough around a nub of salted butter. As it bakes, the butter melts and oozes out of the bun, “frying” and crisping up the bottom. If you can imagine a warm dinner roll meeting a flaky croissant, you’re getting closer.

You’ll often find a range of salt bread, some leaning closer to sturdy bread with a tighter crumb and others resembling a softer milk bread. In all salt bread cases, there are a few key identifiers: (1) a deeply golden exterior, with the aforementioned crisp bottom; (2) the signature hollow in the middle (where the pat of butter once stood) when you tear the bun in half; and (3) a sprinkle of flaky or coarse salt atop the bun.

In this riff, I use an enriched dough, bringing in qualities of a soft milk bread into the mix. With the bread flour, the end result is a lovely, crowd-pleasing bun that’s great for snacking on its own or enjoying alongside a special holiday meal. If there’s one note to highlight: Ensure you are starting with a fresh pack of instant (or “rapid-rise”) yeast. This will make all the difference in the rise and the eventual yield.

Read More: BA Bake Club’s October Recipe Is the Best Dinner Roll We’ve Ever Made

1 hour 30 minutes (plus 3 hours 30 minutes for resting)

Stir 2 Tbsp. (16 g) flour and ½ cup water in a small skillet, preferably nonstick, over medium heat with a heatproof rubber spatula to combine and cook, stirring constantly, until thickened to the texture of mayonnaise, about 2 minutes; remove from heat. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into small pieces and stir until melted. Transfer tangzhong to the bowl of a stand mixer.

Add 2 large eggs, ½ cup whole milk, ¼ cup (50 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) to tangzhong; stir vigorously by hand with rubber spatula until incorporated. Add remaining 4 cups (500 g) flour, attach bowl to stand mixer fitted with a dough hook or paddle, and mix on low speed until dough is smooth and soft (it may stick to bottom of bowl but should mostly clear sides), 20–25 minutes. Pinch off a small piece of dough and stretch it between your thumbs and index fingers on both hands. The dough should be able to stretch thin enough to let light through without breaking. If it tears, the gluten is not yet developed enough. Keep mixing until it can stretch; it may take up to 30 minutes.

Transfer dough to a work surface (no need to flour) and shape into a ball. Lightly grease stand mixer bowl with vegetable oil. Return dough to bowl, cover tightly with a plate or plastic wrap, and let rise in a warm, draft-free spot until nearly doubled in size, about 2 hours. (For optimal flavor, let dough sit at room temperature 30 minutes, then cover tightly or transfer to an airtight container and chill at least 8 hours and up to 2 days to proof slowly.)

Meanwhile, cut 1 cup (2 sticks) salted butter into 1-Tbsp. pieces and arrange in a single layer on a large plate or small baking sheet. Chill in freezer until ready to use.

Transfer dough to a surface (no need to bring to room temperature before shaping if you chilled it). Using a bench scraper or paring knife, cut dough into 70–75 g portions (you’ll get 12–16 portions depending on how much your dough has risen). Working with 1 portion at a time, cup your hand over dough and drag across surface, moving your hand in a rapid circular motion to form into a tight ball (cold dough is easier to work with; rolling into balls on an unfloured, ungreased counter creates friction and helps the shaping process). Place on a baking sheet and cover with plastic wrap; let sit 15 minutes.

Uncover dough (save plastic wrap) and, working one at a time, carefully roll each ball into a cone shape with your hands (you want them about 4" on the wider end). Return to baking sheet and re-cover with reserved plastic wrap. Let dough rest 15 minutes.

Place a cone in front of you on surface with wider end facing toward you (keep remaining cones covered in plastic wrap). Lightly flatten with your palm, then roll out dough lengthwise to make an isosceles triangle about 12" long with a 3½"–4"-wide base (short side of triangle). Place 1 Tbsp. frozen salted butter at base of dough and roll up (not too tightly) like a croissant. Arrange, seam side down, back on baking sheet. Repeat with remaining cones and salted butter (you may not need all of the butter; save it for another use). Let rolls sit at room temperature until slightly puffed, about 1 hour.

Place a rack in lowest position in oven; preheat to 425°. Remove plastic from rolls. Lightly mist rolls with water from spray bottle; sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Bake 10 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back and continue baking rolls until golden brown on top and bottom, 5–8 minutes more (keep an eye that they don’t burn). Remove from oven (there will be melted butter on baking sheet, so be careful) and, using a heatproof pastry brush, brush butter on baking sheet over rolls. Let rolls cool at least 10 minutes before serving.

Do Ahead: Rolls can be baked 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6806. BA's Best Rice Krispies Treats

Perhaps the most nostalgic of all recipes, a classic Rice Krispies treat is hard to beat. There’s just something about the crisp yet gooey texture that can’t be replicated. While the classic back-of-box recipe is a guaranteed winner, we thought it was high time to give the original a run for its money. Introducing our new favorite way to make Rice Krispies treats, with a few small (but dramatic) tweaks to the original formula. For starters, this version increases the butter and browns it, adding a subtle nutty flavor. From there, the marshmallows are split in two: The first set gets fully melted into the butter along with salt and vanilla, while the remaining set gets folded in along with the cereal so you get pockets of stretchy marshmallow throughout. While seemingly insignificant, these small changes make for a Rice Krispies treat that’s perfectly pullable, delightfully sweet yet salty, and just a touch more exciting than the classic.

Read More: The Only Type of Marshmallows I’ll Use for Rice Krispies Treats

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Lightly coat a 13x9" baking pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray and line with parchment paper, leaving overhang on long sides. Cook ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat, stirring constantly, until butter foams, then darkens to a light amber, about 4 minutes. Remove from heat and immediately add one 10-oz. bag mini marshmallows, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and quickly stir until marshmallows are melted.

Add remaining one 10-oz. bag mini marshmallows and 9 cups Rice Krispies or other puffed rice cereal to pot and mix until cereal is completely coated in melted marshmallow mixture and last addition of marshmallows is melted slightly. Working quickly, transfer mixture to prepared pan and spread into an even layer. (Don’t press too hard.) Let sit at least 1 hour before cutting into squares.

Do Ahead: Rice Krispies treats can be made 2 days ahead. Store tightly covered at room temperature.

The Duke of Sussex is trying hard to win his sister-in-law over again.

It’s no secret that Prince Harry and his brother, Prince William, aren’t exactly friends right now—even though Harry has moved back to the UK with his wife, Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, and their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet. But Harry’s relationship with his sister-in-law, Catherine, Princess of Wales, has also come under serious strain amid the fallout.

Kate and Harry were once super close, but they’ve not been seen together publicly since King Charles’ Coronation in May 2023. However, it now sounds as though Harry wants to make amends, with a source close to the Sussexes telling The Times that Harry is “mindful” of the King’s upcoming trip to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) and the Prince and Princess of Wales’ expected visit to India, ensuring his own activities will not clash.

“Obviously with the King going to CHOGM and the Prince and Princess of Wales going to India, he knows about those things and he is obviously mindful of that as he’s planning his own activities as well,” the source said.

The King is currently on a nine-day tour of the Caribbean, which will culminate at CHOGM. Meanwhile, the Earthshot Prize Awards are due to take place in Mumbai this month, and Prince William is confirmed to attend, but it is not yet clear whether Kate will join him. If she does go, it would be her first appearance at the Earthshot awards since 2022, and a likely focus of attention in its own right.

The reported effort to avoid scheduling around major royal events comes after Harry’s GQ interview was published on the same day as the King’s ceremonial welcome for the Sultan of Oman, which raised some eyebrows. A Sussex spokesperson said the publication date was GQ’s decision and not Harry’s, but it sparked off a discussion around how the estranged prince can pull attention away from the working royals.

Against that backdrop, the idea that he is factoring the King and the Waleses’ plans into his schedule could be read as a deliberate olive branch, giving off the vibe that Harry is trying to make space for his family, rather than compete with them for headlines.

As for how Kate in particular features here, it’s reported that she was one of the go-betweens trying to keep the brothers close. In William & Catherine, royal editor Russell Myers wrote (per Marie Claire), “Whether counseling William or having a quiet word in Harry’s ear, she saw it as her duty to keep the two brothers on the same team, as did their senior aides.”

Kate has also carved out a place in the royal calendar with her annual Together at Christmas carol concert, which brings together big names and people doing good in their communities. It’s one of the moments when the spotlight is firmly on her—so Harry reportedly keeping the Waleses’ plans in mind could be an especially meaningful gesture.

#6798. Every New Balance 990, Ranked

The New Balance 990 is one of the greatest sneaker lines ever. First released in 1982, the original took four years to develop and cost around $100—a lot for a running shoe back then. But the Boston brand wanted to make the best one it possibly could, and it wasn't cutting corners. More than four decades later, the series has given us some of its best trainers, with each generation making its own adjustments to the suede, the mesh, and everything underfoot.

And with the seventh-gen 990v7 coming in hot, it felt like a good time to revisit the whole thing. A lot has changed since the OG, and some updates have worked better than others. We took stock—from the early pairs to the latest model, from the one that didn't quite hit to the GOAT—and here's every New Balance 990, ranked.

Well, someone had to come in last place. The 990v5 simplified the paneling and added Ortholite insoles, but visually, it's the one we get least hyped up about. The plastic detailing feels a little awkward, and the cleaner upper loses some of the aura of its predecessors. Of course, it's still a good-looking sneaker—there are just six others we'd pick first.

Putting the OG this low feels a little blasphemous, but being first doesn't automatically mean best. The 990v1's slim sole, big “N” logo, and straightforward suede panelling make it an easy pair to wear. It's a handsome thing. We just prefer the more complicated, slightly nerdier designs that NB came up with afterwards.

The newest 990 gets a provisional fifth. There's plenty to like in the reworked upper, including the leather accents, but the busy sole takes some getting used to. From the teaser photos, the proportions don't look quite as convincing as the pairs above it. With the release still ahead, we're judging the design here. A few good colorways could easily move it up.

The 990v6 made a fairly big change: out went the mid-foot saddle, leaving the “N” sitting directly on the mesh, and in with FuelCell cushioning underneath. The result looks longer and more substantial than earlier versions. That's part of the appeal, especially under wider trousers. But all that sole can dominate a fit, and we'd take the slightly neater proportions of our top three.

The 990v2 is the freaky-looking one, and we mean that in the best way possible. The small “N,” angular panels, and sculpted sole give it a very different feel from the rest of the family. There's a lot going on, but the slimmer upper keeps it from looking heavy. It's the pair we'd choose for someone who already has the obvious New Balances and wants something a little more particular.

The 990v4 is probably the one we'd recommend most often. The shape is beefy without being bulky. The suede overlays leave just enough mesh showing through. It works with jeans, loose chinos, and trousers you'd usually save for the office. Nothing feels oversized or awkward. Second place comes down to a small preference: we like the winner's extra detail a little more.

The diamond-patterned tongue. The ribbed “N.” The way the suede panels spread across the mesh. The 990v3 gives you plenty to look at, and somehow it all works together. It has the most convincing proportions of the seven: broad enough to suit loose trousers, with a sole that doesn't completely overwhelm the upper. Even in the standard grey color combo, there's nothing we'd want to change. Our GOAT.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

#6793. This Revamped Field Watch Is More Fall-Coded Than Pumpkin Spice

Watch collaborations can sometimes feel they have been randomly cobbled together, two disparate brands fusing to make something wholly uninteresting. This isn’t the case for Huckberry or the Canadian military watchmaker Marathon, which supplied timekeeping equipment to Allied forces in 1941. The natural alignment between brands gave Huckberry the perfect excuse to rummage through the archives and collaborate on the all-new, 41mm CeraShell Navigator, a pilot’s watch whose design traces back to the Steel Navigator developed with Kelly Air Force Base in 1986.

Military and heritage references are already a big part of Huckberry’s in-house brands, particularly Flint and Tinder. For its take on the Navigator, Huckberry focused on the dial, color, and tweaked a few distinct details rather than changing the watch too dramatically.

That starts with Marathon’s matte-black CeraShell case, here paired with an Arctic white dial for the first time on a CeraShell Navigator. The familiar 12- and 24-hour scales remain, while Huckberry swaps the usual red seconds hand for its hunter orange. Branding has also been kept to a minimum, with Huckberry’s tree logo placed on the crown instead of the already slightly crowded dial.

Together, the black case, white dial, and orange second hand simplify the Navigator’s appearance, but doesn’t drown out its classic military timepiece pedigree. The case is made from Marathon’s CeraShell, a proprietary combination of bio-sourced plastic and ceramic powder that helps keep the watch lightweight. It measures 11.5mm thick and is fitted with a sapphire crystal, while tritium tubes provide constant illumination for the hour and minute hands, hour markers, and bezel pip.

Inside the 41mm case is an ETA F06.115 HeavyDrive quartz movement, with water resistance rated to 60 meters. The watch comes with two straps, an olive-green DEFSTAN nylon strap and a coyote-brown HANK strap made using neoprene and Kevlar, extending the military influence beyond the case and dial.

The watch sits in the duality of being both rugged and completely refined, which is, in some ways, a perfect distillation of both brands. The Navigator is available now exclusively through Huckberry’s site.

#6791. Do You Need a Night Cream? The 10 Best Picks for Dryness, Sensitive Skin, Fine Lines, and More

Sleep may be free, but great skin takes a little investment. So while you're dreaming about running away to Tuscany or that boy you matched with on Hinge (guilty), your face is quietly clocking in for the night shift. Its objectives? Repairing and renewing with the help of the right night cream—because the right one can turn those eight hours of unconsciousness into a full-blown glow-up, coaxing out collagen and smoothing the fine lines that betray our Netflix habits.

Of course, you could just use a moisturizer, but a night cream is richer, often filled with firming and plumping ingredients that work best overnight. Not sure which is for you? Fear not, because there's a night cream out there for everyone, whether you've got dry skin, wrinkles, dark spots, or anything in between. To help you find your perfect match, I’ve rounded up the best night creams for all skin types and concerns. So, consider the following your skin's version of a silk pillowcase: indulgent, effective, and worth every last dreamy drop.

“This is a heaven-sent nourishing moisturizer for sensitive, dry, and acne-prone skin. My aesthetician, Madalaina Conti, first recommended this for me. I love it not only for acne, but it helps with my tight, flaky skin that I get in the winter months. When I use this overnight, it brings back all the plumpness and hydration. When I’m really dry, I’ll put on a thick layer like a mask and sleep in it.”—JASMINE HYMAN, ASSISTANT BEAUTY EDITOR

“I understand the purpose of a night cream is to be thick and cocoon-like on your face. But when you want all the moisture without your face sticking to your pillow, this ‘cloud cream’ from Kiehl’s is perfect. It’s got a whipped texture that feels really light, yet it’s packed with squalane, rich lipids, and shea butter.”—BETH GILLETTE, BEAUTY EDITOR

“The fine lines around my eyes look less noticeable, and my under-eyes suddenly seems like I’m getting sleep again. I’m 29 and starting to think about taking extra care of my eyes and neck, so I’ve been focusing on those two areas every night for the last two months. And I really notice a difference. My eyes look brighter and more awake in the morning, and my under-eye bags aren’t as prominent.”—BG

“If you have super dry skin and suffer from redness and irritation, this is the night cream for you. The thick consistency is deeply moisturising, cocooning your skin in a rich, soothing layer. The formula itself is infused with Japanese indigo and ceramides, which help to calm irritation, strengthen your skin barrier, and leave you waking up looking like you actually got eight hours of sleep (even if you didn't).”—LIA MAPPOURA, BEAUTY WRITER

“I’ve used up a few tubs of this ultra-rich moisturizer. It’s my go-to in the winter when my skin gets quite dry. It feels so luxe, even down to the glass jar, but is a mere fraction of the price of so many of my other favorites (and I love that I can pick it up quickly from the drugstore whenever I need it).”—BG

“If you're a loyal retinol user, listen up because Medik8's Advanced Night Restore was made with you in mind. This rich yet fast-absorbing cream is designed to be applied after your retinoid, helping to soothe, strengthen, and deeply nourish skin overnight. Infused with ceramides, antioxidants, and a reparative peptide complex, it reinforces the skin's barrier and locks in moisture, making it ideal for dry, sensitive complexions.”—LM

“I randomly started using this when I was very young and had not a single wrinkle on my face. But I loved the rich texture so much; it made my skin look so glowy and fresh. I felt like I woke up with better skin every time I used it. Now at 29, I’m returning back to it, and I realize this is so freakin’ good to add into any anti-aging routine. This cream is loaded with moisturizing ingredients, which is a must if you’re trying to offset dryness from any actives like retinol or AHAs.”—BG

“As a beauty writer, I'm often asked what my favorite skincare brand is. And while I experiment with many daily, my response always remains the same. Cetaphil! The dermatologist-recommended brand is a failsafe option for me, not only for its pared-back formulas that work twice as hard as the fancy brands (and don't irritate my sensitive, breakout-prone skin), but also for its price. I mean, you can't go wrong with a product that’s less than $15. The Rich Night Cream is just that: rich in consistency to hydrate yet not overbear the skin. Breathable yet effective, if you will.”—LM

A night cream is any cream that you use at night before bed to hydrate your skin. The idea is that night creams are thicker and made with rich emollients that work well to seal in hydration overnight versus your standard moisturizer that could be applied day or night. But a night cream can be a cream for nighttime, even if it’s not explicitly called a night cream. FWIW, that’s more of a marketing term than anything.

You absolutely need a moisturizer before bed, even if you have oily skin. But do you need a specific cream that’s called a “night cream”? Not necessarily, so long as your nighttime moisturizer is doing its job of hydrating and locking in moisture while you sleep.

How to choose the right night cream for you

If you have dry skin, the night cream selection process will probably be a breeze for you. Most night creams contain a plethora of ingredients to moisturize your skin. But some of those can be too heavy for oily and/or acne-prone skin. If you want something on the lighter side, avoid anything with a lot of butters and oils, like shea butter or cocoa butter. Lightweight hydrators include squalane, jojoba oil, hyaluronic acid, and panthenol.

Look for a mix of hydrators and sealants.

The key to moisturizing your skin is two-fold: Hydrate, then lock in moisture. Hydration comes from humectants, aka ingredients that pull water into your skin. That’s glycerin, hyaluronic acid, panthenol, and aloe vera. But once you’ve hydrated, you want to keep all that water in your skin, which is where sealants come in. That’s oils and butters. They create a barrier over your skin to keep moisture from seeping out. Together, the two create a formula that offers lasting hydration, not just a quit hit of plumpness.

#6790. Why Is It So Hard to Call Someone Out on the Group Chat?

Read the rest of GQ’s special report on Cornell here and here.

The screenshot, circulated in reporting on the allegation of sexual assault by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell in 2024, is painful to look at, and painfully familiar: a more extreme example of an episode that plays out on our own phones. Someone in the group chat says something fucked-up. You cringe as laughing emojis roll in. You think about saying something. You probably don’t. And you feel worse for it. Northwestern sociologist Aaron Shaw, who has studied how groups talk to each other online, explains why it happens.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

This kind of interaction is seen linked to the general disinhibition effects documented in digital communications: If your face isn’t there, and if you’re not confronted with the presence of other people, it’s a lot easier to behave in ways that may break with normal social conventions. There’s a long legacy of misogynistic groups existing and thriving. Some people might want to say, “Oh, this is a problem because of Snapchat,” but what research in the last 30 years suggests is that people will find ways to connect no matter what digital communication platform they are using. Research about online communities dates back to the 1980s and ’90s, and some of the high-drama incidents occurring in that time were around rape culture.

Gaming is an incredibly heterogeneous space of human activity, but there are some communities where violations of social norms are not just okay, but important: “If you want to play the game, you’ve got to get over it.”

They might be communicating at multiple levels in ways that are hard to see from the outside. By drawing on particular words they’ve used in the past, they might be signaling things to each other, like their membership in the group, their commitment to each other. Their desire to stay connected with each other may be more powerful than the desire to speak in an empathetic way about, in this case, the experience of a young woman.

Some research on bystander effects suggests that the larger the group size, the less likely any one individual in that group is to speak out against it. Individuals may feel like they don’t have control or that they can’t be responsible for the behavior of everybody in the chat. If their sense is that others in the group think this is okay—or would be willing to ostracize them if they were to speak out—they’re less likely to be willing or able to speak out.

There’s also a performative element. They are putting on a show; they are onstage for each other. Group chats really do serve that purpose. It’s hard to know what elements of that performance are, in a sense, fiction and what elements are a factual representation of the events that night in the frat house. The tropes these young guys may be using may be profoundly objectionable, may be hyper-misogynistic, may undermine the humanity and rights and autonomy of women, but it doesn’t necessarily equate to evidence of rape. In some ways it’s like cultural expression.

It might feel comforting to say, “Well, we can’t fix culture easily, but what we can do is kick people out of group chats or ban fraternities from campus.” But there’s lots of reasons to believe that that’s not going to actually address the root causes. There’s evidence that a lot of young men feel left behind or excluded by prevailing cultural and political and economic forces. I’m not saying that’s factually true, but the feeling seems to have made some young men hateful towards those they perceive to be not like them, who they perceive to be threats to their authority. It’s heartbreaking, not just for the alleged victim of sexual assault, but also for the people who engage in the chat. I don’t think that’s going to give them the sense of security and self that might allow them to behave more generously and respectfully towards others, either. ◼︎

Fraternities control access to coveted resources. They use humiliating rituals to bond with each other, enforce hierarchy, and belittle outsiders. Sound familiar?

What people in Ithaca are saying—and not saying—about the sexual assault allegations brought against members of the Chi Phi fraternity.

#6787. Pumpkin Enchiladas With Black Beans

Homemade enchiladas might sound like a laborious weekend project, but with a few clever tricks, this version made with black beans and pumpkin can be whipped up on even the most hurried of work nights. For starters, canned pumpkin creates the base of a quick sauce that requires no precooking. And because they are vegetarian, the filling—a combination of canned black beans, onion, and bell pepper flecked with cilantro—comes together in a flash. In lieu of baking the enchiladas, this version opts for broiling in order to brown the tops while also heating the enchiladas through in the same skillet you cook the beans in. A flourish of pumpkin seeds, sliced onion, cilantro, and fresh lime brightens up everything, although serving them straight from the oven would be just as delicious.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large broilerproof skillet over medium-high. Add 1 large white onion, finely chopped, and 1 medium green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, and cook, stirring often, until browned in spots and fragrant, 7–9 minutes. Add 4 garlic cloves, finely grated, two 15-oz. cans black beans, rinsed, and 2 Tbsp. chili powder and cook, stirring occasionally, just until combined and beans are warmed through, about 3 minutes. Transfer bean mixture to a large bowl; reserve pan.

Smash bean mixture with a spoon or potato masher until about half of the beans are mashed. Mix in juice of 1 lime and ¼ cup coarsely chopped cilantro; season with kosher salt. Set bean mixture aside.

Whisk together one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 1 tsp. Tabasco, and 1¼ cups water in a large bowl; season pumpkin sauce with salt.

Place 1 of twelve 6" flour tortillas on a surface. Scoop out ¼ cup (heaping) reserved bean mixture and arrange in center down length of tortilla. Scatter some of 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup), over, then roll up tortilla into a cylinder. Place, seam side down, in reserved skillet. Repeat process with remaining tortillas. Brush tops with oil.

Place a rack in upper third of oven; heat broiler. Broil enchiladas until tops are deeply toasted and charred in spots, 4–7 minutes (depending on your broiler; watch carefully as they can go from browned to burnt very quickly). Pour pumpkin sauce over enchiladas and spread into an even layer. Top with remaining 4 oz. pepper jack cheese or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about ¾ cup) and raw pumpkin seeds (pepitas; if using). Broil until cheese is melted and deeply browned in spots, 4–7 minutes (watch carefully). Remove enchiladas from broiler and top with thinly sliced white onion and cilantro leaves with tender stems. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

#6786. The 15 Best Moisturizers Perfect for Mature Skin

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Nourishing favorites from brands like Augustinus Bader and ZIIP come expert-recommended

There are plenty of ways to treat signs of aging, but among the most effective is also the simplest: Striking the right moisture balance for your skin. Proper hydration can help reduce the appearance of fine lines and dullness, while also improving skin laxity over time. While almost any face cream can boost hydration, the best moisturizers for mature skin provide targeted, preventative treatments in a jar.

Key ingredients, such as peptides, retinoids, and others, work together to target specific concerns. “Retinoids or plant-based alternative bakuchiol improve and prevent fine lines, increase cellular turnover, improve skin texture and elasticity, and [reduce] discoloration,” dermatologist Morayo Adisa tells Bazaar. “Look for antioxidants such as vitamin C and E to help with collagen production and decrease oxidative stress. Hyaluronic acid, glycerin, and urea to increase skin hydration, softening the appearance of lines and wrinkles. Also, look for an emollient such as squalane or shea butter.”

Several moisturizers feature at least one of these transformative ingredients, so how do you know which one is right for you? To help narrow down your options, we asked Adisa, along with other dermatologists, for their thoughts on some of the best moisturizers for mature skin.

Neutrogena continuously proves that you don't have to spend a ton of money to reap the benefits of wrinkle-smoothing ingredients. This night cream targets the primary causes of wrinkles, uneven tone, and loss of elasticity with a firming and plumping lipid complex called Hexinol, brightening vitamin C, and moisturizing ingredients such as shea butter and glycerin.

Key ingredients: vitamin C, glycerin, hexinol

The clinical studies on this gel cream after four weeks of use are pretty impressive. Co-signed by dermatologist Hadley King, this moisturizer works at a cellular level to restimulate collagen production, diminish dark spots, and significantly smooth deep-set wrinkles.

“It contains humectants and emollients like squalane, as well as niacinamide, which improves tone and texture, and willowherb, which has senolytic properties to help promote skin longevity,” says King. The brand's proprietary combination of plant stem cells targets exosomes, energizes skin through NAD+, and decreases inflammation.

Key ingredients: squalane, niacinamide, willowherb, plant stem cells

Bring the spa home: This do-it-all hydrator makes it a breeze to give mature skin a refresher. Valmont’s Prime Renewing Pack leaves skin with a healthy glow in minutes and uses a creamy formula that reduces fine lines and wrinkles while seamlessly smoothing texture. Use a thin layer of the Pack as a quick five-minute mask, or a thicker layer for a more intensive treatment.

Key ingredients: peptides, RNA liposome, triple DNA complex

Sisley Paris's Black Rose cream is a go-to choice for beauty lovers and makeup artists alike, thanks to its excellent priming capabilities. The star ingredients, alkekengi calyx extract and padina pavonica, work in tandem to plump skin that's lost volume. There's also hibiscus flower extract and alpine rose extract, which help erase dullness, making your skin look more vibrant and glowy before you apply any makeup.

Key ingredients: black rose oil extract, black rose aqueous extract, alpine rose extract, alkekengi calyx extract, padina pavonica extract, hibiscus flower extract, shea and camelina oils

If you’re looking for a longer-lasting alternative for skin hydration, allow us to introduce you to Neuraé’s Harmonie The Sleeping Mask. The nourishing mask is created to rejuvenate dull, dry skin while reducing redness over time. Plus, its emollient-rich formula is the perfect addition to your beauty routine in colder months.

Key ingredients: gardenia jasminoides extract, shea butter, kokum butter, babassu oil

Here’s a top-rated moisturizer from Sulwhasoo that minimizes dullness, fine lines, wrinkles, and dryness simultaneously. The hypoallergenic cream has a whipped texture that works for a range of skin types and delivers up to 24 hours of hydration.

Key ingredients: Korean herb extract, Jisun firming complex, white mulberry, jujube, Chinese skullcap

Augustinus Bader is another worthy splurge, and in a few uses, you'll understand why. The Rich Cream utilizes a proprietary blend of TFC8, which features squalane, argan, sunflower seed, and evening primrose oils to stimulate cellular renewal and deliver targeted ingredients to skin cells.

Key ingredients: evening primrose oil, argan oil, sunflower seed oil, squalane, glycerin

If you’re already a fan of ZIIP’s devices, this moisturizer from the brand deserves a place in your rotation. The brand’s high-tech essential works with your skin’s electrical activity, along with ingredients like encapsulated collagen peptides, argireline, and more, to smooth expression lines while boosting firmness and radiance after six weeks of use.

Key ingredients: collagen peptide moisturizer with argireline amplified peptide solution, marine samphire bioactive

The 2:4:2 in the names refers to the trifecta of two percent ceramides, four percent cholesterol, and two percent fatty acids that work together to rebalance the skin and even out elasticity irregularities that cause sagging, roughness, and enlarged pores. It's a deeply moisturizing formula that replenishes and seals in moisture to help skin look and feel smooth and plump.

Key ingredients: ceramides, cholesterol, fatty acids

You'll see impressive skin-firming results with many of the moisturizers on this list, but this one is specifically designed for those who don't want to wait weeks to reap the benefits of their cream. Over time, the formula stimulates the sirtuin protein within the skin to boost collagen, hyaluronic acid, and elastin production.

Key ingredients: instant tightening sugars, micro-hyaluronic acid, glycerin, sunflower seed oil, grapeseed oil, shea butter

Dermatologist Marisa Garshick notes that some moisturizers contain ingredients that help support collagen production, thereby improving the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles while firming the skin. “A great option is the Mother Science Molecular Genesis barrier repair moisturizer, which uses their patented ingredient malassezin to strengthen the skin barrier, while also containing other ingredients like hyaluronic acid, growth factors, copper peptides, lipids and squalane, which together help to boost hydration, reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles, and offer antioxidant benefits against free radical damage,” she explains.

Key ingredients: malassezin, copper peptides, squalane, hyaluronic acid, lipid concentrate

Mature skin can still experience breakouts, but this formula, which King also recommends, replenishes lost moisture without clogging pores or making the skin oilier. The formula looks to dimethicone for moisture and adaptogenic Chinese herbs to strengthen compromised skin barriers.

Key ingredients: dimethicone, ginseng, gotu kola, dongquai

Another one of Adisa's top choices is this rejuvenating cream from Andalou Naturals. The formula utilizes bakuchiol, a gentler yet equally effective alternative to retinol. “Bakuchiol works to reduce the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles and overall leaves the skin feeling rejuvenated,” Adisa explains. It also features a fruit stem cell complex and super antioxidants to restore and protect the skin barrier. "This has a nice, lightweight whipped consistency that quickly absorbs," notes Adisa.

Key ingredients: bakuchiol, resveratrol, goji berry, aloe vera

This rich moisturizer, created by dermatologist Ben Johnson, is rich in barrier-protecting oils and antioxidants. The cream also contains an effective blend of phosphatidylcholine, raspberry seed oil, and shea butter to keep skin nourished. However, if you require even more moisture, consider layering the brand's face oil, Osmosis Nourish, on top after application.

Key ingredients: phosphatidylcholine, raspberry seed oil, shea butter, apricot oil, blueberry

Here's a top-rated cream that works overnight to smooth and tighten as you snooze. The formula not only evens skin's texture but also repairs its barrier while visibly lifting sagging skin. Plus, since you won't need more than two pumps of the favorite to cover your entire face, a little goes a long way.

Key ingredients: retinol, bakuchioil, vitamin C, hyaluronic acid, antioxidants

Adisa noted earlier that retinoids or the plant-based alternative, bakuchiol, are ideal for improving and preventing fine lines, increasing cellular turnover, smoothing skin texture, and enhancing elasticity—so check ingredient lists for these. Garshick says to also look for moisturizers like hyaluronic acid and glycerin, along with ingredients to support the skin barrier, such as ceramides and squalane, and peptides or growth factors to help with firmness. “Antioxidants like vitamin C can help to protect against environmental stressors, while niacinamide may be added to help calm and soothe the skin,” Garshick notes.

“As we age, the skin barrier weakens, contributing to increased moisture loss, and there is decreased production of sebum, hyaluronic acid, and ceramides, key ingredients that help to keep the skin moisturized. This makes the skin more prone to dryness and dullness,” Garshick explains.

Johnson adds that skin dries out with age primarily due to a loss of circulation. “As the skin ages, it loses about one percent of circulation each adult year, so at 50, the skin has 25 percent less circulation,” says Johnson. “This leads to fewer nutrients, lipids, and immune cells, which result in a porous, dehydrated barrier.”

Incorporating a moisturizer for mature skin helps hydrate the skin while supporting the skin barrier. “Some moisturizers may also contain ingredients that help to support collagen production, improving the appearance of fine lines and wrinkles while also firming the skin,” notes Garshick.

Johnson advises steering clear of alpha-hydroxy acids because they can dry out and damage the skin. Ceramides, while generally good for sealing in moisture, can also be problematic. “They have a feedback-loop effect on the skin that results in them slowing down your epidermal turnover rate,” the expert says. You should also ease off on harsh exfoliants, which can damage the skin barrier and speed up moisture loss, leaving skin dry and crepey.

#6785. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.

#6783. Pumpkin Bolognese

Classic Bolognese, with its multi-hour cook time, can be truly remarkable, if you ever have a stretch to make it. In this version, a scoop of canned pumpkin purée is the head-turning ingredient that gives it full-blown flavor and body, without the wait typical of a nonna-style sauce. Lightly caramelizing the pumpkin in the pot along with tomato paste gives it a nutty, savory edge. Milk is the other surprise ingredient here, especially in the quantity of a full cup. Think of it as a tenderizer, making the final sauce soft and delicate. Pay attention to the order in which the ingredients appear—the milk goes in first with the wine to follow. If you switch the order, the acidic wine will curdle the milk.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Heat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Add 1 large white or yellow onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. freshly grated nutmeg and stir to combine. Cover pot and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are very soft, 8–10 minutes. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until onion and celery are golden around the edges, about 5 minutes.

Uncover pot and add 1 lb. ground beef, preferably 20% fat; season lightly with salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until beef is very lightly browned but not crisp (it will still be pink in spots), 6–8 minutes. Pour in 1 cup whole milk and cook, stirring occasionally, until milk has evaporated and fat is pooling on surface of meat, 7–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup dry white wine and cook, stirring occasionally, until wine has evaporated, 6–8 minutes. Add 1 cup canned pumpkin purée and 2 Tbsp. double-concentrated tomato paste; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, stirring often and scraping bottom of pot, until combined and pumpkin darkens slightly, 8–10 minutes.

Pour in 1 cup water, reduce heat to low, and cook, stirring occasionally, until mixture is saucy, 12–15 minutes. If meat seems dry, add an extra ½ cup water and continue cooking another 3–4 minutes. Taste sauce and season with salt if needed. Keep warm.

Meanwhile, cook 12 oz. fresh tagliatelle or pappardelle or dry rigatoni, in a large pot of boiling salted water. If using fresh pasta, cook about 3 minutes. If using dry, cook until very al dente, about 2 minutes less than package directions.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to pot with sauce. Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid and 2 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about 1 cup). Increase heat to medium, bring to a simmer, and cook, tossing constantly, until pasta is al dente and sauce is slightly thickened, about 2 minutes.

Transfer pasta to shallow bowls and sprinkle with more Parmesan.

#6781. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6780. Michael Kors Still Believes in Magic

The New York native is marking his namesake brand’s 45th anniversary in style.

When Michael Kors thinks back to his 40th anniversary runway show in 2021, he remembers it fondly as a step toward a dream fulfilled. At the time, Covid restrictions had kept audiences from viewing the collection in person, though supermodels like Naomi Campbell and Bella Hadid walked the show, turning New York’s Theater District into a runway. “It was a bit of wishful thinking about how life would be once the city reopened,” Kors says. “Even though we were shut down, I knew that eventually the city would revitalize—and now life has not only returned, it’s returned with a vengeance.”

Five years later, dreams became reality as he hosted his 45th anniversary fall 2026 runway show in one of New York’s most famous cultural landmarks, the Metropolitan Opera House, at Lincoln Center this past February. His return to a theatrical venue marked a full-circle moment, a celebration of life lived in community with others. Kors recalled a recent trip to the opera house where young women in attendance were dressed to the nines, which for Kors was a clear sign of a post-Covid affinity for glamour. “People are celebrating going out, and they want to look great while they’re doing it,” Kors says. “This 45th anniversary show was a love letter to live performance, to New York City, and to going out and making an entrance.” The collection more than lived up to that promise, with leather opera gloves and draped evening dresses. In a fitting throwback, Christy Turlington—who starred in the designer’s first ad campaign—closed the show. Broadway stars like Rachel Zegler and Nicole Scherzinger watched from the front row before heading across the street to another Manhattan institution, P.J. Clarke’s, to celebrate with champagne toasts and a serenade from Rufus Wainwright.

For Kors, famously a patron of the arts, choosing the space as a backdrop for his collections was intentional. Live performance and fashion have always been connected for him, particularly through movement. Just as a performance changes when experienced through a screen, clothes lose something when reduced to a still image. That idea was central to the brand’s 45th anniversary collection. “We don’t live in a still picture, we live in a moving video,” he says. The transporting power of live performance is worth fighting for, particularly as financial support for the arts has been faltering. “We have very few times in our lives when we are in a communal situation,” Kors says. “Anything that allows us to unplug and experience something magical with other human beings is something we can’t let disappear.”

There is another somewhat fantastical engine that fuels Kors: New York. Throughout the brand’s history, he has captured the essence of the city’s dynamic style. “New York is always changing,” the designer says. “The energy has always been a source of inspiration.” Describing the city’s fashion scene as “contradictory,” even comparing it to a “big bowl of potato chips with caviar,” Kors understands the balance between function and glamour, discipline and indulgence. This dance between those opposing impulses is what gives New York its unmistakable character. “When things are strictly casual, it feels boring, and when they’re strictly glamorous, it feels too special for daily life.”

That balance of ease and enchantment has been foundational to the Kors brand since its inception. In a review of the brand’s first runway show in 1984, WWD defined the collection as “haute, classic streetwear” and “elegant but minimal,” sentiments that the designer still identifies with today. “When I read things that were said about me when I first started, you would say, ‘Wow, he’s still using that same playbook,’ and I am.” But while his design ethos has remained steady, Kors is sympathetic to how culture, and thus fashion, has drastically changed. “What is considered casual now versus what was considered casual in the ’80s? Night and day.” From how clothes were designed to how they were styled, the differences were drastic. “When I started,” he points out, “there were no stretch fabrics—jeans didn’t stretch.”

To the untrained eye, Kors’s staple designs, like a camel trench coat, a hand-knit black cashmere sweater, or a flattering red dress, may seem simple. But each design, fabric, and color choice is laced with deep sentimentality. “I love anything that has the possibility of interpretation,” Kors says. “When it comes to color, black is limitless for a designer, and as far as bright colors, red is always what I go to. Red is life-affirming.”

When Kors thinks back on where it all began, his mind goes to Studio 54. He skipped his high school prom to go to the famed disco, and says that was the night that he knew he wanted to be a fashion designer. “Seeing people move in their clothes, feel confident, understand their own sensuality—that was something you saw at Studio 54,” he says. “It really represented the best thing about New York: the mix of people. People from every background, every language, all together in this magical space. And the cool thing was that there was no social media and no judgment, so people could truly let go and have a good time.” Kors is acutely aware of a cultural craving for togetherness and community. Through his designs and runway shows, he aims to highlight the beauty, comfort, and even theatricality that come with living life authentically with one another. Studio 54 has since been turned into a theater, and Kors relishes, once again, New York’s ability to reinvent itself. Voilà: magic.

Lead image: A theatrical look from Michael Kors fall/winter 2026.

#6779. Inside Kering’s First Water Resilience Lab in Italy

This story is part of ‘The Business Case for Nature’, a series exploring fashion’s impact on nature and vice versa. Read more here.

In 1966, the banks of the Arno river burst, causing the most destructive flood Florence had ever experienced. It took dozens of lives, displaced thousands of people, and claimed millions of rare books and art works.

The region has seen many more floods since then. In 2023, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni declared a state of emergency for the worst-hit areas amid Storm Ciarán, which caused an estimated €1.89 billion in damages. One of the fashion suppliers hit was Prato-based Beste Group, whose HQ sits directly on the bank of the Bisenzio river. The company purchased a new machine — worth around €7 million — the month prior, which was then destroyed by the floods. It was only insured for 60% of the price, so replacing it cost the company several million euros. On top of that, the waist-high water brought production to a standstill for three weeks.

When Rachel Kolbe Semhoun, head of sustainable sourcing and nature initiatives at Kering, read about these losses in Vogue Business, it started a chain reaction that eventually led her to create the group’s industry-first water strategy. “They had done everything right inside the factory, but they were still flooded,” she says. “It was a great example of how nobody can make resilience happen by themselves. The only thing that would have helped was collectively investing in better nature infrastructure upriver.”

The luxury conglomerate has outlined a plan to become “water positive”, laying the groundwork for other brands to follow. It’s a bold move, but experts say it’s just the beginning.

When Kering set that strategy 18 months ago, its goal was to become “net water-positive” by 2050, with “measured net-positive water impacts” in 10 priority water basins by 2035. It was a bold aim. No other fashion company had developed a dedicated strategy for water resilience, and there was no blueprint for the French luxury group to follow.

On Monday, Kering officially opened its first Water Resilience Lab in the Arno Basin, outlining a roadmap for building water resilience that it says can be replicated in the other nine priority areas, spanning France, Spain, Türkiye, Mongolia, India, Peru, Argentina, South Africa and Australia. Vogue Business got a first look.

“Most of fashion’s strategic raw materials rely on water,” says Kering chief sustainability and institutional affairs officer, Marie-Claire Daveu. This doesn’t just apply to the growing phase for natural fibers like wool, leather and cotton, but also to the production processes that follow, including washing, dyeing and tanning. “To ensure resilience and business continuity for the fashion industry, we have to support the regeneration and replenishment of the key basins where we operate as an industry, which are home to our suppliers. Ultimately, this becomes a significant driver of long-term value creation for businesses, strengthening supply chain resilience, reducing water-related risks, and supporting the health of ecosystems and communities our industry relies on.”

Kering started with the Arno Basin because of the “irreplaceable know-how” specific to the region, as well as the many local, strategic suppliers it relies on for everything from ready-to-wear and leather goods to accessories and jewelry. “The Arno Basin offers a perfect opportunity to create and test this new model,” says Daveu, “because it has the governance and the stakeholders that can carry through the lab’s ambitious approach.”

That ambitious approach involves bringing together public institutions, businesses, academia, the scientific community and financial actors. In the case of the Arno Basin, that includes Kering’s Regenerative Fund for Nature co-founder Conservation International, environmental consultancy Etifor, the University of Florence and multiple layers of local government, as well as the Northern Apennines River Basin Authority and local land reclamation authorities ANBI Toscana and ANCI Toscana. LVMH and Burberry have also joined the efforts. “It’s been very important for the lab to build on the efforts, understanding and achievements by public authorities in the region,” says Daveu. “The lab is amplifying what has previously been done, while filling gaps and creating new models.”

Kering has officially launched its first water resilience lab, in Italy’s Arno Basin.

There are three main pillars to the roadmap: creating robust and innovative governance structures that allow all stakeholder groups to be heard; creating a financial model that incentivizes change without relying too much on philanthropy; and building out a portfolio of nature-based and industrial projects for various stakeholders to implement, each of which has a strong business case.

Future climate and nature risks are central to that. By 2030, Tuscany is expected to see upward of 50 days of heat stress each year, leaving local communities vulnerable to water scarcity and other water-related risks. But, according to Kering, if 48 million cubic meters of water can be retained in the Arno Basin, the impact of future flooding events will be drastically reduced, with each cubic metre of water retained avoiding approximately €157 in flood damage.

The lab has identified six key intervention points in the local area, where it says investments can generate the greatest impact: Villa Petriolo, Ombrone/Bisenzio, Altopascio/Lake Sibolla, Pisa/Era Basin, Usciana/Pescia River, and Arezzo/Chiana Valley. In each location, “multi-sectorial and private-public consensus has been a real game-changer”, says Daveu.

The roadmap was based on leading methodologies, including volumetric water benefit accounting (VWBA), which allows companies to quantify water stewardship impacts in consistent, comparable units, and the Science-based Targets for Nature (SBTN) of which Kering was an early adopter. These approaches were supplemented by a basin-specific methodology built by the University of Florence, which provides the scientific basis for quantifying risks and outcomes.

It’s a robust start, but some fine-tuning is needed to turn this into a reliable and replicable model other brands can lean on, says Daveu. “A key limitation is the lack of recognition of the role nature-based solutions play in mitigating risk and building long-lasting resilience,” she explains. “This limitation is part of the work the lab will address; innovating the governance and the financial model to go beyond philanthropy to make nature-based resilience a viable investment.”

Moving forward, proving the return on investment for water resilience initiatives like this will be critical to long-term success, she adds. Until now, investments in water resilience have largely been funded by philanthropic foundations, and projects have developed in siloes, minimizing the potential for impact. “Philanthropy will never be enough to support the needed investments for real resilience,” says Daveu. “Efforts need to be coordinated to address water risks in a holistic way [...] and become truly resilient. Amplifying impacts and investments is necessary to have a viable financing model for nature to bring investors to the table.”
