#6754. What Is Swedish Mys? And Where to Experience It

The brutal cold of Sweden’s winters is well documented, but Stockholm has a knack for bringing some special magic even to its gloomiest season. The city, located just 500 miles south of the Arctic Circle, enjoys as little as six hours of daylight during the bleakest months, with the peak of darkness occurring at the winter solstice on December 21—and it’s no coincidence that this is when Stockholm fills with fairy-lit streets and cozy dining rooms illuminated with candles and roaring fireplaces. Add a whole host of invigorating winter activities, from ice-skating on frozen lakes to plunging through holes drilled in the frozen Baltic Sea, and you’ll see why many Swedes claim this as their favorite time of year.

“Winter is a time to hunker down, cook and play vinyl records; to wear something cozy and breathe the crisp outdoor air; to heat up the sauna, cut a hole in the ice, and—well, don't even get me started on how much I love cold-water plunges!” exclaims Hanna Oscarsson, the creative director at Stockholm’s most celebrated cocktail bar, Röda Huset.

“Cooling off on a hot summer day is wonderful too, of course,” she continues. “But winter dips are like a deep breath to reset the constant, hectic pace of modern life.”

Nowhere does cozy like Sweden—so much so that they even have a special word for it. Mys is Swedish for that feeling you get when you curl up under a soft blanket on a deep-cushioned sofa next to a fireplace, your hands wrapped around a giant cup of hot chocolate, or when you wrap up in your thickest knits and mittens and head out for a bracing walk along winter-lit streets, a soft dusting of snow creaking under your boots. It’s not entirely unrelated to what the Danes call hygge—but where hygge has hardened into an international lifestyle aesthetic, mys remains purely a state of mind.

I grew up in Sweden and toughed it out for 20-or-so years until the darkness got the better of me, prompting me to move to Barcelona and never look back. So imagine my surprise earlier this year, when my feed suddenly filled with Swedish “coolcations”, as the whole of southern Europe fled north to escape the stifling heat. “That’s cool,” I thought to myself, but you don’t really know Sweden until you’ve tasted the cold. So grab your furriest coat and woolliest hat, because when it comes to winter wonderlands, nowhere does it quite like Stockholm.

Imagine jetting off to Stockholm to visit your art collector pals in their private waterfront residence. If an invite from said friends doesn’t come through, a stay at Lydmar Hotel is the next best thing. Part hotel, part gallery, the 46-room property is home to one of the largest, privately owned fine-art photographic collections in the Swedish capital. Each of the plushly upholstered rooms—some of which enjoy unobstructed views of the Stockholm waterfront all the way to the Royal Palace—has its own vibe, brought to life through a curated blend of photography, artworks and bespoke furniture. Expect plenty of mys-filled nooks designed for curling up with a book while gazing at your favorite artwork.

When a hotel set in a former bank names its main dining room Bonnie’s (a tribute to legendary outlaw Bonnie Parker), you know you’re in for a good time. Guests at Bank can warm their cockles at nearby Sturebadet, a beautiful Moorish-inspired Art Nouveau bathhouse and sauna complex (access is included for suite guests while others enjoy preferential rates), before whiling away their evenings in the hotel’s Papillon cocktail lounge, a sultry, wood-paneled affair serving warming Old Fashioneds and Negronis. Spacious rooms come with soft slippers for keeping cozy on icy nights.

Set on the easternmost tip of the well-to-do island of Lidingö (one of the 14 islands that make up the city of Stockholm), Ellery Beach House is a former IBM conference center-turned-Palm-Springs-inspired seaside fun palace. If toasty saunas and invigorating sea dunks are your poison, you’ll be in your element in the hotel’s four heated pools and two saunas, one of which is set right on the edge of the Baltic Sea—ideal for defrosting after a glacial plunge. There are countless other activities on offer, from padel to cornhole or boules, to sipping cocktails under a blanket in the firepit-heated relaxation room.

Swedish chef Niklas Ekstedt uses only natural heat, soot, ash, smoke, and fire to prepare the tasting menu at his eponymous Michelin-starred restaurant. This is a meal that will stay with you long after you’ve trudged home through the snowy streets, frost-nipped gloved fingertips in pockets and earlobes tucked under woolly hats. You’ll sample the first courses, such as the Swedish caviar, or vendace roe, topped with crown dill, and be served a cast-iron flatbread in the snug, flame-heated kitchen, before being led to a table for the mains, which include a sublime confit North Sea langoustine, like a smaller, firmer lobster, infused with rose and lingonberries.

Nowhere does mys like this comfy café set in a castle-like structure built for the 1897 Stockholm World’s Fair. It makes a perfect stop for oversized cups of tea and fresh-baked cinnamon rolls in front of the crackling fireplace after a bracing walk along the Djurgården shoreline, past the Kärleksudden (Lovers’ Point) observation deck with its breathtaking views.

Where better to sample a Swedish classic than this low-lit space tucked alongside the Stockholm Opera House? Bakfickan (the back pocket) is an intimate, 28-seater restaurant that serves Swedish comfort food, or husmanskost, including their best-selling meatballs with all the customary accoutrements: creamy gravy, potato purée, lingonberries, and pickled cucumber.

The name Röda Huset (red house) conjures images of a red-painted cottage deep in the Swedish countryside, but this particular house is as urban as it gets, with its bright crimson façade overlooking Sergels Torg, Stockholm’s most central square. The moodily lit top floor is home to an award-winning cocktail lounge, where drinks are laced with hyperlocal Scandinavian produce. Think a Manhattan infused with heather honey from the Baltic island of Gotland or a tart, green tomato-flavored Dry Martini.

Stockholm’s southside, or Södermalm (Söder for short), was once an impoverished district where affordable homes were built for factory workers. These days, it’s best known for its laid-back, unbothered vibe, lively bars, and hip stores. It’s where Swedish actor Alexander Skarsgård grew up and where you’ll often spot him casually hanging out with friends when he’s in town. Start at Nytorget and wander through the trendy SoFo district, where you can marvel at the Christmas lights and the elegant Nordic Classicism buildings. Once you reach Mariatorget, climb the hill to Monteliusgatan Street where you’ll be treated to one of the most magnificent aerial views across the frozen waters of Riddarfjärden to the snow-dusted rooftops of Stockholm City Hall.

Staying in Söder, the area around Nytorget is full of chic boutiques like the 6/5/4 clothing and concept store and menswear brand A Day’s March (to help you perfect that effortlessly cool Skarsgård look). Don’t miss interior design mecca Tambur, where you can invest in some mys of your own, like cozy wool throws and charcoal-scented candles. Meanwhile, Hornsgatan is home to the Slow Fashion District, a collection of some 20 stores selling vintage, second-hand, upcycled and sustainable fashions, as well as skincare and homewares.

Swedes love to tell you “there’s no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing”—and winter is the time to prove them right as you bundle up and get your outdoor mys on. It takes a cold winter for Stockholm’s waterways to freeze over, but when they do, they fill with ice skaters from families teaching their little ones to stay upright to hardcore long-distance skaters. If open water ice-skating is too adventurous, there’s also a public rink in central Stockholm at Kungsträdgården. Meanwhile, winter kayaking is an exhilarating option for milder winters.

Saunas are as beloved here as they are in Finland, but scoring a membership at one of Stockholm’s private sauna clubs is like getting an audience with His Majesty King Carl XVI Gustaf. This year saw the launch of Stockholm’s first-ever public sauna, Bastun Tanto: a photogenic, verdigris-green floating pontoon set on the fashionable Hornstull waterfront that offers icy plunges and steamy warm-ups all winter long (with slots bookable 30 days in advance).

#6753. Everything Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams Have Said About Their Friendship

HBO Max and Crave’s Heated Rivalry has quickly become one of the most-discussed series of the year, catapulting its stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams into the celebrity stratosphere. The two actors portray hockey players Shane Hollander (Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Storrie), who have a secret love affair spanning almost a decade. The series is known for its spicy intimate scenes as well as its beautiful depiction of romantic yearning.

Storrie and Williams have been open in interviews about their experience creating the show, along with their offscreen relationship as they navigate sudden fame together.

“Hudson is my best friend, and I literally can’t fathom doing this without him,” Storrie told W magazine in December 2025. “We were both in similar places in life before this. We quit our jobs within a day of each other. We booked this and flew out the same day. Now it’s turning into two people who are being seen internationally for the first time. This has been the highlight of my life, and meeting Hudson makes that 10 times sweeter.”

Here, everything the two actors have shared about their friendship.

Fans of the show tend to “ship” Williams and Storrie, hoping they end up dating in real life. Storrie addressed this head-on in an interview with Vulture, saying things are strictly platonic.

When asked about the intimate scenes they shot in the show, Storrie said, “For me, it doesn’t feel spicy at all—like, that’s me and my best friend. This is the first time in my life I’m having this many eyes on me. They’ve seen me naked, they’ve seen me kiss, they’ve seen me be in love with a man on-screen—it’s only normal for people to try to transfer that over to mine and Hudson’s real life.” He explained that he intends to keep his private life private, adding, “I feel honored to be able to bring someone to life that so many people feel seen, understood, and represented by, and I think that transcends whoever I’m sleeping with in my real life.”

Williams expressed a similar sentiment to Deadline, saying, “I want queer people telling queer stories, but also, there’s the element of Connor and I—we’re best friends, and we love expressing that physically. You see people who infer or assume, and you kind of have to let that go. But then again, I never wanna stop expressing the love I have for Connor physically, and I’m never really going to, and I think multiple things can be true at once.”

In November 2026, Williams’s interview on The Assembly aired. One of the audience members there asked Williams if he ever had romantic feelings for Storrie. “No,” he replied. “Quickly, me and Connor realized we were, like, platonic soulmates, just completely in love with each other. I think that’s what made our friendship so stable and beautiful, is that we realized we could be completely ourselves, be completely guard down. So, I think the thing that made our relationship as rich as it was is, like, me and that man could cuddle for 10 hours, and it just mean cuddling, just mean we just love each other dearly, but don’t wanna beep each other’s bop.”

He then added playfully, “Who doesn’t want Connor Storrie in their shower? You know, someone needs to get my back. I wish Connor was just with me every day. I’m like, ‘Hey, I have a loofah but I can’t reach [my back].’ If I had Connor with me every day, he could just come in there.”

Sophie Nélisse, who plays Heated Rivalry’s Rose Landry, interviewed Williams for Wonderland magazine in January 2026 and asked him how he and Storrie balance promoting the show with forging their own identities. Williams admitted that they purposely go to different events, in part to keep their friendship more private and their brands separate.

“It’s been really nice, because Connor and I are aligned,” Williams began. “We want to be different artists. We don’t want to be the Olsen twins. We want to be Connor and Hudson, with different filmographies and different deals. As much as we love each other, our friendship doesn’t need to be public. Jacob [Tierney] has that quote: ‘Shane and Ilya are for the public. Connor and Hudson are for themselves.’ And that’s how we feel. People want to see us front row together all the time, but we actively avoid that, because it starts to feel like branding. If you’re always seen together, you become attached at the hip. I FaceTime him whenever I’m free. But if we’re offered the same fashion shows, we’re like, ‘Which one are you going to? Okay, I’ll go to a different one.’ We’re stubborn, selfish artists who want to be our own people. We’re like, ‘I love you. I don’t want to do everything with you.’”

Both Williams and Storrie got into great shape for the show. In a profile with GQ in December 2025, Williams talked about meeting his co-star and being intimidated by his build.

“Connor pushed himself up onto the island in the kitchen,” Williams said. “I remember seeing his arms. They were the size of my legs. I was like, Holy fuck.”

“It’s not true,” Storrie responded. “Because you have crazy legs.”

The show’s creator, Jacob Tierney, also commented on their affection for one another in the piece, saying, “They’re living through a thing right now that is bananas—absolutely fucking bananas—and they’re handling it with grace, with humor, with generosity. They adore each other, which is like, thank fucking God.”

While discussing his own workout routine with Men’s Health in January, Williams had a playful quip about Storrie’s physique: “I’m okay talking about my butt, but poor Connor Storrie—who has the fattest butt I’ve ever seen on a man—I’m sure just wants to stop talking about his beautiful cheeks.”

In a December interview with Entertainment Weekly, the friends discussed a viral video from the Heated Rivalry wrap party where they are rolling around on the floor together.

“Very plainly spoken, me and Hudson are freaks,” Storrie explained. “We’re clowns. We just love to riff and have fun and go crazy, and those were two situations where we were caught off guard doing our thing. The wrap party, that was all improvised. I think we were just putting on a show.”

Williams added, “Also, there might be something else, I think, with—we’re both very physical actors, and movement is a huge part of it.”

During his Vulture interview, Storrie spoke about moving into an apartment next to Williams’s while filming in Toronto.

“We would literally just go to set, go home, cook, work out together, and geek out over how excited we were to finally be working on this level,” he said. “If we were any less close, we probably would’ve gotten annoyed with each other really quick.”

The American actor told Vulture that they leaned into their chemistry while promoting Heated Rivalry’s first season. “If Hudson says something jokingly, like, ‘Spit in my mouth,’ I think that gives everyone else the go-ahead to get in on that too,” he said. “People are ruthless talking about our holes and our butts.”

During his discussion with Interview, Storrie added that spending time with Williams has helped ground them both during their press tour. “Hudson’s been in town, so we’ll have some quality time and come back down to ground zero,” he said. “It’s funny, because all the press and stuff is getting easier and easier and easier. You would think you would get burnt out and exhausted. Even though it’s only been three weeks of doing press for this, I’m clicking into an interesting sort of confidence and appreciation for all of this.”

Williams, meanwhile, credited Storrie for helping him keep the press tour fun during an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. “I have one of my best friends for life right beside me through it all, which is already a luxury that a lot of actors don’t get,” he said. “I’m sure I would’ve probably had a smaller appetite for the amount of stuff we’re doing if I didn’t have him through this. I’m an omnivert, leaning more to an extrovert, but I still get—I have ADHD, I’m unmedicated, currently, for the last while, so my social battery can just tap [out] pretty quick. At the end of the day, I’m pretty forgiving with myself if I’m talking with a reporter in a polite, more boring way. Then when I’ve had coffee, and I’ve had a nap, I let myself be chaotic. I let myself off the leash. I try to say, whatever mood I’m in, just be Canadian, don’t be mean. Whatever they get, they get.”

Timid magazine asked Williams how Storrie’s acting has helped him be a better performer. Williams responded, “He’s so incredibly present and so incredibly truthful. As an actor, it’s so much easier to think of what you should be doing or what you think would be an entertaining version of this or the most dramatic version or make sure you're hitting these lines properly or doing the scene properly or the director wants this and the script says this. But just to actually listen to the person and let what they’re saying affect you—Connor is so good at that. There’s so many moments where I am saying something and the script says he does this, and he does something so unexpectedly emotional or so unexpectedly vulnerable that even if I'm very robotic and going through a scene, he can crack me and change my trajectory in the scene. He’s a huge resource in affecting me and that makes my job way easier because I don’t have to. He makes me be present. He’s so good at that. That’s his superpower.”

Storrie, meanwhile, credited Williams for helping him understand Ilya so quickly in his Interview story. “I feel like I got the character pretty instantly,” he began. “I believed in his circumstances without almost any effort, and I just trusted Hudson so much. It’s so easy to act when you know where you’re coming from and you believe the person opposite you. I mean, I’m so gooey. I’m such a romantic. So any of the really heightened emotional moments—their love or confession or an outbreak or a fight—those are the moments that I really enjoy as an actor.”

Williams listed out all the nicknames he and Storrie have for each other during his Timid magazine interview. “He calls me Huddy, Papi, Bubba, Baby,” he said. “I call him Pookie. I used to call him Pookie a lot. Papi. Oh, Con Con. I call him that both in text form and verbally. But yeah, a lot of nicknames.”

GQ revealed that when the series wrapped, they got matching tattoos that read “SEX SELLS.”

The Canadian star revealed that he stayed at Storrie’s Los Angeles apartment when he came to the U.S. to do some press. “We were like, ‘Oh, my God, if people saw us just getting ready in the morning, giving each other big spooning hugs, just to say we’re proud of each other,’ people would be going crazy,” he told Variety. “If only one fan had access, God forbid. But yeah, we just love each other very dearly.”

The outlet asked him what creating Heated Rivalry taught him. Williams responded, “I think I had my own biases, maybe that would be too strong of a word, but my own discomfort if I expressed myself fully, physically and affectionately, both with women and men. It would feel inappropriate. I realized if you really do love someone—platonically or not—I’m such a tactile, sensory person. There are so many taboos. It’s much harder on men. I had to let that go, and I got to learn how freeing that is. That also went hand-in-hand with being myself, truly as an artist. Connor was also a great person to have at my side. I think we both opened each other up to just be freer, more fully expressive.”

During Williams’s January 2026 appearance on Andy Cohen Live, he revealed that Storrie is an “awful texter,” but they largely keep in touch with frequent video calls. “We'll Facetime each other or call each other randomly, very consistently,” he told the host. “That has sort of been my stability, especially through this. Just having my best friend who is in the same position I am.”

In a November 2025 interview with The Permanent Rain Press, Williams said he would pitch Storrie as “a beautiful little, sensitive little radical, artist boy. Who should be treated with the utmost care and hugs and friendliness because he can’t handle anything else. And that’s perfect. And that’s the way he should be treated.”

He added, “And anyone who doesn’t treat him that way should die.”

In May 2026, Williams and Storrie made their Met Gala debut. They took a bathroom selfie together, which Williams later posted to his Threads account.

The pair’s appearance at the Met Gala excited fans, with one user taking a solo shot of Williams and posting it alongside lyrics from Rihanna’s breakup song, “Woo.” (Williams has a longtime girlfriend, Katelyn Larson.) The post has since been taken down, but Williams responded and wrote, “Rpfing [real person fan fiction] gotta stop y’all.”

#6752. Inside the Underground Harry Styles Hospitality Network

It remains one of Gillian Harmon’s great pop culture regrets that she never got to see One Direction live. The 26-year-old is from Irvington, a small town in Mobile, Alabama, where major artists rarely make so much as a pit stop. “I think the closest they came was either Atlanta or New Orleans,” she says, though at the time Harmon was too young to make the trip across state lines on her own.

A year ago, she moved to New York City, which is more frequently graced with the presence of pop stars. Especially these days, as Harry Styles performs a 30-night residency at Madison Square Garden, with fans coming from all corners of the world to attend. But Harmon, who lives on the Upper West Side, had something many of them don't: an apartment with a spare bedroom. So, in the spirit of fandom and hospitality, she figured she could give someone else the experience she wished she had and started inviting out-of-state Styles fans to crash—for free.

Harmon isn't the only one. Around the city, a small hospitality network has emerged among Styles devotees, with fans opening their apartments to strangers traveling to New York to see the residency. They offer up their couches, guest rooms, and even subway directions, acting as something closer to a tour guide than a host. For fans coming from places where seeing Styles requires a flight, hotel, and a considerable financial commitment, their generosity can make a huge difference. To these fans, seeing Harry Styles in concert is not a luxury. It's an inalienable right.

When tickets for the MSG residency went live this past January, not all New York-based Harry fans were feeling so magnanimous. Some fans who couldn’t get tickets complained of tourists swooping in and snatching them up. Harmon, however, saw an opportunity. If fans were coming all the way to New York City to see Styles command the stage in a rotation of business casual get-ups while singing the hits from his four solo albums, she could help ease the financial burden. When she posted a TikTok offering her spare bedroom to roving fans, the response was immediate. More than halfway through the residency, she has already hosted four people, with more scheduled to arrive for Styles’ final run of shows. Her roommates, who aren’t particularly devoted Harries themselves, were game. After all, they are used to Harmon's adventures in popstar-chasing, and they liked the idea of meeting new people.

Harmon gave priority to people who told her it was their first chance to see Styles, particularly those coming from places where the cost of both travel and accommodations would have been difficult to absorb. When too many fans wanted room and board for the same dates, she would simply spin a wheel.

The arrangement has made Harmon’s five-bedroom apartment a kind of accidental commune. She has personally shepherded some of her guests to the Garden by subway, shown first-time visitors how to navigate the city, and met up with them post-concert to debrief. They’ve gone to pop-ups, ridden boats in Central Park, and explored Roosevelt Island. “It was really wholesome,” Harmon says.

She has experienced the financial and logistical hell of trying to attend a Harry Styles concert firsthand. Harmon has traveled to Nashville for Styles shows herself, sometimes with friends from college, and has been scammed trying to get tickets. She remembers the humbling experience, later, of unknowingly buying bad seats. But she was grateful just to be in the building. The MSG residency marked her fifth time seeing him live. And she recently watched her best friend, who flew from Alabama for his first-ever Styles concert, have the time of his life in the pit.

It’s fitting that friendship has become part of the Harry Styles fan experience. During the 32-year-old’s Wembley show in June, he announced that “being somebody’s friend is the most incredible, beautiful thing you could possibly be to someone.” Throughout his solo career, Styles has returned to the intimacy of friendship as both a thematic linchpin and guiding philosophy: the people you find, the people who stay, the people who make an otherwise lonely life a little less so. Fans have especially latched onto the motto "Treat People with Kindness,” from the Fine Line track of the same title. “They’re happy,” Harmon says. “They’re positive, uplifting, encouraging.”

Across town, 32-year-old Carolina Sanchez saw Harmon’s video and got inspired. Originally from Mexico, Sanchez has been a Styles fan since he was first discovered on X Factor in 2010 and later moved to New York. When she saw a slew of comments from eager fans needing a place to stay under Harmon’s videos, she offered up her own two-bedroom in Staten Island.. Soon, messages came pouring in.

“I just want to be part of something special,” Sanchez told me. Her first guests arrived in early October. At first, Sanchez admits, the idea of allowing strangers into her home made her nervous. But she started vetting prospective guests on Instagram and getting a sense of their connection to Styles and his music. Eventually, she created a Google form asking for basic information and identification to make sure the person she had been speaking with was the person who arrived her the door.

Her husband was initially surprised by the arrangement but understood the compulsion. He had seen firsthand how expensive Sanchez’s own ticket to the concert was. If hosting another fan meant someone could put that money towards a ticket of their own, Sanchez wanted to help. Now, her husband is cleaning their guest room and putting together goodie bags for the people staying there.

Sanchez hopes the connections will last beyond the residency. She imagines visiting some of the women she meets on future trips, including one who is coming from Florida. The idea, she says, is to make friends and treat other people well. In the process, she is also making New York feel a little less like a city of strangers. “When I've told people what I was doing, they're like, Are you insane? Are you crazy?," recounts Zaia Rodriguez, one of Sanchez’s lucky guests. “I think part of it is stan culture; we make these connections on the internet with absolute strangers, and we talk to these people so often, we bond over the things that we love, and we become friends.”

For other fans, the journey is a little more complicated. Maria Miglio, a 29-year-old surgery resident from just outside Detroit, flew to NYC with a coworker and stayed a 15-minute walk from MSG. The hotel was $500-a-night, and tickets to the concert set her back another $200. Residents in Miglio’s program get only four days off each month. She flew out Friday after work and was back in Detroit by Sunday.

“Concerts are just such a community-based thing, especially for me,” says Erowyn Walsten, a 20-year-old student at the Fashion Institute of Technology. For her, the neighborly instincts demonstrated by Styles devotees are innate to One Direction fandom. She attended her first 1D show when she was nine, and even had a Harry Styles doll; he was always her favorite. She saw him again at 16, and is now preparing to go to MSG alone, where she expects to make friends, like she has at other concerts.

“I really think that honestly, as long as I've even been a Directioner, it truly felt like a family,” she says. The fandom’s largely female community, she believes, has made it easier to form lasting connections with people who are, ultimately, total strangers. Some of her closest friendships have grown out of mutual acquaintances met through Styles. “I think it's one of the most beautiful things,” she says.

The residency has also given the Garden a particular significance, the same way it’s Mecca for fans of the New York Knicks. Styles has called the venue “Harry’s House,” a phrase that has stuck with devotees. Cara McDonald is planning to fly from Ireland for the historic residency, the longest single-engagement run in the venue’s history, even with the steep price of hotels and flights. But she’s been saving up. Like Walsten, Mcdonald’s first concert was One Direction, giving the trip a certain emotional resonance. Even the cost of attending has become part of the story: McDonald’s resale pit ticket for the residency cost more than the ticket she bought for his previous tour in Los Angeles. But that's her primary indulgence, she says. “Concerts and rent, that’s it.”

There’s also a sense that this moment might be more fleeting than it seems. In a September 9th email to fans, Styles wrote that he “doesn't know what comes next,” a line that sent fans online into a frenzy of speculation. For those old enough to remember the collective emotional whiplash of One Direction’s indefinite hiatus announcement, there’s a particular appeal in making the trip now, while there's still a chance.

#6747. The Best Men's Crewneck Sweatshirt in 2026, According to GQ

There’s no such thing as ‘the best men’s crewneck sweatshirt,’ at least not in the objective sense. As tactile and quantifiable garments can be, the truth is it’s all open to interpretation, and comes down to personal taste (even if your personal taste sucks). That said… I do have some strong opinions on what makes a good sweatshirt and have tested too many to name. I grew up wearing cheap, serviceable sweats from places like Walmart. I’ve also invested in unreasonably heavy 24-ounce sweatshirts and became obsessed with the unyielding craftsmanship of Japanese reproductions that required rare loopwheel machines.

Through decades of experience, I’ve honed in on what makes a sweatshirt special. A good crewneck sweatshirt should be comfortable, and that all comes down to fabric and fit. The fabric, usually made of either a French terry or a brushed fleece, should be both dense and soft. The silhouette shouldn’t squeeze, but should be relaxed enough to layer over a T-shirt or even a button-up. I’ve also dialed-in on the things you should avoid, like when sweatshirts are too tight in the neck, especially as a guy with a thicker gullet for my frame. And I really hate when sweatshirts are too long. As a long-torso individual, you’d think this wouldn’t be a problem, but it’s something that feels endemic to the genre.

Now that I’ve given you a brief tour of the weeds, let’s get into what you came here for. Through rigorous research and far too much time on our hands, here’s what’s what in the world of crewneck sweatshirts.

Reigning Champ has been in the sweats game for generations, producing some of the absolute finest hoodies, sweatpants, and crewnecks around. When I was first introduced to the brand an unspeakable number of years ago, it left an impression on me. The idea that something so basic could be so good revealed to me that my base line for quality was much lower than I’d realized.

Though we here at GQ have adored their slim-fit crewnecks for years, Reigning Champ's more classic-fitting sweatshirt is one that will stay steady through the fickle fashion trend cycle. It's made with custom-knit midweight French Terry fabric, cut with a relaxed but clean fit, and sewn with super smooth flatlock seams to cut down on bulk. While most sweatshirts will opt for either raglan sleeves or set-in sleeves, Reigning Champ’s crewneck stands out for its unique construction that uses both techniques. The result is a more tailored set-in sleeve look at the front with raglan details at the back to give the wearer a freer range of motion.

The brand’s name alone sets high expectations, and in every aspect, Reigning Champ’s crewneck sweatshirt meets and exceeds them. While $125 isn’t by any means cheap, the stunning quality from the fabric to the fit and finish all equate to a sweatshirt that punches well above its weight class. If I really had to nit-pick, though, I'd like to see the color palette expand a little more, especially for such an essential piece of kit.

If your sweatshirt budget is decidedly smaller, your first stop should be Russell Athletic, the Alabama sportswear stalwarts who literally invented the crewneck sweatshirt way back in 1926. Almost a century later, they're still turning out the best bang-for-your-buck fleece crew on the market. It's got all the classic details that made Russell a household name: ribbing at the cuffs and hem, a V-insert collar, and a classic cut (size down if relaxed ain't exactly your thing).

The midweight 9 oz. fleece is pleasantly soft and warm, and it's moisture-wicking and breathable so if you run a little hot, it won't emphasize the sweat in ‘sweatshirt’. The thing I like most about Russell’s crewnecks is that they still fit like the vintage joints—but you don’t have to work yourself to death bobbing between vintage stores trying to hunt one down.

No list of the best crewneck sweatshirts would be complete without Champion's reverse weave joint in the mix. Todd Snyder’s legendary collab (see below) has got style and function down pat for the new-school, but the OG heavyweight pullover deserves a crown of its own. The sturdy cotton-poly blend is soft but will hold its shape after countless wash cycles (loungewear and pizza go hand in hand—residual stains do not). Fabric aside, the fit is just right: not too slim, not too baggy, and with slightly dropped shoulders to make your neckline really pop. We pick quality over quantity any day, but with this classic sweatshirt you get the go-to year-round layering piece for the fewest amount of dollar bills.

If you’re expecting a soft, motherly embrace, I hate to tell you this, but Champion’s iconic Reverse Weave sweats aren’t the softest. In fact, they’ve got a pretty rough hand. But don’t worry about that too much because that’s just straight out of the box. What you get in return is an unquestionably beastly durability. And the longevity you get out of them means they’ll only get softer and luscious with age.

You can’t ignore the impact that vintage clothing has on the modern fashion landscape, not just for the endless references and inspiration it gives designers, but also for the sheer explosion of secondhand style. Vintage-obsessed dudes like myself will search high and low for forgotten garments with esoteric details, from jeans left in abandoned barns to rare leather jackets tucked away in grandpa’s attic. And if you’re thrifting skills aren’t up to snuff or if coughing up the dough to a dealer is too big of a hit, the best thing to do is to look to Japan where they’re even more obsessed with reviving the grails of bygone eras.

While many repro brands deserve their flowers, I’m particularly keen on Buzz Rickson’s' interpretation of the perfect vintage sweatshirt. The fabric is made using ultra rare loopwheel knitting machines that knit the terry material methodically and slowly, using the natural tension of gravity to achieve a product that’s shockingly soft for its density. It also results in a fabric that’s totally seamless around the torso, an old-school detail that’s hard to come by but oh-so-satisfying once you do. The crewneck sweatshirt also features low-profile flatlock seams, tall ribbing at the cuffs and hems, and the throwback V-neck insert for easy donning.

HAVEN's Excel crewneck employs the label's telltale details like custom ribbing and underarm gussets for increased range of motion. But the star of the show has to be the fabric which comes from rare 1980s Azume knitting machines, lauded for producing low-tension French terry with unrivaled softness and character.

Lady White Co.'s methodical approach to jersey knits has brought them to the top of the heap not just for tees and sweatshirts, but for the entire wardrobe. It's mini crewneck uses custom-milled terry fabric that's cut to a flattering cropped silhouette and garment-dyed for depth.

Look, I'm just as surprised as you are that Gap's heavyweight sweatshirt is not only $70, but actually that good. It's legit heavy and will handily knock out other sweats in beefier weight classes, especially since you can often find it on a mega discount.

The kings and queens of American-made cotton fleece at Camber make their crewneck from a beefy 12-ounce cotton fleece with just enough elastic in the body panels to make it feel like a big hug. Plus you can get it in 11 colors.

Dyed one at a time by hand, each sweatshirt from the New York-based indie label Buckets is completely unique and certainly distinct from the droves of potassium-dyed, sun-faded, vintage-inspired sweats that have flooded the market in recent years.

NYC-based 3sixteen has built out a line of carefully dialed-in menswear, like this hardy crewneck made with a fleece that's, quote, "some of the heaviest available on the market." And yet it's the pockets, surreptitiously slipped into the side seams, that have us nodding in appreciation.

Known for its chef-approved T-shirts, Whitseville's reproduction sweats deserve equal praise for its heavy all-cotton fleece, tubular construction, and double-V gussets that reference rare vintage crewnecks.

Quince's 70-30 cotton-poly blend recalls vintage sweats of yesteryear, the kind that were as soft as they were durable and didn't break the bank. Its Everyday fleece crew ticks all the boxes.

There are levels to sweatshirts, as humble as they are. What we look for in high-quality sweatshirts comes down to fabric, construction, and fit. Sweatshirt fabrics should be soft, certainly, but many high-quality options are quite burly and stiffer than you'd think. Most of the time, that means the more material goes into the sweatshirt the longer it'll last. And if you're willing to commit to them, they'll get softer and more comfortable the more you wear and launder them.

Most garments are made by overlapping fabrics and sewing them together. That may be fine for a dress shirt, but sweatshirts are made of a thicker, knit fabric which can bulky and irritating when it's sewn like this. We like sweatshirts that are made with flatlock seams which are made by butting two fabrics next to each other rather than overlapping; the result is a smoother, flatter seam. On rarer occasions, some sweatshirts are made the old-school way on either tubular knitting machines or very rare loopwheel knitting machines which produces a sweatshirt without any side seams on the body. Garment nerds go gaga over this kind of detail, but it's by no means a requirement for a good sweatshirt.

Sweatshirt fabrics are typically made from terry cloth, French terry, or brushed terry. (If that sounds familiar, it's because terry cloth is the same stuff that's used to make bath towels.) Terry cloth features loops of yarns which are absorbent and insulating. But the main difference between your bath towel and your sweatshirt is that sweatshirts only have the loops on the inside of the garment. Often, those loops are either brushed or shorn to give the material a luxuriously fluffy hand.

Fit is always subjective, but classic-fitting sweatshirts will fit somewhat relaxed all-around and fall at the hips. Slimmer sweatshirts will fit better if you want to layer them under a jacket and look cleaner with slim-fitting pants. For a fit that's more of-the-moment, opt for a sweatshirt that's boxier and cropped to go with some high-waisted, baggy trousers.

The humble crewneck helped Steve McQueen evade capture in The Great Escape, cemented John Travolta’s heartthrob status in Grease, and made Eddie Murphy a badass in Beverly Hills Cop. Paul Newman, the patron saint of laid-back menswear, wore one religiously. And today, a roster of famous—and famously stylish—dudes still put their trust in it. The only difference now is that it comes in a rainbow of different colors and silhouettes, not to mention fabrics far beyond the staid French terry.

Like many menswear staples, crewneck sweatshirts were born from athletics and have transcended into everyday leisure. You could style a crewneck with baggy jeans and sick sneakers for a streetwear-leaning aesthetic, dive headfirst into a preppy look with a pair of chinos and loafers, or turn up the lounge-factor and double it up with some sweatpants and classic sneakers.

Like The Bachelor, we had a flock of hopefuls vying for our love. But instead of hot singles, we had to dole out roses to a gaggle of cozy sweatshirts. One by one, we got to know each sweatshirt, taking them out on dates (literally), and looking intently for rock-solid characteristics, flaws, and dealbreakers. We wore every sweatshirt like any other piece of clothing in our closets, styled them with our favorite pants, scrutinized their fits, put them through harsh laundry cycles, and repeated the whole process over again. What we ended up with is this A-team of great crewnecks, from budget options to luxurious upgrades, and everything between.

#6743. The Best Men's Jean Jacket 2026: 12 Fall Layering Essentials

Adding the best men's jean jacket to your closet is like drafting Lebron to your rec league team: you’ll end up with a ‘ship no matter how bad the rest of the squad is. Whatever you want to call ’em—jean jackets, denim jackets, trucker jackets—the all-American stalwarts are the layering MVPs of every outfit on the brink of an L. Makes sense considering blue jeans, the jacket’s southern equivalent, can do the exact same thing for your wardrobe. Workwear roots bestow the humble piece of outerwear with utilitarian features, durability, and classic proportions—a surefire formula that churns out menswear icons like double-knee pants and chore coats.

What started out as a work jacket to accompany the blue jeans made from the same burly denim material, jean jackets have grown out of their pragmatic uniform and are more of a fashion statement these days. Be it a luxurious runway riff, an upgraded take, or a down-home workhorse, every flavor of denim jacket has the potential to make every outfit pop. Of course, the trucker jacket is what comes to mind first. But denim jackets come in many forms and aren’t limited to the Levi’s version you likely have in your mind’s eye. Denim’s enduring appeal and boundless applications have seen it merge with chore coats, trenches, Harringtons and more, expanding the scope of jean jackets. That’s great news for anyone looking to find one that truly speaks to themselves, but terrible news for anyone attempting to wade through all the options.

So we did the denim digging for you. We went out and scraped the market for the absolute best men’s jean jacket, from the tried-and-true to the new-age startups and everything in-between.

This shouldn’t be a surprise to anyone. And if it is, as this company’s self-proclaimed Denim Guy, it’s definitely my fault for not teaching you. Levi's is the grand daddy of all jeans which puts them on a rarified level few others could ever hope to approach. The brand’s iconic 501 jean gets most of the (deserved) praise, but the Levi's trucker jacket also warrants recognition.

The very first iteration of the Levi's trucker jacket debuted in 1905 and has since gotten several updates, but the one most ubiquitous today is known as the Type III. It's the picture you have in your head when you think of a trucker jacket and it's great for so many reasons. The midweight denim is ideal for year-round wear, the trim and cropped silhouette has transcended trends for decades and, like the five-pocket blue jean, pairs with just about everything (and looks better the more you wear it). If you only have a hundred bucks to spare and enough room for just one denim jacket in your rotation, it had better be this one.

A chore coat isn’t what most people think of as a ‘jean jacket’. But I’m proposing this as a more practical, no-less stylish alternative to the usual trucker jackets you’re used to seeing. And if you’re taking the term ‘denim jacket’ liberally, any outerwear made of denim would count. Anyway. Chore coats are more commonly made of a sturdy canvas or heavy moleskin cotton fabric, but denim's resilience make it another reliable option for the workwear genre. It doesn't get much better than this one from Alex Mill.

The brand's range of modern menswear staples is no slouch when it comes to fabric and construction and its line of chore coats is among the best out there, even compared to the multi-generational stalwarts like Carhartt and Dickies. This one’s made with sturdy, yet broken-in 100% cotton Japanese denim and comes with dual chest pockets and hand pockets, not to mention a stealthy phone pocket. The relaxed fit borders on boxy and is roomy enough to layer over a sweater or thick hoody once the temps drop. But if you're not the denim type (why are you even here?) Alex Mill makes its work jacket in a range of different fabrics, too.

To me, Alex Mill’s chore coats are nearly perfect. They fit like a dream and come with just the right vintage details that make guys like me swoon. I’ve compared it with my vintage French chore coat and not only are the details almost identical, the craftsmanship is virtually the same. So you could search for hours for a vintage one, or you could save the time and money and just get Alex Mill’s.

Levi’s may be the dominant denim trucker jacket, but they aren’t the only ones with a classic trucker jacket etched into the annals of menswear history. Lee’s left an indelible mark on the American denim landscape and is rightfully considered one of the so-called Big Three along with Levi’s and Wrangler. Lee’s famed Rider jacket was first introduced in 1948 and is considered one of the best denim jackets of all time.

Today’s modern reproduction is made by the brand’s retro sub-label, Lee 101, and features the same left-hand twill denim the brand is famous for, this time woven by a storied Japanese denim mill. The signature zig-zag stitching details at the collar and front placket still remain, as do the cateye buttons at the waist, and the slim, hip-length silhouette. If you’re hardcore, I’d recommend you go with the raw denim version and earn those fades yourself. But if you can’t be bothered to put in the work for five years straight, then stick with the light wash version.

Fans of the Japanese brand Kapital are quick to point out the brand's head-spinning takes on denim. From painstaking boro patchwork stitched by hand to far-out interpretations of blue jeans, the cult-loved label is a true innovator in the denim space. Its catalog is chock full of certified grails, but if you’re focusing in on jackets, it doesn’t get any crazier than its boro jacket. From the outset, it looks more like an antique pile of fabric than a jacket—and that’s kind of the point. The jacket is made of dozens and dozens of fabric scraps, each one meticulously distressed—and then repaired— to look like worn-out vintage textiles before sewn back together as a single garment.

As you can imagine, the process is extraordinarily time-consuming. That immense dedication results in a jacket that’s truly not for the faint of heart or those with shallow pockets. This particular jacket takes inspiration from Type I denim jackets and features a single flap pocket, rear cinch, and a boxy cropped fit. It may look shredded, but putting it on feels like absolute butter thanks to the custom, boro-printed satin interior.

Kaptain Sunshine has long been known for its loving recreations of heritage American workwear, but the artful way it approaches its designs has earned it a ton of crossover appeal with the fashion crowd. Case in point: This one-pocket denim jacket, which is constructed according to classic selvedge standards, but has enough interesting details (including a buckle back) to inspire the envy of any runway show attendee. Wear it carefully—you never know which menswear nerd could be nearby and hoping to swipe it from your chair.

The circle of iconic denim jackets is small. Even so, there’s one that doesn’t get as much attention it ought, and that’s the Type II trucker jacket. Levi’s introduced the Type II in 1953, the long-awaited follow up to the Type I. The features were much the same, but the main difference was the addition of a symmetry-imposing second pocket and adjustable waist tabs instead of a cinch back. The result is one of the most geometrically pleasing jackets ever. The boxy fit and spare details are very much in line with workwear designs, but there’s something also very minimalist about it, too. No wonder it still gets referenced and duped by modern designers.

Levi’s will always be the OG when it comes to the Type II, but if you really want to get one, The Real McCoy’s is the one to get. The Japanese brand is known for going insane lengths to reproduce the most coveted and iconic pieces of vintage menswear and their rendition of the Type II is a prime example. The denim was designed from the ground up, using a specifically sourced vintage loom that was able to deliver the kind of slubby character of ‘50s denim at a consistent clip. The result is one of the most accurate reproductions you can get. That is, if you can even find it. Thanks to the limited fabric production and high demand, the jacket is so sought after that it’s been sold out for ages.

Don’t let Gap’s iconic khakis ads make you forget that the iconic brand got its start in denim. That DNA is still prevalent today as Gap’s stable of denim offerings is as strong as ever. Case in point, this faithful take on the famous Type II trucker jacket featuring knife pleats, dual chest flap pockets, and a boxy cropped fit—all done in a hearty all-cotton denim.

If we didn’t tell you, you might not realize this was denim too. But even though it's finished in soft corduroy, there's a full denim jacket inside, taking trompe l’oeil to a new level. While most attempts would easily fall flat in the uncanny valley, Jeanerica's result offers the best of both worlds (and textures).

Before Ralph launched his western-inflected RRL line, Polo was still making workwear hits. And denimheads could easily miss this pitch-perfect take on the Type II trucker jacket with its impeccable cut and spot-on vintage wash.

J.Crew and Lee's collaborative iteration on the denim jacket is a true sleeper hit, featuring a mix of details from a corduroy collar, trendy (and practical) plaid lining, and those beautiful, unmistakable Lee trucker pockets. This is the denim jacket to take with you into fall.

Ralph's premium ranch-hand line has been quietly making the best faded denim in America for decades: The 'Leeland' wash has genuine depth to it, and even better—the buttons are embossed with “Cowboy.”

Material and construction: With denim jackets and jean jackets, the most important factor will be the denim itself. Make sure that the denim feels substantial and weighty. Good quality denim shouldn’t be too thin or loosely woven. Though I personally prefer denim without any sort of elastane, you may want to consider opting for a jacket with some stretch built into it for ease of movement. Even then, I’d advise you to limit the percentage of stretch to no more than 2%. Selvedge denim and Japanese denim are often a good sign of a high-quality fabric, but non-selvedge and non-Japanese denim can be well-made too, so don’t put all your trust in provenance.

Fit: Fit is subjective, but most trucker jackets follow a tried-and-true formula with a hem that hits right at the hips. They may have a leaner silhouette or a boxier cut, but a hallmark of trucker jackets is truly the cropped length which helps emphasize your natural proportions and lengthens your legs (without having to spend tens of thousands of dollars and months of agony). Denim jackets with hand pockets are often a little longer than those without, so if you may want to factor that into your decision.

Silhouette: Sizing is key, as well. Most denim jackets are cut on the more tailored end and around hip length. Make sure that the shoulder seams line up with your shoulder bones if not a little past. Keep in mind that you may want to layer underneath, since that will affect how snug the jacket will feel. With time, the sleeves of a trucker jacket will tend to get shorter as the elbow creases set in so if the sleeves are a tad long, you’re probably in a good place.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

Soft Services has shrunk its beloved exfoliating Buffing Bar down to miniature proportions, with four little bars in a very giftable set. A posh way to keep skin in check, and low-key great for travel.

Caraway isn't the first to make a coffee maker with an all-glass-and-steel brewing system, keeping hot coffee away from plastic. But it might just be the best-looking of the bunch, which counts when it's one of the first things they see in the morning.

#6736. Boyedoe Lagos Spring 2027

Across several African nations, fashion plays a significant part in shaping ceremonial attire. Ghanaian designer David Kusi Boyedoe is reimagining how heritage and culture can exist in today’s world. For spring 2027, he was heavily influenced by the Asante Kingdom, a Ghanaian ethnic group, and their dynamic relationship between an Asante King and the Asante man. “It’s also a return to our ideology, which is about going back and restoring, and making known our silhouettes,” he said. With this collection, titled ‘Oath’ (or ‘Ntam’ in Twi, a Ghanaian language), Boyedoe is swearing a pledge to his craft.

Often, there’s a monolithic perception of African fashion: it’s either experimental and bold or lacking commerciality to the Western world. But there’s a cohort of African designers that are offering a counter perspective, and Boyedoe is one of them. “Instead of creating a spectacle, I’m focused on designs that sell,” he said. Even though this collection is more commercially-driven and wearable, there’s still an interesting story rooted in culture, community, and craftsmanship—particularly as the majority of his pieces are handmade by local artisans in Ghana.

Overall, this collection wasn’t about spectacle. Upcycled denim, sourced from textile waste dumped in Ghana, was reworked into his signature patchwork design. Standout looks included a mini patchwork dress and a pair of barrel jeans paired with an off-white blazer. The denim was another avenue into accessories in the form of medium-sized patchwork bags. Boyedoe also introduced a new earthy color palette in silhouettes like an ivory coat and a moss green suit.

#6735. 4 Epic New Watches Every Watch Guy Is Salivating Over Right Now

Welcome to Watch Guy Watches, GQ’s monthly curation of high-end timepieces for the true watch nerds among us. This month, Moser goes retro(grade); Lange brings back a beloved bracelet; Biver drops its first hand-wound three-hander; and Breitling puts a pair of vintage-inspired watches in its core catalog.

There are only a few firm absolutes in the horological sphere. One of them is “never bet against H. Moser & Cie.” The high-end independent maker never ceases to amaze with its creativity, wit, and technological prowess. From a mechanical timepiece that bears a suspicious resemblance to a certain famous smartwatch to one the coolest integrated bracelet-bearing luxury sports watches on the market, Moser consistently delivers the Swiss-made goods.

Building upon its Pioneer Retrograde Seconds Midnight Blue release from two years ago, three new models with retrograde seconds join the collection this month in the Pioneer, Endeavour, and Streamliner collections. While all three are beautiful, however, it’s the latter whose aesthetics pair particularly well with this steampunk-esque complication—one in which a small hand tracks the passing seconds in an arc and then jumps back to its starting position at the top of each 30-second period.

Housed in a 40mm brushed stainless steel cushion case with a serpentine integrated bracelet, the Streamliner Retrograde Seconds offers a potent mix of Streamline Moderne and futurism before one even considers its dial. Executed in midnight blue fumé enamel, it features applied indices and the brand’s signature modified syringe handset, with a faint “H. Moser & Cie” signature appearing in white beneath 12 o’clock. The lower half of the face, meanwhile, is given over to the retrograde seconds display. Inspired by instrument gauges such as automotive speedometers, it features smooth action powered by the cal. HMC 252, a product of movement specialists Agenhor. (Flip the watch over and you can view its tungsten rotor whirring away via a sapphire caseback.)

One of the coolest features of the Streamliner collection is that despite the presence of numerous complications; of the use of fumé dials; and of high-end pricing, these watches are meant to be used. With 120m of water resistance, steel constriction, automatic winding, and 72 hours of power reserve, the Streamliner Retrograde Seconds is effectively a high-end tool watch. (Though at a sticker price of 29,900 CHF, maybe take it off if you’re, like, climbing Mt. Everest or whatever?)

While retrograde seconds displays don’t have the same utility as calendar readouts or GMT complications, they do demonstrate horological competence on the part of the watchmaker…and more importantly, they’re wild fun to watch in action. And if you can’t have a little fun in your watch-collecting journey, well—then what the heck are you even doing here, anyway?!

If you’ve been waiting years for the return of platinum bracelet options for A. Lange & Söhne’s Datograph Perpetual watch, we give you permission to rejoice: a new version of the timepiece—made in honor of the model’s 20th anniversary—is equipped not only with a diamond-studded black dial, but with a fresh matching platinum bracelet. Designed with five links rather than the seven of early-2000s models made by German jewelry manufacturer Wellendorff, said bracelet is perhaps more notable than the watch itself, which features the brand’s manually wound manufacture Calibre L952.1 movement and is limited to just 50 pieces.

When watch-world elder statesman Jean-Cladue Biver and his son Pierre co-founded their eponymous firm in 2022, their introductory product was a half-million-dollar automatic tourbillon and minute repeater. Having since added a simple automatic three-hander to their lineup in the form of the Automatique, they’re now expanding their offerings with a hand-wound three-hander in stainless steel. Dubbed the AB, it measures 38mm wide and 9.8mm tall and features a beautiful black multi-level onyx dial with gold accents, plus a cool stainless steel bracelet with an angular five-link design and a patented micro-adjust system. Powered by the new Calibre JCB-004 designed in collaboration with Le Cercle des Horlogers, it’s the brand’s entry-level model…though it’ll still set you back roughly the cost of a BMW M3. (Naturally, it’s already sold out.)

On the slightly less eye-watering—but no less compelling—end of the watch-guy spectrum is the new Breitling Navitimer B09 Chronograph 41. Why does it look so familiar, you might ask? Effectively, it’s a modern version of the famed ref. 806 “Twin Jet”-logo chronograph from the 1960s, only this time, it’s available as a non-limited edition—a fact that will surely excite deep Breitling aficionados. Measuring 41mm in stainless steel, it’s manually wound just like its vintage namesake, and comes paired to a brown leather strap for $7,900 or to a handsome steel bracelet for $8,400. If you fancy something a bit more left-field, there’s also a hand-wound, non-limited version of the Cosmonaute, a riff on the Navitimer equipped with a 24-hour dial that was famously worn by astronaut Scott Carpenter in 1962 ($10,600-$11,000).

#6729. Fruché Lagos Spring 2027

It was an exciting summer for Frank Aghuno, founder and creative director of Fruche. After winning Berlin Fashion Week’s contemporary prize, Aghuno travelled some 3,000 miles to the German capital and held his first international showcase. Still riding that high, the Lagos-based designer was eager to bring the collection home and present it to his Nigerian audience.

This collection asked us to embrace our natural quirks and imperfections. At times, that took on a literal meaning; “handwork can be imperfect in its natural state,” he said, be it naturally occurring holes in the wood carved beads or imperfections from dyeing. “There are quirks everywhere, from the perfectly styled looks to the looks that are more twisted and knotted,” he said.

Inspired by Nigerian boarding school uniforms, gingham featured heavily throughout the collection and came in several iterations, including cotton gingham; aso oke (a Nigerian textile) gingham; beaded gingham; and adire gingham, a traditional resist-dyeing technique. While the silhouettes felt contemporary, traditional crafting techniques remained a key component. From the fabric to the local wood carving, Aghuno was keen to collaborate with artisans based in Nigeria. The cotton used was sourced from Katsina and milled in Nigeria. “Everything is sourced here, and every look was made around the country,” he said, adding that he searched high and low for the right team to help develop the collection (including discovering craftsmen on TikTok). “It just goes to show the richness of our culture and the work we are doing today,” he said.

Standout looks included a satin dress and shirt featuring hand-painted artwork by Aghuno’s twin brother Dricky, an artist based between Lagos and London. At the show’s end, we heard the final look before it appeared on the runway. A model wearing an outfit made out of wood-carved shells walked out as the music drew to a close. The crowd fell quiet as they perched up in their seats and listened closely to the soothing sound of the beads brushing against each other. It was the first time I’ve heard Lagos that silent.

#6726. Inez and Vinoodh Mark 40 Years With a CFDA Lifetime Achievement Award

The celebrated photography duo and couple will be honored at the annual ceremony.

This evening, celebrated photography duo Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin will be given the Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award at the CFDA Fashion Awards. The pair, who are married, have been working together for 40 years, creating ad campaigns for brands like Gucci, Chanel, and Saint Laurent and shooting for major magazines.

“We didn’t know it was possible for [the Geoffrey Beene award to be given for] photography because it was always designers until now,” Matadin tells ELLE. “We’re just so happy that the CFDA is recognizing photography as such an integral part of the industry we all work in. The fact is that we as photographers translate a designer’s vision into an image or a film, so their designs live on in another world, in another way, in other media.”

This year also saw “Can Love Be a Photograph,” a museum retrospective of their work at the Kunstmuseum Den Haag in the Netherlands. Below, Van Lamsweerde and Matadin spoke with ELLE about the award, working together as spouses, and how digitalization is changing how we connect.

Inez van Lamsweerde: What was so unbelievable about that experience of choosing 200 works to reflect on our 40 years of working together was that now there’s a new baseline. Now this is from where we keep going, keep growing, keep having new ideas.

Vinoodh Matadin: At one point we said it’s not a retrospective, it’s a futurespective.

IVL: In most of the works in the exhibition it feels like there’s an element in this work that we could explore more, that asks for more new work to be made. It’s incredibly energizing and exciting to see that ideas from the mid-’90s can still be developed more.

VM: We realized when we did this exhibition that our work is almost timeless because it deals with the real and the unreal.

IVL: What’s so exciting every time is to step into someone’s world and hear about their influences, their inspiration, who they want to talk to, who they want to relate to, and what part of our work represents that for them. Then together, we form the ideas for a campaign. It always starts somewhere and then it ends somewhere completely different because as you go along together and work with the models or stylists, there’s new input all the time.

IVL: There is a series we made called “Thank You Thighmaster.” It’s large-scale photographs of a model shot nude in the studio that we then combined with faces of mannequin dolls from the ’70s. We took away all the orifices to show a hermetically closed person that still has all these feelings inside of her, but no way to communicate, because computers are the way we now are in contact with each other, and physicality is less and less important.

IVL: The title of the exhibition and the book that goes with it is “Can Love Be a Photograph?” To us, it’s not a question, it’s a statement. The exchange that we have with the person that’s sitting in front of our lens and then the viewer’s relationship to what they see on the photo is actually the most important thing. It’s this triangle of relationships, of emotion, of trust, of reflecting back on yourself that really drives everything for us. The bottom line of that is we love people. It’s just the most wonderful life to learn from everybody every day.

VM: The sad part of all this digitalization is that it was invented to connect us all. Now, we’re all disconnected while we’re all connected. No one can communicate with each other, and we don’t know what’s the real and what is the unreal anymore, and what is the truth. The only thing that we still have left is human contact and being in the now.

IVL: If you’re both rigid, it doesn’t work. You have to give and take one or the other way. I think a lot of people say to us like, “Oh my God, I could never work with my spouse.” We’re just constantly thinking, How could you not? For us, this is our way of living, and we’ve now also been together and worked together longer than we weren’t together.

VM: We still have the feeling we just started.

IVL: We still feel like young photographers.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6725. The Vogue Business Funding Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business Funding Tracker, a running list highlighting the most notable and intriguing investment and M&A activity in fashion and beauty. From emerging disruptors to legacy giants undergoing major changes, we spotlight the deals that are shifting the dynamics of the sectors we cover, including fashion, beauty, tech and sustainability.

Company description: Touted as London’s first functional smoothie bar, Elevate launched at the Royal Exchange in June 2025, before opening in Selfridges in April 2026. Founded by Julia Baldet, its bestselling smoothie, The Glow, made with collagen and hyaluronic acid, has grossed close to half a million pounds since rollout. Elevate has collaborated with brands such as Nike x Skims, Adanola, Ouai and Medicube, as wellness continues to crossover into beauty and fashion. The new funding will be used to open additional London sites next year, after finishing its first full year with over £1 million in sales.

Investor(s): JamJar (portfolio includes: Innocent Drinks, Deliveroo, Humantra), Active Partners (portfolio includes: Tala, Healf, Salad Project) Cassius, Soho House founder Nick Jones.

Investor comments: “Elevate’s proposition is perfect: delicious smoothies that look great while meeting real nutritional and wellness needs. It’s clearly working; loyal customers love the brand. But most of all, we’re backing Julia. She’s focused, ambitious, creative and commercial, and we’re thrilled to support her as she builds Elevate into a category-defining brand,” JamJar partner Adam Balon said in a statement.

Company description: Frasers Group has successfully taken control of Hugo Boss. Following a rejected takeover bid of €2 billion (€38 per share) in June, the British retail conglomerate has raised its stake to approximately 50.08% — an additional purchase of 198,666 shares, equating to €7.63 million, according to the stock market filing. The German fashion company will now become a subsidiary of the Mike Ashley-owned business.

Hugo Boss believed the June takeover proposal to be “financially inadequate”, urging its shareholders to reject. Though Frasers continued its efforts, gradually raising its holding once again to 48% in mid-August (up from 30.3% in June, alongside the initial takeover bid). Frasers Group CEO Michael Murray assumed the Hugo Boss chair position last month, after Stephan Sturm stepped down.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has adjusted its stake in Burberry from 7.4% to 6%. This comes after the growing British retail group raised its position in the company from 6.3% last week, after upping it from 4.2% at the end of September. This marks a potential pullback from its current luxury brand spending spree.

Investor(s): Frasers Group Luxury (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Matches).

Company description: Frasers Group has acquired a 8.78% stake in US-based sports brand Under Armour, continuing a string of cross-category investments in recent months. Earlier this week, Frasers upped its investment in Burberry to 6.3%, having also taken on ownership of esteemed department store Harvey Nichols in August. The Frasers portfolio spans discount retailer Sports Direct through to The Webster, House of Fraser, and Flannels, as well as a strong stake in Hugo Boss — upped to 47.89% in August. Under Armour’s share price has risen since the SEC filing was made on October 1.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct, The Webster)

Company description: Frasers Group has upped its economic interest in Burberry from 4.2% to 6.3%, with the British brand now part of a new luxury division launched in early October. Also part of the luxury portfolio, Hugo Boss — of which Frasers now owns almost 48% — continues to reject the retail group’s takeover bids; it may be looking elsewhere for potential acquisitions.

Investor(s): Frasers Group (portfolio includes: Flannels, The Webster, Harvey Nichols, Sports Direct).

Company description: Activewear brand 437 was founded in 2016 by co-CEOs Adrien Bettio and Hyla Nayeri. Initially founded as a swimwear brand, 437 moved into activewear in 2023, which is now the core of its business. The Toronto-based brand is the top-selling activewear brand on Revolve, and has fast become a celebrity go-to.

Funding and round: $15 million CAD, minority stake

Investor(s): Revolve (portfolio includes: Alliance Apparel, Alexandre Vauthier)

Investor comments: “437 is still a small player, but is already outselling nearly every activewear brand on our site, including billion dollar brands. The brand is great and the aesthetic and products are great — it’s really just building on their core momentum and continuing to gain awareness. Hyla and Adrien had built something very special, but had also reached a point where they needed additional capital, infrastructure, and a thought partner who had been through the same journey,” said co-founder and co-CEO Michael Karanikolas.

Company description: Founded by former fashion executive Yasmin Sewell, Vyrao launched in 2021 as a fragrance brand blending aromatherapy and neuroscience principles. The brand was ahead of the curve tapping into the cross-section of fragrance and wellness, by offering customers something more than just a scented mist. Following the acquisition, the genderless brand will embark on its next development phase under its new owner.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Company description: Based in LA, Arey launched in 2021 under entrepreneur Allison Conrad and celebrity hairstylist Jay Small, offering vitamin, antioxidant and peptide-infused products to help delay and repigment aging hair. The funding will support Arey’s new product development, ongoing clinical research, and expansion through retail partnerships.

Funding and round: Series A, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Unilever Ventures (portfolio includes:), Greycroft, Female Founders Fund.

Company description: AI-driven discovery platform Slayd launched in Gurugram, India, in 2025. Targeted at Gen Z, the startup sorts fashion items from more than 300 marketplaces and brands by theme and curates personalized feeds that enable product discovery across multiple sites. Slayd claims to currently have more than 200,000 users, and can identify emerging trends through its proprietary tech software. The investment will help strengthen its team and accelerate the growth of its private-label business, Slayd Originals.

Investor(s): AJVC (portfolio includes: Midcase, Bubble Me, Trufides).

Company description: ISDIN is a product of pharmaceutical company Corporación Químico-Farmacéutica Esteve (CQFE) and beauty group Puig, who partnered to launch the skincare brand in 1975. Since then, both families have supported ISDIN’s evolution into a global dermatological skincare business focused on scientific formulation and innovation. In acquiring CQFE’s 50% stake, Puig will obtain complete ownership of the Spanish brand.

Investor(s): Puig (portfolio includes: Charlotte Tilbury, Byredo, Penhaligon’s, Dr. Baraba Sturm).

Investor comments: “Expanding our presence in dermocosmetics is a strategic priority for Puig. ISDIN is a unique company, with a strong management team, a clear strategy and a distinctive position in dermatology and skincare. Full ownership will give Puig the best platform to support its next phase of growth and continue investing behind the science and innovation that have made ISDIN successful,” Puig CEO Jose Manuel Albesa said.

Company description: Founded in 2021, Talm (“To All the Mamas”) initially focused on bodycare products during pregnancy and postpartum, however the brand has gradually expanded to offer sensitive skincare for all stages of life. It currently offers around a dozen products, operates in roughly a dozen countries, and reports double-digit revenue growth. This marks the first acquisition for Caudalie, which plans to accelerate Talm’s global expansion and product development by leveraging its pharmacy network, sales force and infrastructure.

Company description: Medici Brands, owner of David Protein and newly launched confectionery brand HallPass, will use its Series B funding to enter the next phase of growth. This includes expanding HallPass’s retail presence, alongside the remainder of its product portfolio — extending David into new formats and categories, advancing product innovation, and enabling the launch and scaling of new brands such as Rowdy.

Funding and round: $250 million, Series B.

Investor(s): Greenoaks (portfolio includes: Stripe, Canva, Discord, Robinhood), Valor Equity Partners (portfolio includes: GoPuff, SpaceX, BitGo), Peter Rahal, Iconiq, Imaginary Ventures.

Investor comments: “Two years ago, David Protein showed customers they no longer had to choose between great macros and great taste, and it became one of the fastest-growing CPG brands in America. Now, Medici is bringing that approach to the rest of the store, building a house of brands that delivers the taste consumers adore, without making the compromises they have grown to accept,” said Greenoaks partner Neil Shah.

Company description: Truly Beauty is a plant-based personal care brand founded in 2013 by Maxx Appelman. Known for its viral, Gen Z-focused bodycare and social media marketing, Truly Beauty combines high-performing active ingredients with a luxurious but playful aesthetic. It is headquartered in Los Angeles. For razor company Dollar Shave Club, this marks its first acquisition as it extends beyond grooming.

Investor comments: “By layering Truly’s fast-turn product engine onto our AI-driven inventory planning and backend logistics, we are building a high-velocity innovation model that legacy CPG conglomerates simply cannot replicate,” said Dollar Shave Club CEO Larry Bodner.
