Investor comments: “Vera Wang is a legend. Her name is synonymous with modernity, artistry and impeccable style. We are honoured to partner with Vera Wang and look forward to building on the brand’s remarkable legacy with new business opportunities around the world,” said Yehuda Shmidman, chairman and CEO of WHP Global.

Company description: Founded by the eponymous PR guru in Paris in 2006, the agency represents over 100 of the most exciting brands across fashion, beauty, lifestyle and art, including Jacquemus, Coperni and Loewe. Pagès opened a New York branch in 2019.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): The Independents (portfolio includes: Karla Otto, Lefty, Bureau Betak).

Investor comments: “We’re delighted to welcome Lucien, who is the perfect addition to the puzzle we’ve been building for some years now,” said The Independents CEO Isabelle Chouvet. “Today’s clients are so global that it’s no longer possible, I think, to stand alone. So we have to be able to work together to meet these needs.”

Company description: Tangle Teezer was founded in 2007 in London, and has grown to become one of the most popular hair detangling brush makers in the UK thanks to its two-tiered teeth technology that claims to reduce damage. Since 2021, the brand has been owned by Mayfair Equity Partners. The company has reportedly doubled in size over the past four years, with net sales worth approximately €70 million as of 2024.

Funding and round: Acquisition, €200 million.

Investor comments: “We are excited to acquire a market-leading business in a dynamic, high-growth market where we can drive significant value. Both companies share a deep spirit of joy, innovation, entrepreneurship and a common vision for growth. With a consumer-first approach, together we aim to redefine personal grooming by creating personalised haircare solutions that enhance daily routines,” said Bic CEO Gonzalve Bich.

Company description: About You is a German e-commerce company founded in 2014 specialising in personalisation and influencer marketing. The company offers business-to-business tech services for online retailers and its annual sales reached €1.9 billion in 2023 — it’s now Hamburg’s first unicorn.

Funding and round: Acquisition, €6.50 per share (approximately €1.13 billion).

Investor comments: “I’m excited about how together we’ll be able to cover a larger share of the fashion and lifestyle market. In B2C, we can offer customers and brands distinct and rich shopping experiences. In B2B, combining our complementary software capabilities — Tradebyte and Scayle — will create an even more advanced e-commerce operating system that enables brands and retailers to manage their multi-channel business across Europe and beyond,” said Robert Gentz, co-CEO and co-founder of Zalando.

Company description: French boutique hotel group Les Domaines de Fontenille was founded in 2016 and owns 11 properties with strong heritage across France, Spain and Italy, including Tuscany, Marseille and Menorca. The group’s clientele includes young travellers looking for a premium experience.

Funding and round: Minority investment, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): LVMH (portfolio includes: Louis Vuitton, Belmond, Cheval Blanc) and Anaïs Ventures (portfolio includes: IB2).

Investor comments: “This financial investment by LVMH in Les Domaines de Fontenille is an opportunity to explore a complementary realm to the hospitality offerings we provide through our brands. We are pleased to support the founders, Frédéric Biousse and Guillaume Foucher, as well as CEO Linda Hazi, in writing the next chapter of the brand’s development,” said Jean-Jacques Guiony, CEO of Moët Hennessy, LVMH’s wines and spirits division.

Company description: Beauty brand Pañpuri was founded in Bangkok by Vorravit Siripark in 2003. It is known for its premium skincare, haircare, bath and body, and fragrance products inspired by Thai wellness traditions.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Kosé (portfolio includes: Tarte, Decorté).

Investor comments: “With this acquisition of shares, we will accelerate the global strategy set forth in our medium to long-term vision and aim to establish a presence in the Global South markets and further enhance our value,” said Kazutoshi Kobayashi, president and CEO of Kosé.

Company description: London-based resale startup launched in 2022 by Warwick University graduates Woody Lello (CEO), Felix Jackson (COO), Jack Cardwell (CIO) and Connor Mattinson (CTO). The Truss platform uses artificial intelligence to identify the specific product in an image and then shares detailed information about that item, with the goal of improving searchability and conversion rates. Thanks to the new investment, Truss has secured the match funding to activate a £1.1 million grant from Innovate UK. The startup previously raised £345,000 in pre-seed funding.

Investor(s): Figr Ventures (Truss is its first investment).

Investor comments: “We believe the fashion sector needs to change, we believe circularity is the answer and we believe Truss is the way for businesses to achieve this,” said Fiona Humphries, managing director of Figr Ventures.

Company description: Norwegian premium luggage and travel bag brand Db was founded in 2012, originally called Douchebags, and has risen in popularity among surfers, skiers and other outdoor sports fans. The brand is stocked in Selfridges, Harrods, End, Goodhood and more. The funds will go towards Db’s international expansion, design innovation and store openings in Europe.

Funding and round: Minority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): LVMH Luxury Ventures (portfolio includes: Our Legacy, Lyst, Aimé Leon Dore).

Investor comments: “Db is a reference in the bags and luggage sector, combining truly distinctive designs with high quality and functionality, and is geared towards a close community of outdoor enthusiasts, athletes, creative people and passionate travellers. Db has a strong position in Scandinavia with an untapped growth potential in the rest of the world,” said Julie Bercovy, CEO of LVMH Luxury Ventures Advisors.

Company description: Brand Architekts is a beauty group that counts drugstore brands Skinny Tan and Super Facialist among its portfolio. In October, the company reported a 15 per cent drop in sales for the year ended 30 June as it shifted its focus to fewer, larger brands.

Funding and round: £13.9 million, acquisition.

Investor(s): Warpaint (portfolio includes: Technic, W7)

Investor comments: “As part of a larger group we believe applying our established supply and distribution channels and approach to Brand Architekts will improve efficiency, reduce costs and drive profitability,” said Warpaint CEO Sam Bazini.

Company description: Founded by French makeup artist Violette Serrat in 2021, New York-based Violette_FR exclusively offers a 14-piece core collection that includes makeup, skincare and haircare. The brand has risen to popularity thanks to Serrat’s signature ‘French girl’ aesthetic.

Funding and round: Series B, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Silas Capital (portfolio includes: Makeup by Mario, Herbivore, Wonderbelly), Experienced Capital, Monogram Capital Partners, Felix Capital.

Investor comments: “Violette_FR stands out in the beauty landscape for its aspirational French brand appeal, driven by Violette’s authenticity and credibility, which resonate deeply with consumers,” said Brian Thorne, partner at Silas Capital.

Company description: Launched in 2018, Korean womenswear platform Ably has tripled its value to over $2 billion over the past three years, and is now considered a unicorn under Alibaba’s investment.

Investor(s): Alibaba Group (portfolio includes: AliExpress, Tmall, Taobao)

Company description: Indian clean beauty brand Earth Rhythm offers plastic-free packaging and biodegradable products, as well as vegan and cruelty-free formulations. Founded in 2019, the brand has 250 offerings spanning skincare, haircare and cosmetics. In 2022, Nykaa acquired a minority stake in the brand.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Nykaa (portfolio includes: Kay Beauty, Pipa Bella, Dot & Key)

Investor comments: “Earth Rhythm represents an exciting addition to our portfolio and presents an opportunity to expand our play in the clean beauty space, a category with immense long-term potential,” said Adwaita Nayar, co-founder of Nykaa and CEO of Nykaa Fashion.

Company description: H&M Group’s digital fashion outlet launched in 2018. Due to a lack of demand, the group announced that Afound would be discontinued in August, but it will integrate with Secret Sales under a December relaunch, offering over €5 billion in revenue sourced from 3,800 premium brands.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): Secret Sales, an off-price marketplace within private equity firm Perwyn’s portfolio.

Investor comments: “Bringing Afound into the Secret Sales family reinforces our commitment to growing our premium off-price solution across Europe. This acquisition is another step towards transforming the off-price landscape,” said Chris Griffin, CEO of Secret Sales.

Company description: Manchester-based men’s streetwear brand founded by brothers George and Michael Heaton in 2011. The brand has scaled quickly with a compound annual growth rate of 64 per cent since 2020, delivering double-digit profit margins, and expects to generate around £100 million in revenue by the end of the fiscal year. In 2021, Represent launched its ‘247’ performance line and in 2024 it introduced its first retail locations in LA and Manchester, with a London store planned for 2025. The brand aims to use the funding to fuel retail expansion and improve operational capabilities.

Funding and round: Minority stake, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): True (Portfolio includes: Formerly Known As Haeckels, Boy Smells).

Investor comments: “Represent is a real success story for British fashion. The team’s track record of developing culturally relevant products and acquiring loyal customers to the brand, despite the challenging consumer environment, is remarkable,” said Ejike Onuchukwu, investment director at True, who has joined Represent’s board.

Company description: Paris-based lab-grown leather startup founded in 2021. Faircraft manufactures leather using cellular biology that replicates the structure and cellular composition of animal skin. The funding will be used to expand Faircraft’s team, recruiting more engineers and biologists to scale its operations.

Funding and round: €15.8 million, Series A.

Investor(s): Kindred Ventures (portfolio includes: Poshmark, Postmates), Cap Horn, BPI, Sake Bosch, Entrepreneur First, Alliance for Impact, Heirloom.

Investor comments: “Leather has long been the cornerstone of the fashion industry, valued for its timeless appeal and durability — but its production comes with steep environmental costs. Faircraft’s lab-grown leather is a breakthrough for brands and consumers who refuse to compromise between quality and sustainability, and we’re proud to support them as they scale operations and bring this revolutionary product to market,” said Kanyi Maqubela, managing partner at Kindred Ventures.

Company description: Founded in 2019, Clean Skin Club is a mass skincare brand known for its single-use disposable facial towels, stocked across Amazon, Target and Beauty Bay, among others. The brand was inspired by an aesthetician’s complaint about the bacteria in spa towels. The funds will be used to expand the brand’s bricks-and-mortar retail, new product development and grow the team.

Funding and round: $32 million, Series X.

Investor(s): Astō Consumer Partners, Amberstone (portfolio includes: Bloom Nutrition, Crown Affair).

Investor comments: “Clean Skin Club is ushering in a new era of skincare through reimagining the category and delivering straightforward, science-backed solutions that truly work. The disruptive brand has amassed a cult following, ranking as a bestseller on Amazon and breaking through the large, high-growth skincare market,” said Clayton Christopher, co-founder of Astō Consumer Partners.

Company description: Prestige haircare brand founded in 2020 and known for its promotion of haircare as a selfcare ritual. Crown Affair previously generated $5 million in Series A funding in 2022, also led by True Beauty Ventures. The Series B funding will be used to expand Crown Affair’s offering at Sephora, build out its team and scale marketing initiatives.

Investor(s): True Beauty Ventures (Portfolio includes: K18 Hair, Caliray, Maude).

Investor comments: “As a long-time supporter, I have witnessed Crown Affair consistently demonstrate the strength of its brand with a unique blend of elevated, clean haircare innovation, thoughtful hair rituals and authentic storytelling,” said Cristina Nuñez, co-founder and managing partner of True Beauty Ventures.

Company description: Beauty supplements and wellness brand, founded by influencer Tati Westbrook in 2018. Westbrook departed the company in August 2024 after settling a four-year legal battle in which her business partner, Clark Swanson, accused Westbrook and her husband of fraud, negligence and breach of fiduciary duty to Halo Beauty.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor comments: “We’re honoured to carry Halo Beauty’s legacy forwards by expanding its mission of clean, effective beauty and wellness. This acquisition marks a new era of innovation and commitment to empowering consumers with products that enhance both their beauty and overall well-being,” said the private investor.

Company description: Skincare brand known for peptide-infused anti-ageing products. The brand claims its signature OS-01 peptide can reverse the skin’s biological age ageing by preventing senescent or “zombie” cells, which are cells that are alive but damaged. OneSkin was founded by four PhD scientists: Carolina Reis de Oliveira, Alessandra Zonari, Mariana Boroni and Juliana Carvalho. The recent investment brings OneSkin’s total funding to $20 million.

Investor(s): Selva Ventures, Plus Capital, Unilever Ventures, Able Partners, Camila Alves McConaughey (Brazilian-American model and wife of actor Matthew McConaughey), tech entrepreneur Kevin Rose, plus previous investors.

Investor comments: “As a Brazilian woman, I am thrilled to invest in a brand founded by four Brazilian female scientists — my heritage is something I’m incredibly proud of, and I am honoured to support those who are executing this work. The OneSkin team has built a line of products that hold a unique space in the massive skincare market. I fell in love with the products the moment I saw the results on myself, and I knew I had to be a part of it! I’m so looking forward to seeing their future innovations and continued success with the help of this funding,” said McConaughey.

Company description: Wholesale vintage clothing marketplace founded in 2021 by Abhi Arora and Sanket Agarwal. The platform connects retailers and resellers to inventory from verified vintage wholesalers around the world.

Funding and round: £17 million total, £4.7 million in seed and £12.3 million in Series A.

Investor(s): HV Capital (portfolio includes: Depop, Zalando, Hello Fresh), Andreessen Horowitz (portfolio includes: Instagram, Pinterest, Roblox), Y Combinator (portfolio includes: Snap, Airbnb), Shopify president Harley Finkelstein, former Depop CEO Maria Raga.

Investor comments: “We are proud to invest in Fleek, a company that is redefining the secondhand fashion landscape. Fleek’s innovative approach to scaling the secondhand market globally reflects tremendous potential for growth. The marketplace not only addresses current industry needs but also paves the way for a more sustainable future in fashion. We’re excited to be part of this journey,” said Felix Klür, general partner at HV Capital.

Company description: Founded in 2005 in Stockholm by Jockum Hallin, Cristopher Nying and Richardos Klarén, Our Legacy is known for high-quality menswear with intricate design signatures. The brand has around 200 stockists and seven of its own stores, and has risen in notoriety thanks to buzzy collaborations with Stüssy and Emporio Armani.

Funding and round: Minority stake, terms undisclosed.

Lead investor(s): LVMH Luxury Ventures (portfolio includes: Aimé Leon Dore, Lyst, Heat).

Investor comments: “Our Legacy is the epitome of what we could call the ‘quiet cool’ tendency, featuring a unique blend of contemporary minimalism and creative subversion,” said Julie Bercovy, CEO of LVMH Luxury Ventures Advisors.

Company description: Californian premium athleisure brand Vuori was founded in 2015 by Joe Kudla. The brand is known for its unique fabrics and is certified as carbon neutral by Change Climate. Following this investment, the brand’s valuation has reached $5.5 billion, building on a $400 million investment by Softbank Vision Fund 2 in 2021, which brought its valuation to $4 million.

Funding and round: $825 million, secondary tender offer.

Lead investor(s): General Atlantic (portfolio includes: Gymshark, Sézane, Tory Burch), Stripes (portfolio includes: On, Reformation, Khaite) and existing investors.

Investor comments: “Vuori encapsulates everything we look for in a Stripes investment — the products are amazing and beloved by the consumer, the team is fanatical about quality and innovation, and the market for athleisure is global with durable tailwinds,” said Chris Carey, partner at Stripes.

Company description: Secondhand peer-to-peer marketplace founded in 2008 by Milda Mitkutė and Justas Janauskas in Lithuania. The platform is Europe’s largest clothing resale marketplace. The recent investment brings Vinted’s valuation to €5 billion.

Funding and round: €340 million, secondary share sale.

Investor(s): TPG Tech Adjacencies, Hedosophia (portfolio includes: Monzo, Go Puff), Baille Gifford, Invus Opportunities (portfolio includes: Coupang, Chrono 24), FJ Labs (portfolio includes: Farfetch, Uber, Klarna), Manhattan Venture Partners (portfolio includes: Discord, Epic Games, X), Moore Strategic Ventures.

Investor comments: “We’ve seen that consumers are increasingly choosing secondhand as a core part of their wardrobe, as sustainability and flexibility become top of mind for many people. Vinted’s customer focus, leading product experience, and sophisticated approach to logistics have made this market accessible to an even broader population,” said TPG partner Andrew Doyle.

Company description: Biotech-powered prestige skincare brand Reome was founded by beauty editor and acupuncturist Joanna Ellner in 2023. The UK-based brand is known for its sensorial products and is stocked in Space NK, Liberty and Moda Operandi among others.

Investor(s): Rianta Capital (portfolio includes: El Rayo, Home Cooks).

Company description: UK-based women’s shirt brand launched in 2017 by a former Vogue stylist and Tatler editor Pip Durell. The B Corp-certified brand, which is known for timeless designs inspired by men’s tailoring and British heritage, launched its first pair of trousers earlier this year and plans to expand further with blazers and knitwear at the start of 2025. With Nothing Underneath was named one of Walpole’s Brands of Tomorrow in 2022.

Lead investor(s): Pembroke VCT (portfolio includes: Tala, Me+Em, Bella Freud) and JamJar Investments (portfolio includes: Deliveroo, Oatly, Spoke).

Investor comments: “With Nothing Underneath (WNU) holds a unique position in the womenswear market. Pip and her team have built a fantastic brand around one staple item, the shirt — an essential in most women’s wardrobes. It has become a standout in the fashion industry and early growth metrics have given us conviction in the brand. This investment will enable this emerging British heritage brand to enhance its product range, assist with growth and support WNU’s international reach,” said Andrew Wolfson, CEO of Pembroke Investment Managers.

Company description: UK-based luxury retail platform that stocks a curation of independent brands. The retailer is known for its selection of vibrant eveningwear. Founded in 2019 by Nina Briance, Cult Mia initially received $3 million in seed funding in November 2023 led by Fuel Ventures, with participation from Morgan Stanley and David Wertheimer of the Chanel family.

Funding and round: $2 million, seed (bringing total seed funding to $5 million).

Investor(s): H&M Group Ventures (portfolio includes: Goop, Klarna) and existing investors.

Investor comments: “We are delighted to invest in Cult Mia on their mission to launch independent and diverse designers from around the world. We have been incredibly impressed by all that Cult Mia has achieved in such a short space of time,” said Nanna Andersen, chief of new growth and ventures at H&M Group.

Company description: Founded in 1997 by Dr Gregory Brown, Révive is known for its luxury serums and creams powered by bio-renewal technology. The brand was previously acquired by Shiseido in 2016, before it was sold to Tengram Capital Partners in 2017.

Funding and round: Acquisition, terms undisclosed.

Investor(s): S’Young Group (portfolio includes: Evidens de Beauté, Pier Augé).

#6723. Mashed Sweet Potatoes

Sweet potatoes are a fall classic, and they make up some of the best dishes of the season, from dishes like sweet potato pie to sweet potato casserole. But the flavors of the sweet potato still shine in its simplest form. When we’re craving the flavors with no distractions, we turn to this simple, satisfying side. Blended with plenty of butter and half-and-half, these easy mashed sweet potatoes are creamy while being just sweet enough, but you can even turn them savory if you’re missing classic mashed potatoes.

Add the potatoes to a large pot and cover them with at least 2" of water. Sprinkle in a generous amount of salt. Bring everything to a boil, then cook the potatoes until they're very tender—this usually takes about 15 to 20 minutes, depending on their size.

Mash the potatoes with a potato masher. Pour in the half-and-half, add the butter and syrup, and stir everything together. Season with salt and pepper to taste, then finish by sprinkling some thyme on top.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you’re looking for a make-ahead Thanksgiving side to help your holiday go smoothly, these mashed sweet potatoes are perfect. Simply make them the night before, store in the fridge in an airtight container, then reheat when you’re ready to serve. When reheating, you may want to add more liquid to loosen it up.

#6721. Can the Brooklyn Nets Convert a Generation of Newly Minted Knicks Fans?

At the Brooklyn Nets’ home opener against the Charlotte Hornets last week, one longtime fan pointed out the strange dynamic inherent to New York City basketball fandom. He was jealous of places like Boston and Philadelphia, he said, because the entire city organizes itself around one team. Sports franchises, after all, are avatars of civic pride, and the very best organizations come to reflect the values of the cities they represent. (Think the Showtime Lakers or the Grit-and-Grind Memphis Grizzlies.) But in New York, home to both the Nets and the Knicks, fan bases are pitted against each other by fans, media, and sometimes even franchise leaders.

For a long time, the Nets could take solace in their cross rivals' decades-long stretch of ineptitude. That vanished when Jalen Brunson and company lifted the Larry O’Brien in June, leaving Brooklyn with some soul searching to do. “It doesn't make us feel very good,” Nets owner Joe Tsai told NetsDaily over the summer. “It irates our fan base and it is embarrassing.” As The Ringer’s Zach Lowe pointed out on his recently launched Substack, the Knicks’ title cost the Nets “an entire generation of fans.”

I, for one, have never understood why commentators are so obsessed with the size of Brooklyn’s fanbase. I am, obviously, a hugely biased homer, but you don’t hear the same concerns when it comes to other little-brother teams like the Clippers or teams, like Wizards, whose games are sparsely attended. Even as they’ve tanked these past couple of years, the Nets have maintained a 99% attendance rate and are the eighth most-valuable franchise in the entire league. Still, I have to hear talking heads argue that the team should move back to New Jersey? I might be salty, but that’s stupid.

Nevertheless, there is clearly angst about building up a coalition of Nets faithful. On his podcast Curious Mike, where I wish he would be less curious, the team’s star forward Michael Porter Jr. recently said, “When we play Knicks, Celtics, Philly, Lakers, it's mostly their fans. It's crazy.” And he’s not wrong: it's a weird time to be a fan of the Brooklyn Nets—the team’s fallen twice in the lottery and is trying to kickstart a rebuild in the shadow of one of the most storied franchises in the NBA. So I made my way over to the team’s training facility in Sunset Park to see how the Nets are tackling this problem with pillars of the present and future.

“I don't give a shit,” says Julius Randle, tucked into a glass room in the corner of the Nets’ famously photogenic training facility, when I ask him about the invasion of opposing fans at Barclays. “I've been on teams that weren't good and didn’t have the excitement around them. Then you start winning and the whole arena is there to see your team and cheer. So I think that's just part of being a fan. For us as a team, we got to give them something to root for.”

Randle, who played an integral role in the Knicks rebuild before being shipped off to the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2024, has seen New York City basketball fandom from both sides of the river. “It doesn't really matter what team I play for. I was at my son's basketball game yesterday and it was like, Man, I'm a Nets fan. You’re going to kill it this year. Then I get on the other side and it's, Thank you for everything you've done for the Knicks."

Randle, now on his fifth team in 13 seasons, also downplayed the idea that the Nets-Knicks intercity rivalry mattered all that much to players. “From the locker room, basketball is basketball,” he insists. “It's not like college or high school where we play our rival on Friday or whatever. You play 82 games a year. You feel the energy during the game, but I definitely think it's a bigger deal from a fan perspective than it is from a player's perspective.”

I can’t even finish my next question before he cuts me off. Do you see part of your role as growing this next generation of fans or are you just here to—

“No, hell no,” Randle says. “I definitely want to be a part of establishing a culture and giving the city of Brooklyn something to be proud of. I'm not here just to come out and get my numbers or whatever it is. I'm here to win a championship. I'm here to help these young guys excel and speed up their growth process.”

One of those young guys is the anointed prince of the franchise, Mikel Brown Jr., the Orlando-born point guard the Nets took sixth overall in this year’s draft and who fans are already calling “the best prospect in franchise history” (I agree.) Another prominent member of Nets Twitter, moved by preseason action, described him as a mix of CJ McCollum and All-NBA regulars Tyrese Haliburton and Kyrie Irving. (I love that tweet, and I love this fanbase.)

With the Nets, Brown came into a peculiar situation. Not only does the future of the franchise’s success hinge on whether he can reach his star potential—so does the team’s ability to cultivate a new generation of fans. It’s a challenge Brown recognizes and embraces. Many fans, myself included, took note of a phrase he kept repeating on draft night: “I’m home.” It felt like a full-throated endorsement of the franchise and its mission. “Most of the [Nets] fans are there in the arena for a draft night,” Brown says when I ask him what he meant. “So to hear the crowd pop and just to see the energy, it brought me a whole bunch of joy.”

Brown is 20 years old, and looks even younger, but he understands just how much is riding on his rookie season. “I embrace it,” he says. “At the end of the day, we're just kind of focusing on what we can control and then let everything else play on. Whatever happens after that and whoever comes along with us, enjoy the ride because we're going to go to war.”

Everyone I talked to believes Brown has the goods to deliver on both his promises and his potential. Randle, too, told me he’s been texting his friends back home to tell them how gifted Brown is. “I've been thoroughly, thoroughly impressed with not just his talent level, but his maturity and his IQ at such a young age is really, really impressive.” Typically, Randle continues, young players are single-mindedly focused on scoring. But Brown understands that there’s more than one way to contribute. “He just knows how to make the right play every single time. He just knows how to play good basketball.”

Brown is the type of prospect us Nets fans have been waiting to call our own. I loved rooting for every iteration of this team, but what the franchise’s best players—Jason Kidd, Deron Williams, Joe Johnson, Kyrie Irving, and Kevin Durant—have in common is that none of them were drafted by the Nets. Developing a homegrown star is a different task altogether, and the Nets have solid reason to believe they've found one.

On Wednesday night against the Boston Celtics, we caught a glimpse of what Brown can do . The 20 year-old was “not human,” as Nets longtime commentator Ian Eagle likes to say, in the fourth quarter. After pouring in several clutch baskets, he sent the game to overtime with a falling-to-the-side three with just 0.2 seconds left. Brooklyn lost the game, but if Brown’s development keeps trending in this direction, maybe we can win the war.

My Nets fandom is the result of perfect timing. I mostly grew up in California but spent my formative sports-team-choosing years in New Jersey when my family and I moved across the country for my dad’s job. After moving back to the Bay Area halfway through elementary school, I clung even more tightly to the Nets to stay connected with the friends and the place I left behind: the Snoopy fishing rod I used at the local lake, the fireflies in my New Jersey-sized backyard, the cul-de-sac that seemed to have a friend in every neighboring house.

During the Nets home opener, with the team wearing their excellent ABA-inspired red-and-blue jerseys, the game seemed all but decided as the Charlotte Hornets started to pull away at the end of the fourth. But with just over a minute left, the crowd started to pop as Randle bullied his way into an and-one layup and starting center Day'Ron Sharpe blocked a shot at the other end.

I thought back to the simple philosophy both Randle and Brown echoed: just win, and people will show up. The Nets eventually lost that game against Charlotte, and a few other heartbreakers since (against very tough competition, for what it’s worth). It’s unclear whether the Nets will ever convert a generation of fans spellbound by the Knicks, or even win the Finals. But I know I’ll be there.

#6720. Burgundy Ballet Flats Are Trending—5 Ways to Style Them for Fall

Burgundy has been flexing its might on the fashion scene for quite a few seasons now. We’ve seen the shade crop up on leather jackets and dominate the handbag conversation. Lately, it’s making its way south to ballet flats. Seen at Phoebe Philo, The Row, and Alaïa, burgundy footwear hits a useful sweet spot: It’s not quite a neutral, but it’s nowhere near as outfit dominating as a punchier shade like red or cobalt.

Caroline Trentini (Photo by Claudio Lavenia/Getty Images)

Clara Kong Vila (Photo by Edward Berthelot/Getty Images)

The color feels especially well suited to the ballet flat, a shoe that has become a bona fide wardrobe staple. After seasons of black mesh, metallics, and classic leather styles, burgundy offers a way to make the familiar silhouette feel fresh. It’s also an easy way to introduce a little color into your fall wardrobe. Burgundy flats look just as good with denim, black, brown, and gray as they do with some of the season’s less expected shades, like pale pink or chartreuse.

Below, shop some of our favorites and take a look at the five ways we’re wearing them now.

The Row’s Stella slipper in burgundy lends a fashion-forward finish to classic blue jeans and an everyday wool jacket.

Burgundy pairs surprisingly well with pale pink, lending the sweeter shade a more sophisticated edge.

A graphic black-and-white look benefits from the subtle addition of a burgundy ballet flat, which keeps the combination from feeling too severe.

Burgundy fits easily into an off-duty wardrobe too. Pair it with army green cargos and a gray knit for an easy yet polished combination.

Proenza Schouler’s chartreuse dress may be the star of the show here, but burgundy is an ideal complement, keeping the look dynamic and colorful.

#6719. A Retractable Makeup Pen That Does More Than One Job

ELLE editors think Alleyoop’s innovative product is a game changer.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Growing up, I had exactly one prized possession: a gel retractable multi-pen. To my 10-year-old brain, it was a marvel. I could write one word in sparkly sky blue, then the next in lime green, and the following in hot pink. If I wanted to get crazy, I could change the color of each letter while I scrolled. Twenty years later, my taste in writing utensils has gotten much more practical (almost all of my pens are boring, one-color black ones). But beauty brand Alleyoop has managed to bring a retractable multi-pen back into my life in the most practical way: with a makeup touch-up version that has eyeliner, lip liner, highlighter, and a brow pencil.

The Alleyoop Pen Pal 4-in-1 Touch-Up Pen comes in three different variations (though they all have black eyeliner and champagne highlighter): In a Rouge, which is made for light skin tones and has taupe brow pencil and nude pink lip liner; Make a Mauve, meant for medium skin tones, which features dark brown brow pencil and mauve lip liner; and Berry Busy, a deeper option that has berry lip liner and dark brown brow pencil. The ELLE team put this innovative tool to the test. Read our unfiltered thoughts below.

“I can’t believe how much I like this pen. It’s so easy to click through the different options. Each tip is small and sharp, so you’re able to draw precise lines, and the formulas are creamy, glide easily, and last all day. Being able to basically do your entire face with one product is incredible. I want to keep one in my travel case, gym bag, and purse for easy touch-ups on the go.”

“This fun little pen totally took me by surprise! What I expected to be a bit gimmicky turned out to be a super convenient and well-formulated makeup product. To start, I lined my lips with the pink shade. The mauve color was beautiful and pigmented; it glided on smoothly, and actually lasted throughout the day. Next, I took the champagne shade and used it to highlight the tip of my nose, inner corners of my eyes, and my brow bones. The small tip was especially helpful for precise placement. After filming, I even tried using the black shade to create a little winged liner. It wasn’t super pigmented, but it definitely helped to lift and elongate my eye shape. I can definitely see myself throwing this tool in my bag for on-the-go touch-ups across my entire face.”

“My makeup bag is essentially a black hole, so you can imagine my delight at discovering that this clever little pen replaces four of the beauty essentials I find myself rummaging around for every morning: brow pencil, eyeliner, lip liner, and eye highlighter. The Make a Mauve shade is a perfect match for my everyday makeup routine, featuring a dark brown brow pencil, black eyeliner, champagne gold highlighter, and rosy pink lip liner. Each formula glides on effortlessly with great color payoff. The eyeliner is particularly easy to blend if you’re after a smoky, smudged-out look, but as someone who rarely leaves the house without a little wing, I’m pleased to find that I can still achieve a precise flick with the help of a straight-edged piece of card. The lip liner is another personal favorite, delivering smooth, even color without any dragging or skipping. And when one of the pencils starts to wear down, all it takes is a quick twist to reveal more product—no sharpener required. Suffice it to say, the next time I’m jet-setting somewhere, I’m leaving my assortment of pencils behind and making room for this multitasking Alleyoop pen instead.”

“The only way I can describe this pen is that it is an all-in-one makeup product designed for the girl on the go (a.k.a. me). Not only was I delighted by the novelty of clicking through the different products, but I find it incredibly useful for someone who needs to do a touch-up every now and then before a work event after a day at the office. And no, I'm not over the nostalgia for the pen, either.”

“I love the idea of having an all-in-one tool I can just throw in my purse or bag on days when I’m not sure if I want to wear makeup or not. In fact, I might get a second one of these pens to just leave at my desk.”

#6717. Better American Sunscreens Are Here—But We’re Still Way Behind the Best

Anyone who’s applied sunscreen only to be left with a chalky white cast, a greasy finish knows American sun care has long been a frustrating experience. The US is decades behind European and Asian counterparts, which have long been blessed with sunscreens that are lighter, more luxurious, and easier to wear every day. For skincare obsessives (this writer included) trips abroad are also opportunities to stock up on superior sunscreens they can’t find at home.

The root of the problem is regulation. The Food and Drug Administration classifies sunscreen as a drug rather than a cosmetic. Because of that distinction, more time and testing is required to get new sunscreens on the shelves, dramatically reducing innovation in American sun protection. But for the first time since the ‘90s, we’ve had some movement on that front. In June of this year, the FDA approved a new sunscreen filter called bemotrizinol—also known as Tinosorb S or BEMT—after years of lobbying in the states by dermatologists, skincare brands, and Congress members. It’s a meaningful step toward better sun care, but the US is still lagging behind.

Bemotrizinol is prized for its ability to provide both UVA and UVB protection while remaining stable in sunlight. That’s a significant advantage over some existing US-approved filters, which offer protection against one type of UV radiation more effectively than the other. BEMT also has the potential to make sunscreen more pleasant to wear: “And because it’s a large, oil-loving molecule, it mostly stays on the surface of your skin instead of soaking in, and it blends into lightweight, non-greasy formulas with no white cast,” says Dr. Joel Spitz, co-founder, chief medical officer, and board-certified dermatologist at Honeydew, a virtual dermatology platform.

Bemotrizinol might be new for the US market, but it’s already been used in sunscreen formulations abroad for 20 years, Spitz says. That long track record helps explain why consumers in the US have spent years coveting the more cosmetically elegant formulas available in countries like South Korea and France. While most consumers would love if major brands like Neutrogena, La Roche-Posay, or Beauty of Joseon brought their European or Asian formulations to the US, those SPFs still contain filters that the FDA hasn’t approved. As a result, many brands are developing entirely new BEMT-centric formulas for use stateside.

Australian label Ultra Violette was the first brand to release a BEMT sunscreen in the US with its Unblock Screen SPF 50 in August 2026. Neutrogena debuted its Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 in September. Earlier this month French drugstore staple La Roche-Posay put its Anthelios UVDefense Sunscreen SPF 50 up for sale online. Don’t mistake the relatively quick arrival of these products after the FDA’s approval for ease in which brands can develop new formulations. According to Emanuella Louis, La Roche-Posay’s public relations manager, the brand had been working on its new formula for more than two years.

That long lead time reflects the way sunscreen development works: Brands can research and test formulas in anticipation of regulatory changes, then move a product forward when a particular filter gets the green light. Louis says La Roche-Posay has access to filters the FDA may be considering for approval and is “actively working, playing, testing on what possibly those formulas would be.” When a filter is approved, she explains, a formula already in the testing pipeline can be moved up.

Some brands are still tinkering with BEMT formulas for the US. Round Lab, one of South Korea’s most popular sunscreen manufacturers, has sold a version of its SPF in the US since 2024, and is hard at work on a new version of those formulas that contains bemotrizinol.

“Bemotrizinol’s approval in the US is a meaningful change, but it does not mean a Korean formula can simply be brought to the US market as is,” says Koochul Kwon, Round Lab’s chief technology officer. Beyond incorporating the newly approved filter, brands must ensure the ingredients keep the UV filters stably dissolved and working alongside other components, including moisturizing ingredients. The finished product must then meet US requirements for SPF and broad-spectrum testing, product stability, and labeling. With those considerations in mind, Kwon expects Round Lab to release its own bemotrizinol sunscreen sometime in 2027.

A sunscreen is only as useful as a person’s willingness to wear it consistently. Bemotrizinol’s ability to protect against UV damage is important, but its potential to make formulas lighter, less greasy, and more comfortable could be just as consequential to get people to implement it in their everyday skincare routines.

“One of the strengths of Korean sun care is how naturally it has built sun protection into the everyday skincare experience,” Kwon says. “For people to apply enough sunscreen and reapply it when needed, the way it feels matters as much as how well it protects.”

But better filters alone won’t transform American sun care. The real breakthrough will be sunscreens that people actually enjoy wearing—and, as a result, are more likely to apply generously and reapply throughout the day, a key step to ensuring its effectiveness.

Charlotte Palermino, cofounder and chief brand officer of skincare brand Dieux, has been an advocate for easier sunscreen filter approvals ever since she tried her first Japanese sunscreen, Biore UV, a decade ago. She realized sunscreen could stave off skin issues after her dermatologist told her that her hyperpigmentation had been the result of failing to use sun protection. In the years since she has publicly pushed for regulatory reform. She’s hesitant to put an estimated release date on Dieux’s upcoming BEMT-centric sunscreen, simply because the brand is dialed in to ensure its able to deliver a quality, wearable product.

“We’ve gone through this with [Dieux’s] SkinMercy, which is an OTC colloidal oatmeal cream, but for sunscreen, the stability of your sunscreen is so fucking important,” she says. “If my sunscreen separates or if it’s not at that stated SPF 50, if that degrades at all with broad spectrum protection, I would be mortified.”

Palerimo cites brands like Korea’s Beauty of Joseon, which is more popular in the US than in its home country, as evidence that Americans have long been on the hunt for better sunscreen. And though BEMT is a step forward, we still have a way to go. Board-certified dermatologist Jane Yoo has been lobbying Congress to get new sunscreen filters approved for the US and is tracking the FDA’s progress in making those approvals. Currently there are seven other filters—bisoctrizole, drometrizole trisiloxane, octyl triazone, amiloxate, diethylhexyl butamido triazone iscotrizinol, ecamsule, and enzacamene—under the agency’s Time and Extent Application (TEA) pipeline. Those filters are part of the 2014 Sunscreen Innovation Act meant to speed up the process of determining if ingredients are Generally Recognized as Safe and Effective, or GRASE. But here we are 12 years later, and we’re still waiting for their approval.

“A good analogy is we’ve been making sunscreens with both of our hands tied behind our backs,” Palermino says. “We’ve now had one hand released. I would like both hands released.”

#6716. Emmy Kasbit Lagos Spring 2027

Crowds of men and women gathered outside wearing their best Emmy Kasbit looks. The brand has amassed a cult-like following over the years and its signature akwete, a traditional Nigerian fabric, is hard to miss.

For spring 2027, founder and creative director Emmanuel Okoro, Emmy Kasbit found inspiration in an Indonesian designer with whom he worked earlier this year, drawing similarities between Akwete women and the Javanese women of Indonesia. “We’re very particular about culture and its preservation,” he said, adding that the two cultures might be very different on the surface, but are united in perseverance, community, and heritage. The overlaps motivated the collection’s blending of traditional Nigerian handwoven textiles and Asian silhouettes. Lightweight trousers inspired by a sarong and a poncho made out of two different types of akwete exemplified this fusion.

“It’s a fresh start for Emmy Kasbit,” he said. Indeed, it was the first season since the brand’s start 13 years ago that Okoro did not design with matching sets in mind. While the uniformity has historically performed well with his customers, he wanted to try something new. “The client doesn’t have to take the look as they see it on the runway if they don’t want to. They can take [individual] pieces.” Highlights included a white silk fringed dress and orange fringed blazer, as well as green tailored suits.

#6715. Lisa Folawiyo Lagos Spring 2027

The Lagos fashion crowd loves to be entertained. Throughout the week, designers have found interesting ways to showcase their collections, from celebrities walking the runway to live dance performances. Closing out the program this season was the star Nigerian designer Lisa Folawiyo, who returned to the schedule after several years away (she last showed on schedule in 2019). To mark the occasion, she invited guests for a candle-lit dinner and a unique fashion show experience at White Space, a gallery-turned-creative studio.

Mirrored tables filled the room, each decorated with handwoven flowers, which brought a welcome touch of craft to the proceedings. Shortly after the first course, the lights dimmed, orchestral pop music queued up, and a handful of models wearing Folawiyo’s latest collection walked down the makeshift runway; this pattern repeated over three additional courses. Standout looks included a fully beaded patchwork dress with feather detailing, a black embellished lace dress, and a raffia zebra set.

The collection, titled After Rain, was designed with Africa’s tropical countries, which do not experience the four seasons, in mind. For years, many local designers have tried to fit into the seasonal calendar that brands adhere to in the West. This collection was a rebuttal to that system. Nigeria typically has only two seasons: one rainy and one not. “The main objective was to coin our season,” she said during an interview in her studio, where artisans were hand-beading the new collection. “Everything after the rain is color, sunshine, and that’s really who we are as a brand.”

The collection marked Folawiyo’s first foray into animal prints (snake, leopard, and zebra prints all featured). At first glance, several pieces looked like knitwear. A closer inspection revealed that they were made from strands of raffia dyed and intricately woven together. After some 20 years in business, Folawiyo once again reminded us of her creative prowess.

#6713. Beyoncé Shares a Rare Look at Blue Ivy Carter’s Casual Style in a New Family Photo

Earlier this month, Blue Ivy Carter joined her father, Jay-Z, during night one of his Jay-Z 30 Tour in Los Angeles, playing piano for “The Story of O.J.” and “Dead Presidents.” While the 14-year-old didn’t take the stage for night two, she was still at the show, supporting him.

Beyoncé recently posted personal family photos of the night on her site, including a shot of Blue with her and her mother, Tina Knowles. Blue is dressed casually, wearing a striped jersey with shorts and tan boots. Beyoncé, meanwhile, opted for a LaPointe look from the brand’s spring/summer 2027 collection.

Last week, Beyoncé also posted photos from night one of Jay-Z’s Los Angeles tour stop on her site, where she included another shot of Blue with her and Knowles. The three women held hands backstage.

Blue is eager to perform, her dad told GQ back in March. He reflected on her musical talent, saying, “Blue is a crazy pianist, but she won’t let us get her a teacher. She doesn’t want it to be a job. But she has perfect pitch. If she hears a song, she’ll be like ‘Play it again’ and then she’ll teach herself. That’s just talent, she doesn’t work at that. She worked at this [being a dancer on Beyoncé’s tours], and it makes me proud that she fought for something that she really wanted to do. I don’t think we’re going to be able to get her off that stage now.”

Beyoncé also spoke about her eldest daughter’s interest in performing during her 2024 GQ interview. “Blue is an artist,” she began. “She has great taste in music and fashion. She is a fantastic editor, painter, and actress. She has been creating characters since she was 3. She’s a natural, but I did not want Blue onstage [dancing during my tours]. Blue wanted it for herself. She took it seriously and she earned it. And most importantly, she had fun! We all watched her grow more and more every night before our eyes.”

#6712. 30 Gifts for Dads Who Swear They Don't Want Anything 2026

Your old man is funny about gifts, ain't he? That guy will wear the same jacket for 20 years, spend a small fortune on something you've never heard of, and insist he doesn't need a thing. More often than not, finding the best gifts for dads involves putting your thinking cap on to mentally trawl through all of the very practical things they already own, along with the stuff that they’d just never use. Fortunately, we've got a few good dads on the GQ staff. Opinionated dads. Handsome dads. Great dads. And they've actually got some ideas.

Still no dice? We'd suggest perusing the rest of our gift guides and signing up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas worth your money.

Simple, generously proportioned, and blessed with a great collar, this checked shirt from Japanese label Frizmworks gets all the little things right. And the price? Legendary.

It's a good idea to pay closer attention to what's been happening at Filson lately. The brand's been digging into its archives and finding fresh ways to offer up its outdoorsmen roots, as evidenced by this Tacoma jacket, an old-school silhouette recast in a handsome denim.

There's a reason a Burberry check scarf costs what it does. The pattern is destined to outlast every passing trend and come back into fashion again and again. And the cashmere? Every bit as luxurious as he'd hope.

A Shaggy Dog for the shaggy ol' dog, y'know. J.Press's sweater is the real deal, made from Shetland wool that's hand-brushed to achieve its signature fuzzy texture. And yes, it's still made in Scotland, where the wool comes from. Tradition is tradition.

There's always a good reason for another pair of work boots, so why not make 'em Western? These meet the safety standards for commercial construction but look handsome as hell doing it.

I love this genre of slipper, the travel kind that zips into its own little case. And these from Luca come at an incredible price, with a perfectly shaped toe box and rubber soles that make them handsome enough to wear out.

Of all the tech you could get him this year, a portable cassette player is probably the last thing he'd expect. This one comes from the nostalgia peddlers at Retrospekt. And if he doesn't appreciate the format, he'll at least appreciate the transparent casing that puts the inner circuitry on display.

Five generations in, JBL still hasn't found a reason to make the Go any bigger. And why would it? The pint-sized speaker continues to deliver outsized sound, with the latest iteration adding 10 hours of battery life and USB-C wired audio support. Still the one to beat in its size class.

Nocs Provisions is the first name in cool binoculars, and now it's got a lo-fi digital camera to match. It's a fun little shooter in its own right, but I love that you can take photos straight through a pair of binoculars or a monocular.

String 'em up or stake 'em in the ground—BioLite's solar-powered site lights make illuminating a campsite (or a backyard, balcony, or any outdoor area) a cinch. If he's a camper, he'll be a happy one.

Twelve South is known for its AirFly Bluetooth dongle for flights, and now it's coming for your car. The new AirFly Drive is a clever little device that does away with the cords, letting him connect to Apple CarPlay or Android Auto wirelessly.

I've reached the point where I trust Anker with just about anything that plugs into a wall. This nifty universal charger uses GaN technology to power up to four devices at once, with interchangeable plugs for the US, UK, and EU. Australia, regrettably, remains off the itinerary.

I'm of the mind that you can't have too many fragrances, and of the three versions of Bleu de Chanel, the original EDT is the one I recommend most. It's the brightest and most citrus-forward of the lot, before settling into something warmer and woodier.

Byredo's new body mists offer a more casual way to wear scent, with a lighter touch and a shorter lifespan than your typical cologne. Mojave Ghost leans the most masculine to my nose, though there's nothing gendered about smelling good.

What a great form factor for a shaver. Panasonic's ARC5 Palm packs five Japanese stainless-steel blades and the power of a full-size electric razor into a handsome little device that fit in the palm of his hand.

A hangnail is a small indignity, but an indignity nonetheless, especially when you're a thousand miles from home. German grooming specialists Mühle have been at it since 1945, and this handsome travel manicure set comes equipped with a nail clipper, scissors, tweezers, and file.

Vermont-based Ursa Major comes up a lot in our grooming coverage, and that's no accident. This set brings together a few of our favorites, including its vitamin C serum, night cream, and face wash. A very solid skincare routine, all in one box.

This beef tallow balm from Sky High Farm, the upstate New York agricultural project with a fashion-world following, is as good as anything for soothing and restoring dry skin.

ICYMI: Menswear's patron saint Todd Snyder linked up with West Elm for a stirring collection of homewares this past year, and the hands-down standout is this walnut valet chair. A handsome place to hang tomorrow's outfit—or yesterday's, if we're being realistic.

No man in his right mind would turn down a pair of L.L.Bean's Wicked Goods, which is practically its own category of slipper. Sometimes the obvious choice is the right one.

I've been meaning to take up sewing for years, but my excuse has always been a lack of space. Then I spotted this mini sewing machine at the MoMA Design Store, and suddenly that excuse isn't so convincing.

It's always better when you make it yourself, and that's certainly true of shibori. This beginner-friendly kit comes with bandanas, tenugui cloths, indigo dye, rubber gloves, and easy-to-follow instructions. Might as well throw a few white tees into the mix while he's at it.

Now that's one helluva coffee mug. Made from stainless steel with double-wall construction to keep it cool to the touch, this industrial number from Copenhagen-based design studio Service Projects comes with a generously proportioned saucer that does double duty as a serving tray.

Before there was John Wilson, there was Phaidon's photographic ode to the world's most ubiquitous building material. Give him a nudge and a wink and tell him it's a “solid” gift. He'll appreciate that.

He should absolutely wear these sunnies from Satisfy and Oakley while running. But does he have to? Not in the slightest.

You might think running requires little more than a pair of sneakers, but you'd be surprised. This vest from Lululemon has pockets aplenty for all the little things he needs to bring along, without weighing him down.

It wouldn't be the holidays without a little tension. Therabody's new massage gun is made for the face, combining gentle percussion with heat to help relieve tightness around the jaw, temples, and cheeks.

A few minutes of cold therapy can work wonders on a puffy, sleep-deprived face. Quiet Hours' facial ice roller makes the ritual dead simple: chill it, roll it across the skin, and let the cold do its thing.

Electrolytes have gotten awfully sophisticated lately. Freaks of Nature's zero-sugar powder goes beyond hydration, with a formula designed to support gut health and the skin barrier, too.

Google's new Fitbit Edge splits the difference between its screenless fitness bands and full-fledged smartwatches, adding a bright OLED display to a slim, handsome tracker. There's built-in GPS, heart-rate and sleep tracking, and up to seven days of battery life.

#6710. Want to Take Your Voting Plan from Drab to Fab? Tack On A Little Treat

I’ll be the first to say that voting in American elections is both an increasingly urgent civic duty and, let’s face it, a bit of a drag sometimes. Still, I haven’t missed my chance to vote since I turned 18 (no small feat for a chronic procrastinator with ADHD). My secret? Tacking on something more fun—an embarrassingly over-sweetened seasonal latte at my college coffee shop in Ohio, a mani-pedi at my favorite queer salon in Austin, a shopping trip at Wasteland in Los Angeles—to help get me out the door.

My plan for this year’s midterms has been set in stone for weeks. First, I’ll cast my ballot at the Los Angeles LGBT Center—a wonderful community resource for harm-reduction supplies like Narcan and test strips, as well as theater and breakfast burritos. Then I’ll take the bus to LACMA to check out the new David Geffen Galleries and repair to my favorite Ethiopian spot afterward for injera and a glass of tej.

Would I vote in the midterms even if I couldn’t do anything cute after? Of course. But given the overall grimness of the current political climate, I’m snatching pockets of joy where I can—especially if they’re accessible by public transit.

As it turns out, I’m not the only one attaching a little side quest to my voting plan. Sophie, 35, threw a voting party so that she and her friends could fill out their Oregon mail-in ballots together, with her husband dishing out homemade curry and, she says, making “a silly PowerPoint about different issues on the ballot.” Hannah, 39, is going to bring her young child to her polling place and possibly host a party of her own.

For Nina, 26, voting in person has always been “a task I sometimes come close to forgetting, even though I desperately care about our country’s political future.” So she’s resolved to take advantage of the fact that her New York polling place is near Tiny Doll House—arguably the city’s best miniatures store—and buy herself the mini chaise lounge she’s been eyeing after she casts her vote. James, 19, who is voting in New York’s midterm elections for the very first time this year, wants to mark the occasion with a showing of Wicker at Cobble Hill Cinemas, followed by dinner at Sam’s Italian Cuisine on Court Street.

Given the ongoing issue of low voter turnout in key states, I think we could stand to make voting a little more engaging—and thanks to my long-held “vote + something fun” ritual, I now associate that privilege with the quick dopamine hit of little-treat culture. Sure, it would be great if all Americans were champing at the bit to exercise their voting rights, reward or not—but if getting your favorite sandwich before you cast your ballot or seeing a movie afterward gets you to the polls …why not?

#6709. 11 Best Men's Dress Shirts 2026, According to GQ Editors

Even if your closet is ninety percent fleece, the best men's dress shirts are non-negotiables. At some point, you’ll face an occasion that requires one—a laid-back wedding, a high-stakes job interview, a weirdly formal middle-school piano recital. But the right dress shirt won’t just save you in a pinch or help you sneak past upper management at your new corporate gig. (Especially if said corporate gig is working at GQ.)

Because the superlative versions of the style aren’t simply dress shirts—or, at least, not exclusively dress shirts. Buy one equipped with the right fit, details, and fabrics, and even the most formal of the bunch can kick it in less stuffy environments without eliciting snickers. We’re on-the-record fans of throwing one on with a groovy tie and crisp trousers, but toss a dress shirt over a graphic tee and baggy shorts, and suddenly, your otherwise schlubby fit looks exponentially more considered—and exponentially more stylish.

For starters, polos aren’t dress shirts just because they have a collar. We know, we know—finding the line between casual shirts and formal shirts is hard. Then there’s fabric, little details like cuffs, plackets, and color. And on top of all that, “the perfect fit” is so subjective. Take a deetp breath. We’ve got you. We’ve done the dirty work, buttoned more buttons than we thought was possible, aggregated a heap of our favorites, and wore ‘em every which way possible to determine, once and for all, the absolute best dress shirts for men.

We’ve wholeheartedly recommended J.Crew’s Bowery dress shirts for a long time. But it was up until just recently that the revered preppy label quietly released a new button-up that we had to do some internal reckoning. The Slim Portuguese cotton Oxford dress shirt doesn’t enjoy the distinction of being named after a New York City street (e.g. the Ludlow suit, or the 770 jeans). But don’t let the straight-forward, flavorless nomenclature fool you. Let’s start with the obvious: the fabric. It’s an all-cotton Oxford cloth woven exclusively for J.Crew by the respected Portuguese mill, Solemos. It’s smooth and luxurious with an elegant drape. Plus, the thicker yarns of an Oxford cloth makes it versatile enough for less formal occasions when you want to wear it with a pair of jeans, untucked, even.

It gets better from there. The shirt is a tastefully trimmed down to a silhouette that’s not skin-tight nor 2010s #menswear slim, but svelte enough to look clean without a blazer. But the real star of the show is that 10-out-of-10 collar. Most of J.Crew’s shirts are designed with wimpier collars that are likely, for better or worse, a product of those aforementioned #menswear times. This newcomer, however, extends it enough to a more classic size that bridges the blazer-collar gap so it sits neatly below a jacket lapel. That larger collar means it’s more proportional when paired with a tie.

We’re not a part of J.Crew’s internal meetings, but if anyone there is reading this, we think this needs to be expanded into more fabrics, colorways, and silhouettes—perhaps, it should even be dubbed with a new name.

If it comes as any surprise that Uniqlo sells one of the best bang-for-your-buck dress shirts on the market, you’re likely new to GQ Recommends—and the Japanese retailer’s assortment of eminently affordable men’s clothing staples. Unlike its Calvin Klein counterpart, Uniqlo’s riff on the genre isn’t available with the added benefit of Prime shipping, but what you get instead is a dress shirt that’s worth exponentially more than what you pay for.

You might only go to Uniqlo for the basics—tees, underwear, socks, maybe a hoodie. So I'd understand if you thought dress shirts were too refined a category for Uniqlo to be any good. But every I time I encounter a dress shirt from the Japanese retailer, I'm reminded of just how surprisingly solid its fits and construction are. Unlike most of its price-conscious competition, Uniqlo’s dress shirt is made from 100% long-staple cotton with absolutely zero stretch involved. While you might think of a little elastane as a good thing, generally speaking, it tends to mean that corners were cut. Plus, if a dress shirt fits well, you won't need any stretch.

The fabric is treated for wrinkle resistance, which is great if you're the kind of guy who has a “clothes chair”. But there's a funny sort of sheen that comes with wrinkle-resistant shirts that can be off-putting. That said, the details redeem it completely: no sloppy stitching, exposed seams, or wimpy collars here. Perhaps most crucially, the slim fit isn’t so svelte that you’ll look like you got dressed in 2010.

Both our overall pick and budget pick are solid options no matter your budget or snobbery. But if you're ready to graduate or just feeling like skipping ahead to the finer things, Todd Snyder's line of in-house shirting is where we'd point you. A great dress shirt starts with great fabric and Mr. Snyder's collection is full of top-notch poplins, twills, and broadcloths sourced from Thomas Mason, a revered mill that's been around since 1796 and have been the go-to for grail shirtmakers like Turnbull & Asser, not to mention the Royal family.

In the hands of American menswear nobility, the fabrics are given that distinct yet trend-averse Todd Snyder flavor. It's cut with a tastefully slim silhouette that's not Slimane-skinny, but not what your dad thinks of as skinny, either. The back features comfy side pleats, which are sewn into a split yoke (a fairly uncommon, but appreciated detail for the menswear nerds). Fine stitching and single-needle construction throughout, the shirt is built with a ton of delectable details for stylishly discerning, but what we love most is the extended collar. It's a detail that feels refreshing but also recalls shirts from the 1930s, arguably a golden age for tailoring in the States.

This beauty will run you a bit over $200, which ain't nothing. But that's a resonable sum compared to the heritage shirtmakers whose reputations have been built on shirting alone. Often, their shirts can cost you as much as your car's mortgage. That said, Todd Snyder's will get you like, 90% of the way there for a third of the price.

Got a last-minute invite to a swanky event and need a dress shirt ASAP? Not to fear, Amazon is here (and there, and pretty much everywhere). Calvin Klein’s no-frills slim fit shirt is cut from high-quality cotton that’s just a tad more stretchy than our overall pick, and comes equipped with plenty of next-gen specs its counterparts eschew—including moisture-wicking properties to keep you cool and a non-iron coating to keep it looking crisp. (You’re short on time, right?) Mercifully, the added spandex offers a little give without making the shirt look too shiny.

Throw it over your finest chinos or the dress pants you impulsively splurged on or wear it with jeans on a relaxed Friday in the office. Even if you bought it at the eleventh hour, it won’t take long for it to supplant the pricier competition.

When you’re rolling with the movers and shakers of the world, you need a dress shirt that can keep up. And that’s exactly what the vaunted Parisian chemise-makers at Charvet specialize in, to the delight of royalty both literal (countless French kings) and cultural (Sofia Coppola is a well-known fan). This breezy cotton number is no exception: It’s cut on the looser side and features an extremely classy double cuff for when you're ready to break out the cufflinks you inherited from your old man. Even with the tres formale flourishes, though, we wouldn't shy away from rocking it in a more casual context. When you slip on this sucker, you don’t need to meet with the boss—you are the boss.

“Charvet does not fuck around,” Grossman says bluntly. There’s no shortage of reasons why it remains the first name in old-world dress shirts—and its centuries of pedigree barely cracks the top five. Sure, the brand has outfitted kings, presidents, and titans of industry in equal number, but its core value proposition comes down to one exceedingly simple principle: uncompromising quality. Every dress shirt is still made by hand in Charvet’s wood-paneled Parisian townhouse, which is worth the cost of a flight to visit, Grossman notes.

If you’re not quite ready to drop half a grand on a dress shirt your grandkids will fight over, he also recommends a more wallet-friendly hack: These days, Charvet’s shirts are all over the vintage market, and “you can reliably score one for a lot less than retail”.

Proper Cloth’s been an open secret to menswear heads for years thanks to its surprisingly granular made-to-order service which offers a wide range of custom options from fabric to design details to sizing. Beyond the near-bespoke service, Proper Cloth’s quality will turn the heads of the keen-eyed tailoring nerds. 80s two-ply pinpoint fabric made from American Supima cotton, split yoke construction, and a handsome semi spread collar all come together for one of the best dress shirts you can get for the price.

One of the most compelling arguments we’ve seen in favor of dressing up right now comes straight from Paris, where Husbands outfits its worldly clientele in exquisite dress shirts exactly like this, a masterclass in retro ‘70s swagger so good it clinched a spot in GQ’s inaugural All-Stars class. It looks rad unbuttoned to the navel, and even groovier with a hefty foulard tie.

One of the best things about a cutaway collar? It gives you more room for a declaratively large tie knot.

The J.Crew pick up top is incredible. But it's slim. This Ludlow dress shirt has all the same reliability, but is also cut to a fuller shape.

Given the brand’s stellar reputation in the tailoring place, it shouldn’t come as a shock that Sid Mashburn hawks a grip of bang-up dress shirts, too. This bengal stripe number is a tried-and-true riff on a traditional office-ready pattern, but the spread collar and Goldilocks cut imbue it with Mahsburn’s signature Southern charm—and yank it firmly into 2025.

While this nicely-priced shirt does also come in white, it's also a good reminder that dress shirts can still have some edge, too.

As with any garment, “good” is subjective—but as a general rule of thumb, it comes down to three crucial factors: fabric, construction, and fit. Men’s dress shirts are no different. Michael Hill, Creative Director of Drake’s says, “Versatility is important. Customers need to understand fabric and context. For instance, Oxford cotton is going to be more versatile than poplin, which is typically a bit more formal.” The fabric will help dictate the occasion (or the other way around?). There are so many at your disposal from herringbone to end-on-end to pinpoint, not to mention stripes to plaids. So if you’re not sure, ask the sales staff.

Hill also emphasizes that fit is essential to a good dress shirt and to pay attention to the details like “The way the collar sits on your neck and against the body of the shirt. Does it stay tucked in throughout the day? How do the cuffs sit against the wrist?”

He goes on to give this absolute, “Great dress shirts are never made from synthetic or stretch fabrics.” The majority of good dress shirts eschew synthetic materials in favor of natural long-staple cotton, woven tightly for extra durability. Cotton, of course, is not a prerequisite—but almost every single great dress shirt we’ve swaddled our torsos in has been made from some riff on the fabric, from poplin to pinpoint Oxford cloth.

Other reliable indicators of quality shirts? Telltale details like French or felled seams, which are sleeker and more durable; mother of pearl buttons; and a denser or finer stitch count, usually commensurate with the amount of craftsmanship involved. Seph Skerritt, CEO of Proper Cloth also notes to look out for less common details like reinforced shirt tail gussets, a split yoke, tight and straight stitching, and emphasizes the importance of buttons. “Are the buttons shanked so they won’t come loose? Are the buttons a durable enough material that can withstand your cleaners repeatedly?” These small details reveal whether a shirtmaker is paying close attention.

One unique difference between dress shirts and other garments comes down to the collar. Skerritt says the collar “often has the largest impact on how the shirt makes you look.” That’s because it frames your face and interacts with directly with your suit jacket and its lapels—no small job for a garment. While Skerritt advises to look for fusing (the way that the collar is attached or glued to its interlining) that’s crisp, and a collar that stands up well around the neck, ultimately it “should look natural and effortless. The end result should be [that] you like how it makes you feel in the way that you like to dress.”

As any menswear wonk will tell you, dress shirts boast no shortage of nuances. So in the name of brevity (and general wonk-avoidance), we compiled a handy-dandy glossary to the terms you’ll encounter most often. As a rule of thumb, the less adornment a dress shirt has, the more formal it is.

Like all of menswear, collars are susceptible to the whims of the trend cycle, swelling and shrinking with any given era’s silhouettes du jour. Collar sizes are prone to change, too (see: the massive collars of the power-suited ‘80s; the ultra-shrunken collars of the indie-sleaze 2010s). These are the three you should know.

Cuffs are the small pieces of additional fabric at the end of the shirt sleeve; they're often constructed with stiffer linings to give them structure and thoroughly cover your wrists. These are the two you should know.

Plackets are the strip of fabric that runs down the front of the shirt, designed to be fastened with buttons, snaps, or zippers. (When it comes to dress shirts, you’ll almost always encounter the former.) These are the three you should know.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)
