#6708. How to Choose a Graphic Print Bag That Won’t Go Out of Style

Exploring the power of pattern through the lens of Dior’s Cigale.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

A printed accessory can bring color, dimension, and personality to an outfit without requiring much else. The key is finding a design that works with the clothes you already own, suits your daily needs, and feels relevant beyond a single season. Dior offers an interesting case study, particularly when it comes to houndstooth, a motif closely associated with the house’s history and Christian Dior’s use of menswear-inspired fabrics in women’s fashion. The Dior Cigale bag, Mini Lady Dior Bag, and Bow bag give us a starting point for exploring the appeal of graphic prints and what makes a patterned accessory a worthwhile long-term purchase.

A graphic print should have enough character to stand out, but it should also work with the clothes you already wear. Houndstooth has a strong geometric pattern that can look just as good with denim as it does with formal, more tailored styles. If you prefer something more playful, a colorful or embellished design can make a familiar outfit feel different.

The bag’s shape and construction matter, too. Consider its size, how you plan to carry it, and whether the materials suit your lifestyle. A bag you intend to use regularly should be practical enough for your routine, with craftsmanship that holds up to frequent wear. The Cigale, for example, has a sculptural silhouette inspired by the architectural lines of a 1952 Christian Dior gown. That connection to couture gives the design a distinct identity, while its silhouette offers something to consider beyond the print alone.

A graphic print bag can work with a range of outfits, particularly when its colors complement the rest of your wardrobe. A black-and-white houndstooth pattern, for instance, pairs naturally with neutral knitwear and sharp separates. More colorful prints can coordinate just as well, provided you give them room to stand out.

The simplest approach is to keep the rest of your outfit relatively restrained. A printed bag can add interest to a white shirt and trousers or break up an all-black look without requiring a complete wardrobe overhaul. If you prefer a more coordinated outfit, pick up one of the bag’s colors in your shoes or another accessory. You don’t need to match everything. Just a little repetition is enough to make the look feel deliberate.

No accessory is immune to changing tastes, but some patterns have been around longer than others. Houndstooth, for one, predates Dior, but the designer incorporated it into his collections alongside other fabrics traditionally associated with menswear. He used these materials in women’s suits and dresses, pairing their masculine character with silhouettes that emphasized the female form. The brand continues to revisit houndstooth, including on the Cigale bag.

If you’re buying a graphic print bag to carry for years, think about whether you’ll wear it with more than one or two outfits. A pattern that works with your everyday wardrobe will get more use than one that calls for a specific look. It’s also worth considering whether you like the bag’s shape on its own. Trends come and go, but a bag you enjoy carrying for reasons beyond its print has a better chance of staying in rotation.

Start with the clothes you already wear. A graphic print bag can add interest to everyday staples like straight-leg jeans, a simple knit, and loafers, or bring some personality to office staples like tailored trousers and a crisp shirt. For dinner, try one with a black dress or a streamlined suit. The idea is to let the print add something to your outfit without making getting dressed more complicated.

You can mix prints, too. A fine stripe or small check can work with a bolder graphic, especially when the colors complement each other. If the combination feels too busy, simplify the rest of the look. With the Cigale, clean lines and structured tailoring can play off its sculptural shape. And remember, the bag doesn’t need much competition. A few well-chosen pieces will let it stand out without overwhelming the outfit.

A graphic print can draw you to a bag, but the details are what make it worth the investment. Look closely at the stitching, hardware, lining, and finish. The materials should feel appropriate for the price, and the construction should hold up to regular use. Consider how the print is worked into the design, too. The pattern should feel like part of the bag, not an afterthought.

With Dior, the appeal also lies in how the house approaches familiar motifs. Its graphic patterns are part of a broader design vocabulary, reinterpreted through changing silhouettes, materials, and embellishments. That gives the Cigale context beyond its appearance alone. Ultimately, a bag’s value comes down to what it offers in design and execution, not just the name on the label.

#6707. Designer Susan Alexandra Made Her Dream Butter Yellow Gown for Her Wedding at a Historic French Villa

Susan Alexandra Korn and Andy Nahman officially met in March 2023 at writer Naomi Fry’s birthday party in Brooklyn. But as it happens, Susan actually caught Andy’s eye more than a year earlier, when he attended the October 2021 opening of her Lower East Side store featuring her namesake jewelry and accessories.

“I walked into this magical polychromatic dream world, well over capacity, with her family, friends, colleagues, and collaborators,” says Andy, who was invited to the party by his sister, writer and editor Haley Nahman. “Susan’s energy was palpable, not only because it was like standing inside her mind’s eye, but in the community surrounding her. I remember going home feeling in awe of her magnetic energy and vision.” But it was at that birthday party, held at artist Al Freeman’s home, where they really “clicked,” says Susan.

Andy proposed to Susan in September 2025, on a trip to the South of France. He had a plan: “Take a short drive from our hotel to the Matisse chapel, surprise Susan with my proposal, and subsequently toast to our future with some bubbles,” says Andy, who is a VP of data science at Disney. But when they arrived at the chapel, it was closed—and the fluted glasses had broken in the car trunk. “Andy improvised quickly,” Susan says, “and proposed on the curb outside of the chapel as a few people looked on quizzically from a bus stop.”

The mishap only made it all the more special. “I think we will equally remember my kneeling proposal alongside the scene in the trunk: exploded flowers, broken flutes, and rapidly melting ice. Luckily, the bottle was still intact and we opened it,” Andy says.

Susan and Andy were married on August 29 at Villa Magnan in Biarritz, France. They chose the historic venue because, as Susan says, “it’s dripping with rustic charm and special touches. Hector the Donkey ambling around the lawn while two elder dogs lazily bark from their sun spots. It’s beautiful and old but very inviting.”

From the beginning, when envisioning the celebration, Susan—who is known for her candy-colored creations—zeroed in on the floral design. “I am obsessive about flowers and about only using flowers in season,” she says. She envisioned a “cake of flowers”—a living sculpture of sorts. The family who owns the villa pulled it off, along with a flower-covered chuppah for the ceremony. In addition to the villa’s in-house team, Susan and Andy worked with event producers Mathilde and Ann Charlotte of Sauce to bring it all together.

Festivities began on Friday, when they had their guests board a “petit train to a secret location,” says Susan. “The train zigzagged through Biarritz and dropped us at the lighthouse. We drank Champagne as the sun dipped into the ocean.” From there, they took buses to the nearby town of Saint-Jean-de-Luz, where they rented out a restaurant called Denen Kanttua for a welcome dinner of classic Basque cuisine: pâté, eggs with roe, tuna crudo, mussels, financiers, and lots of wine.

The cherry on top? “We commissioned a local artisan to sculpt our Chihuahua, Pigeon, out of French salted butter,” Susan says. “He was delicious, served with radishes and hunks of bread.”

For the Friday night event, Susan wore a nude tulle and paillette-embellished dress by Jenny Packham, sourced from Vinted. “Everyone asked if I designed the dress because it was so quintessentially me,” Susan says. She paired it with vintage Beverly Feldman Lucite heels. Andy wore a natural linen suit and shirt from Stoffa and chocolate suede loafers from Morjas.

As a designer, Susan always knew she would make her own wedding dress. She worked with her director of production to bring it to life. “Over the course of six months, Melissa and I worked with a patternmaker, a couturier, and master of embellishments to create ‘The Dress’ and the after-party gown.”

For her ceremony, Susan designed a gown made of a soft butter yellow duchesse satin. “The silhouette was based on a gown from the 1930s. We gussied up the dress with rhinestone flowers and cherubs holding roses. The cherubs represented Andy and me, and the roses represented our ever-growing love,” she says. She accessorized with a pair of Art Deco–inspired pearl drop and enamel pansy earrings of her own design, a borrowed diamond tennis necklace, and golden Manolo Blahnik kitten heels from The Real Real. She also carried a floral sequined purse with her and Andy’s names embroidered in pink on the inside.

Andy wore a custom suit from Saman Amel in a deep earthy brown with a RRL shirt and a vintage Hermès tie emblazoned with tiny carrots and radishes that Susan gave him for his birthday, plus loafers from Our Legacy. Susan’s after-party dress was custom-made by the artisans who make Susan Alexandra jewelry and bags. It was “a sequined manifestation of the future I want,” Susan says. “It featured a house surrounded by an abundant garden and Pigeon embroidered on the tush.”

Alison Roman, who is a close friend of the couple, officiated the ceremony. They walked down the villa staircase to a gentle live piano rendition of “Avril 14th” by Aphex Twin. “The incredible power that is Alison Roman married us under the chuppah,” Susan says. “She read a heartfelt speech about observing Andy and me in our natural states, coexisting in harmony, holding different parts of the coin of life. Alison said that in marriage, the colors grow deeper and richer with time. It was so tender and so loving. It is a special person who can officiate a wedding with such ease and grace, and she is that special person,” says Susan.

In Andy’s vows, “he promised to never let me go too long without flowers and to always fill my cup, both with coffee and love,” Susan says. “Both our vows had so much overlap, so much hope for our future and so much love. Many mentions of Pigeon were made, which made me cry,” she adds.

“I am not drawn to public speaking and had anticipated nerves around sharing our vows,” Andy adds, reflecting on the ceremony. “What I learned is that it is extremely comfortable to speak publicly when what you are saying is your truth from the heart.”

For dessert, the newlyweds decided on a “pavlova the size of a small country,” Susan shares. “Every guest grabbed a spoon, and we dug in and ate it communally, leaving plates untouched.” Susan’s sister, Janie Korn, made them a custom cake topper of miniature versions of themselves.

After dinner and dessert, the couple and their guests danced to a set by DJ Alex Chapman, followed by a special impromptu DJ set by Jason Stewart (a.k.a. Them Jeans), who was a guest at the wedding. “We danced, drank, ate sandwiches, and talked until the moon began to set,” Susan says.

We asked guests to meet at Le Grande Plage for a surprise. We boarded le petit train, which zigzagged through beautiful Biarritz.

The trolley brought us to the Biarritz Lighthouse! We sipped Champagne as the sun dipped into the sea. Magnifique!

A sweet stolen moment. I suspect we are out of body here.

We orchestrated many (delightful) twists and turns throughout the evening. Here, our guests are being ushered into buses for the next surprise.

A reenactment of the final scene of The Graduate, but less forlorn.

The joyful gaze as we jet off to our next locale!

Making our Chihuahua, Pigeon, into a demi-sel beurre sculpture was Andy’s brainchild. It was adorned with hunks of bread and radishes, and I’ve never had a more delicious dog. The mini butter cake is that same divine French butter infused with Espelette pepper, which is unique to Basque country. Created by Bonjour Gateau.

Wedding guests shmoozing outside of the restaurant Denen Kanttua. We were in a charming Basque town, Saint-Jean-de-Luz. Another person who married here: King Louis XIV.

Welcoming everyone to the wedding and sharing how surreal this moment was.

Hugging all these beautiful people from my life and Andy’s life and now…our life?

My sister, Janie (with her husband, Punit), gave a delightful toast. She declared, “If I’m going to be under anyone’s thumb in this life, I’m glad it’s Susan’s.” I’m not sure she will ever forgive me for making her speak in public.

Andy’s dad, Vance, bestowing final touches to the groom.

My friend Kim’s Nightshade bag, lounging with my veil. Spoiler: The bag did not make it back to NYC in one piece.

Doria insisted on a veil. (“When else in your life will you wear a veil?!”) So here I am, veiled.

Weddings feel like a portal to another time. As I was designing my wedding ensembles, I thought of black-and-white photos of ancestors in gilded frames. With this in mind, we created an Edwardian-style veil worn low on the head. Satin rosettes with beaded stamens secured the veil in my hair.

I spotted a dark aubergine calla lily in the bouquet and had to yank it out right before this picture was taken. It was disrupting the harmony of the other bright flowers.

The Dress was inspired by 1930s Hollywood sirens and the sun—two things I worship. I sketched floating flowers and cherubs, and the artisans re-created the drawings with rhinestones.

The veil was made from a yard of fabric I found balled up in an antiques shop in Connecticut. I asked the store owner about the origin of the fabric: “It’s 60 years old, from a now-closed boutique on Madison Avenue.” I have a shop on Madison Avenue and thought it was beshert.

Dear friends who showed up in my room as I was getting ready. I felt so loved and supported. Women are so magnificent. From left: Sarah, Rachel, Lisa, Kim, me, Sierra, Doria, and Alison. Aren’t they lovely?

A statuesque Andy, awaiting his grand entrance.

Reciting my vows, flanked by oleander bushes. I assume this is where I was telling Andy that I promise to always harmonize on improvised songs about Pigeon.

No one tells you how delightful vows are. It’s just standing and listening to someone wax poetic about you.

Our dear, special friend Alison Roman officiated the wedding. She made such a beautiful speech about how the colors of marriage deepen as time passes. She is so soulful and was with me the night Andy and I met. Here I am asking her if it’s okay if we kiss. She was like, “Do whatever you want!”

What a surreal moment. We had just left the altar and were suspended in this unbelievable moment of disbelief, joy, and love.

Andy and flowers: two things I deeply love.

Me and my new family members: Avi, Haley, Andy, Matt, Kelly, Kathy, Vance.

A sister pic! Andy and I are so lucky to have sisters. From left: Kelly, Andy, me, Haley (little Dove is in there!), and Janie.

From left: Adam, Mom, Andy, me, Rick, and Janie.

Weddings are not known for great food, and we wanted ours to be the exception. The food at our wedding was a priority. The restaurant at Villa Magnan is extraordinary; every bite was divine. This is a platter of Sucrine lettuce, smoked anchovies, raw cream, and wild herbs.

Every single touch at Villa Magnan was considered. They scattered big dahlias everywhere the eye lands.

The custom sequined bag was perfectly attuned to my gown. Our wedding dates and names are embroidered in the lining of the bag, a surprise touch from the artisan.

This greenhouse-cum-kitchen is where all of the beautiful food was made (with love).

Perfect in situ at Villa Magnan. A bundle of Espelette peppers, dried flowers from the garden, a hand-painted fruit mirror, and strings of beads.

Did we purposely align our wedding with tomato season in France? Perhaps.

My friend Lisa handmade the place cards using seashells and a healthy smattering of googly eyes. The shells were a nod to our seaside locale. Every setting was adorned with a different beaded charm: an Espelette pepper, a pigeon (for our dog), or a donkey (Hector is the resident donkey at Villa Magnan). I illustrated the menus and Andy developed a custom font.

Janie made custom ceramic vases for my wedding and, in an act of extreme love and devotion, shlepped them from London. It was no small feat. Her work made the tables majestic.

Janie’s seashell creature place card was among my favorites.

A glowing moment before the food was served.

Listening to my friend Brian give the speech of a lifetime.

Everyone said such wonderful things. It’s like, “Wow, people actually love us?” Tears were shed.

Danny’s speech was so soulful, so wise, so tender. Every woman asked for his number afterward. You see, a well-delivered wedding speech is the ultimate dating app.

My pops, David. His speech integrated all the French words he knows, c/o Pepé Le Pew, Amélie, and the Madeline books.

After dinner, Andy and I slunk back to our room, where I changed for the after-party. I made this sequined dress, which was a manifestation of our future: a cottage with a garden, flowers, and butterflies. On the back was a bedazzled Pigeon.

I did my own hair and makeup and got ready in 45 minutes. I’ve been doing my hair and makeup for 100 years, so I figured I may as well do it on this day. Looking back, I’m really impressed I was able to adhere false lashes for the first time ever on my wedding day.

Some of the favorite moments from the wedding were the short bottle episodes where Andy and I were alone together. Back in our room, drinking Champagne, the party is on the horizon.

Janie made us hand-sculpted custom cake toppers! Nothing is more special. I will cherish them forever.

Our cake toppers look on with glee and perhaps pride.

The wedding cake was sublime: Vanilla bean gateau was layered with caramelized praline paste. We scattered raspberries on top as guests cheered. The cake wore a skirt of meringue puffs and, as a final touch, a dusting of powdered sugar by Andy.

A shower of sugar as “Chapel of Love” played.

Michelle and Karolyn are two people who make every event a party.

My dear friend the illustrious Alex Chapman, DJ’d the first part of the night, followed by a special Them Jeans set. A highlight of the evening was Jason playing (the song of the summer) “Pink Blush” by Dolly Babe.

Dancing with my mama and Andy. No better feeling!

My former Chicago crew, Lisa and Alex. We became adults together and now, here we are, elder adults. Aww.

See my above note about Michelle. Steph is also joyful, glowing.

All I ever wanted for the night: color, love, joy.

#6705. Hailey Bieber’s Gold Saint Laurent Look at the CFDA Fashion Awards Is Actually Not a Dress

Hailey Bieber celebrated Halloween weekend with her husband, Justin Bieber, and their son, Jack Blues Bieber, in Los Angeles. But by Monday evening, the model had traveled across the country for the CFDA Fashion Awards. She stepped out at the New York City event in a luxurious, gilded look with a twist.

While her gold Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello ensemble seemed like a dress in photos, it is actually multiple pieces. Per the fashion house, Hailey wore a long-sleeve brocade top with animal-free fur-trimmed cuffs, a lace flower cabochon buckle belt, and an embroidered baroque midi skirt. She tied it all together with Salomé sandals in metallic leather.

It marks Hailey’s first time back at the ceremony in nine years. She attended for the first time in 2016, then again in 2017.

Hailey is fresh off her appearance at the Academy Museum Gala on October 17, where she wore a pink Chanel gown.

For Halloween, she did a flirty take on an angel costume, pairing a white feather bra with black shorts, dark sheer tights, and giant angel wings.

In February, the model spoke to ELLE about how she feels about being considered a style icon. “I think my focus has always been about the confidence and freedom to play with different looks,” she said. “Ultimately, your own style comes through when you feel good in what you’re wearing.”

Her style mood board has many references, with one ’90s supermodel standing out among the rest. “Inspiration can come from anywhere in life—photography, travel, food, music, and film can all spark something for me,” Hailey shared. “However, Kate Moss is always going to be iconic. She’s someone who truly stands the test of time and will always be a sartorial reference.”

#6704. Nobody Wants to Have a Baby Boy Anymore

It began, innocently enough, with a cake. In 2008, American blogger Jenna Karvunidis threw a party to announce the sex of her unborn baby. The reveal came when she cut a slice and found pink inside. She wrote about the experience online, the post went viral, and a new ritual was born.

Nearly 20 years later, we all know the drill. If it isn’t a cake, it’s a balloon or a cannon. Friends and family gather. Someone counts down; something explodes in blue or pink; the parents-to-be hug; a grandparent enters the frame looking thrilled and slightly confused. And, of course, there’s a camera rolling, meaning my daughter could have in theory earned her first “like” long before she drew her first breath.

For the first time in a century, nearly less than half of parents are circumcising their newborns. New dad Kevin Lincoln investigates how America’s favorite elective surgery became as debated as childhood vaccines—and considers his own decision.

The gender reveal has evolved from a modest party trick into a full-blown genre of internet spectacle, complete with its own newborn industrial complex. Private ultrasound companies now sell “gender-reveal experiences,” with rooms that glow pink or blue and teddy bears containing recordings of an unborn baby’s heartbeat. Online, the reveals have become more elaborate: smoke bombs, pyrotechnics (one of which started a wildfire in South California in 2020), choreographed dances, skydivers and, in one particularly memorable case, a Louisiana alligator called Sally biting through a blue jelly watermelon.

But the spectacle has moved on. A new kind of gender-reveal video is becoming a genre of its own, one in which a particular reaction is the main event. A recent compilation racked up 33 million views and three million likes on TikTok. Expecting couples do not scream with delight when the color appears. They scream in horror. They collapse and cry. The reason is nearly always the same: it’s blue. They’re having a boy.

What looks like internet absurdity may actually point to something much bigger. Last year, The Economist published data showing that in mostly higher-income countries, the centuries-old preference for sons is starting to reverse. And in some countries, the data shows that opinion has fully flipped: Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Portugal and the Czech Republic are showing evidence of a preference for girls.

In the US, the same trend appears among adoptive parents. According to the National Bureau of Economic Research, prospective parents were willing to pay an average $16,000 more for a girl than a boy. Among couples having IVF in the US—where, unlike the UK, sex selection is legal— leading clinics have reported that 75–80% of patients want a girl.

This is a big demographic plot twist. On one hand, it’s what progress looks like. For most of human history, boys have been the prize. They inherited the family name and property. They were expected to earn money and carry the family line into the future. Girls, in turn, were generally expected to marry out or care for relatives.

In the worst cases, the preference for sons has had lethal consequences. In China, where a one-child policy enforced by the government lasted 35 years, and in India, sex-selective abortion and the killing or abandonment of female babies has led to generations with far more boys than girls. Misogynist discrimination has been so pervasive that in 1990, the Nobel Prize–winning economist Amartya Sen estimated that more than 100 million women were “missing” from world history. (Researchers have since questioned the precise figure and methodology, but the point still stands.)

But there is another, stranger side to the reversal. You don’t have to spend long reading the 20,000-plus comments beneath a viral gender-reveal video to realize that some of this isn’t simply about girls finally being valued properly. There is a growing and increasingly open distaste for boys—a sense that they are inherently problematic, undesirable by default.

Having a son, in certain corners of modern parenthood, has become unfashionable. A curious society might ask itself why this is—and where it might lead.

Ruth Whippman is the mother of three boys. She grew up in England but now lives in America, in what she describes as a “progressive area of the country [with] very progressive school districts”. As she writes in her 2024 book, BoyMom, friends and neighbors kept saying versions of the same thing: “I hope for your sake this one is a girl.”

“We were a year into the [first] Trump presidency,” she tells me. “There were incels on the news. There was just this huge backlash against toxic masculinity. So it wasn’t even just a sense of, ‘Oh, boys, their clothes aren’t as nice; you don’t get to play Barbies.’ It was this sense that boys are actively toxic and harmful.”

My son and I were calling to each other across a great distance, a distance that I was aware might never close.

When Whippman’s first son was due, she had the standard worries about raising a child of the opposite sex. Would they have enough in common? Would she know how to navigate experiences she hadn’t had? As a lifelong feminist, she tells me, the additional sense of cultural disapproval made everything worse. “It was really horrible, because nobody likes to be pitied,” she says. “Nobody likes to think that their children are second best. But I think it played into something in me as well, if I’m totally honest. I had my own fears and feelings about [having boys], and hearing everybody else’s reaction just made it much worse.”

Nearly a decade on from #MeToo, with Donald Trump back in the White House and male chauvinism metastasizing across the internet, it’s unusual to hear the word “masculinity” without the word “toxic” prefacing it. So parents can end up feeling—even if they’re guilty about it—that having a son is more complicated than it was for previous generations.

“When you hear about boys at the moment, at best, they’re this underachieving lunk who won’t go to college, is doing badly at school and will fail to launch,” says Whippman. “And at worst, he’s deep in the manosphere, commanding his AI girlfriend to let him choke her, or whatever. It gets to this wider consumerisation of parenthood. [The idea that] girls are better consumer products, in a way—which is a terrible, terrible way to talk about human beings.”

I’d be lying if I said it hadn’t crossed my mind, when I discovered I was having a daughter, that if I could raise her to be a confident, secure, kick-ass girl, I’d win the approval of the types of circle I move in. “Girl dads” who let daughters paint their nails are the subject of endless kind TikTok videos.

Parents of boys, not so much. Whippman, who has heard more and more fathers say they would prefer daughters, recognizes the problem. “Parenting a son is almost seen as a harm reduction project, rather than anything empowering,” she says. “That’s really at odds with our modern parenting culture, which is about encouraging [our kids] to reach for the stars and be happy and access all the world has to offer.”

And like everything else in 2026, the random, happy event of your unborn child’s sex can somehow thrust you into the us-versus-them culture war. “In the States and in the UK, there’s a sense that if you are on the progressive left, you are on the side of girls and women… any time you’re defending boys and men, it has this sniff of something right-wing, or being a bad actor,” says Whippman. “That’s a really hard thing to hold as a progressive, feminist parent of a son.”

There are other theories for why parents in Western countries, in particular, are increasingly downbeat about having boys. Millennials are having fewer children than any generation in history, and we’re doing it later in life. In other words, by the time it happens, we’re already exhausted. And boys are often perceived as more work, especially when they’re little: more physical, and harder to keep occupied and under control.

Lara Miller has been a midwife for more than 20 years. She uses social media to demystify pregnancy and childbirth. She thinks there is some truth to the idea that older parents may be wary of boys. “When you see older people having babies, they tend to be more controlling about everything to do with it,” she says. “I say this without judgment—I was an older mum myself—but you become used to doing things your own way and to your own routines.”

Of course, it would be silly to assume every girl will be content quietly coloring in while every boy spends his childhood trailing dog shit through the house. But according to Alex Trippier, a kids’ club leader who runs the social media account Be A Happier Parent, there can be real differences in behavior. “You get testosterone surges around age two, which I really see with the kids that I look after in my groups,” he says. “All of a sudden the boys come in and they’re going crazy. Parents who are on the quieter side can be overwhelmed by the sheer energy. Some people insist this is all nonsense, and [boys being more boisterous] is completely socialized. I think it’s a mixture of both. You’ve got that developmental layer going on, and you’ve got all the socialization on top of it.”

Trippier, who has two boys and a girl, thinks culture has shifted. Parents have always worried about teenage girls. But now, they have a whole new list of concerns for boys: porn, gaming addiction, exam results, algorithms. “There are all these fears we have for our sons, this kind of moral anxiety about the impossibility of raising good men,” he says.

In 2024, Zach Baron documented his long journey to fatherhood via IVF in GQ. Now, he reports on the mind-altering chaos (and occasional brilliance) of life with two walking, talking young boys.

Miller, who had similar feelings when she was pregnant but is now the happy mother of two sons, thinks there’s another factor: Schools aren’t always very good at accommodating boys. “We have changed as a society and we’re not as accepting of boys,” she says. “Boys don’t tend to fit the school model. You get worse reports. [Our school] gives the boys set days to be allowed to kick a football. Well, you don’t remember that at school, do you?”

She recalls being summoned by a headmaster after her son made a gun sign with his fingers. “The girls do better at school,” she says. “They’ve read 20 books; my boys have only read two. The teacher’s gone, ‘Well, if you buy a football magazine, do you think they’d read that?’ You’re like, ‘Oh, fuck off. Just fuck off.’”

There’s something else unusual about today’s parents, beyond grappling with the manosphere and Parkrun injuries. We’re the most psychologically literate generation to have ever lived. If we haven’t done therapy ourselves, we’re at least sufficiently fluent in the language of therapy to take a stab at self-reflection (or, as Boomer parents might call it, self-absorption). We know about childhood trauma. We know about attachment styles. We know that our parents’ behavior has consequences. We know that our childhoods don’t simply disappear when we become adults. It gives us an enormous number of things to worry about.

One of the most interesting conversations I’ve had on this subject is with a colleague who is expecting a son. He’s delighted now, but initially, the prospect of having a boy unnerved him—as it did me, before I knew the sex of my baby. We both agreed this probably came from remembering difficult experiences with our own fathers, and being afraid of repeating them. For me, it may have gone a step further. The idea of having a son scared me because I had a pretty broken relationship with myself.

Dr. Chrissy Jayarajah is a psychiatrist and the author of the world’s only academic paper on “gender disappointment.” She’s quick to point out that the term is not a clinical diagnosis, but what you might call a “known phenomenon” (particularly on TikTok, where thousands of videos are tagged with it).

“Something I always say is that becoming a parent will undoubtedly make you reflect on the way that you were parented,” she says. “Whether it was a good relationship, a bad relationship, an indifferent relationship or a non-existent relationship—they all play a part. An absent father is still very present in your mind. We are more psychologically minded and reflective compared with, maybe, the generation before. But I also think we don’t know what to do with that reflection.”

This can manifest in different ways, explains Jayarajah. “Working predominantly with mothers, I would say they fall into two camps,” she says. “They either want to emulate exactly how their mother was, from recreating those childhood memories, making those family favorite meals on a Sunday, and so on. Or they’re: ‘Oh my God, I’m turning into my mother.’”

That can produce powerful feelings about your baby’s sex. “We see that with women who have experienced abuse of some kind,” says Jayarajah. “Some absolutely do not want to have a girl, because they don’t want their daughter to experience what they went through. On the other hand, I have had women who say, ‘No, I definitely want a girl. I don’t want to have a son,’ because a son [would remind] them of the perpetrator.”

The sex of your baby, in other words, can become a vessel for all sorts of fears that existed long before the baby did. Then, there’s the demographic problem. There just aren’t enough babies. A rapid collapse in birth rates and fertility is playing out across the world. In 1990, global fertility was about 3.3 children per woman. Today it is around 2.2 to 2.3. More than half the countries in the world are already below “replacement level.”

The consequences will be huge. Labor shortages. Pressure on pensions. Rising social and healthcare costs. Less of the innovation and forward momentum traditionally associated with younger populations. In that context, favoring one sex over the other seems beyond counterproductive.

Maybe we are retreating into old, narrow assumptions. “We’ve never thought about gender more as a society than we do at this present day,” says Jayarajah. “Ideas about gender are in our face all day long. There was no such thing as a gender reveal party 20 years ago, let alone putting it online. What’s happening, in my opinion, is gender essentialism. This sexist idea of what it means to be a man, what it means to be a woman, is playing out in what we expect for our children.”

The following week, I saw this in action. I took my 19-month-old daughter to a soft-play morning, where she likes to roll around on the multicolored shapes and go down the slide on my lap. A few minutes after we arrived, I heard a scream. “Aaaargh!”

At one end of the ball pit, a little boy was staring at his own reflection in a mirror. “Aaaargh!” he went again, hammering his fists against the perspex and making the entire frame shake. A few feet away, my daughter watched him quietly. I made a mental note to keep them as far apart as possible.

The boy’s parents were nearby, deep in conversation. They seemed oblivious, or perhaps simply immune, to their son’s King Kong routine. A dozen judgmental thoughts zipped through my head. Why aren’t you keeping a closer eye on him? What kind of irresponsible shit are you pulling at home for him to do this? If he harms her, I swear to God…

I took a sip of my coffee, scrolled through my phone, then turned around, ready to rescue my sweet, innocent little girl. The boy who had been screaming a moment ago was now shyly handing her a dumper truck with a missing wheel. She closed her eyes, grinned, and took it with both hands.

A version of this story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of British GQ with the title “For Centuries, Everyone Wanted Boys. Now, Not So Much”

#6702. Sinéad O'Dwyer Spring 2027 Ready-to-Wear

The body in motion has long fascinated Sinéad O’Dwyer. For spring 2027, a central piece was a shimmering sequin-covered slip dress onto which blurred photographs of bodies in the throes of performance were transposed. The photos, lensed by Ottilie Landmark, originated from Knead, a movement piece O’Dwyer developed with choreographer Grace Nicol at London’s Barbican Centre in 2025, which explored the dynamics of watching and being watched, and the desire to be seen. The influence of that dance performance could be felt throughout Notice Me, a collection concerned with how clothes cultivate, capitulate to, or coalesce with bodily brilliance.

First presented in the Victoria and Albert Museum’s Raphael Court, and subsequently captured in an intimate lookbook by Landmark, the collection traced an ongoing shift in O’Dwyer’s approach to making clothes. “There’s a lot of newness, but I suppose for me it’s in a direction of making things a bit more easy to buy and wear,” she explained. O’Dwyer’s practice is built around richly technical, body-inclusive construction; here, she refined her methods rather than relinquished them.

A dance of spectacle and practicality played out most in tailoring, a growing category for O’Dwyer. A double-breasted jacket with a masculine silhouette featured a sensual inward curve at the waist, while zippered jackets and corset tops, paired with matching trousers and hip-skimming pencil skirts, amplified the utilitarian approach. O’Dwyer developed the tailoring by padding out the back and seat of a mannequin, using that exaggerated curvature to inform the cut of jackets and shirting that retained their masculine, oversized proportions.

Meanwhile, pourable sequin dresses with sweat-like surfaces were constructed on stretch mesh, and satin-y, icy blue and green slip dresses and other fine knit gowns moved freely while retaining sculptural shapes. Sporty stretch fabrics were put to work on pale dresses and separates, with softly gathered bustlines and shapes that caressed rather than encased. The pattern cutting, O’Dwyer explained, was intended to accommodate a wider range of proportions without relying on fixed cup sizes or extensive alterations. The aforementioned zippers allow wearers to adjust fit and exposure. Micro-shorts with doubled waistbands introduced a more athletic note. Clothes with a certain toughness were offset by the delicate details of lingerie, and even sheer mesh bralettes were adorned with tiny satin buttons and long, trailing ribbons.

Those buttons were among the collection’s most labor-intensive achievements. O’Dwyer has been developing an embroidery technique in which they are chain-stitched into the garment as it is constructed, with approximately 4,000 featuring on each of two intricate long-sleeved gowns. Such pieces now belong firmly to the designer’s bespoke and made-to-order offering, rather than ready-to-wear. It is a pragmatic distinction for a house where occasionwear is becoming an increasingly important part of the business.

This was a season that built upon a new brand identity, including an updated logo, and reflected the designer’s awareness that the customers who have worn her label since its beginnings have grown up, too. The collection will be sold exclusively through her own e-commerce platform, giving O’Dwyer greater control over pricing and the pace of its release. Rather than abandoning the craftsmanship that has distinguished her work, she is finding more appropriate homes for her techniques, while making the rest of the wardrobe more accessible. O’Dwyer’s allegiance to the ever-amorphous body remains as insistent as ever, but spring 2027 suggested that accommodating its realities can be every bit as compelling as showcasing them.

#6698. The Vogue Business People Moves Tracker

Introducing the Vogue Business People Moves Tracker, a running list highlighting the key executive appointments and exits across the fashion and beauty industries. From CEOs to creative directors to other key C-suite hires, we track the leadership shifts that are reshaping the industry.

Background: Daisy Shaw-Ellis has been appointed CMO of Malone Souliers, where she will oversee the brand’s global marketing and communications, with an emphasis on expansion in North America. Shaw-Ellis joins from Condé Nast, where she was most recently accessories and jewelry director for Vogue and Vanity Fair.

Company comments: “We are delighted to welcome Daisy to Malone Souliers as global chief marketing officer,” CEO Andrew Wright said in a statement. “Her experience in executive positions at some of the industry’s most established and influential titles, alongside her exceptional eye and proven track record in luxury brand-building, will both enhance and amplify our voice globally. This is a pivotal moment for Malone Souliers as we embark on a new and exciting trajectory, and we look forward to presenting the brand in new and exciting ways in the coming seasons.”

Background: Clarisse Godbillon, who was CFO and COO of Lemaire from 2020 to 2025, is returning to the brand as managing director. She left Lemaire in 2025 to become COO of Jacquemus, and made the move back to the French label after Laetitia Mergui stepped down from the head job earlier this year.

Company comments: “Clarisse possesses an in-depth understanding of the company’s various activities and a profound knowledge of its identity,” the house said in a statement. “As managing director, she will oversee the development of the brand and lead its strategic and operational direction, working closely with [the house’s artistic directors and majority shareholders] Christophe Lemaire and Sarah-linh Tran.”

Background: Lady Gaga has moved into the CEO role at Haus Labs, the clean beauty company she founded in 2019. This comes after co-founder and former CEO Ben Jones exited the brand in early October. Gaga will now lead all commercial aspects of Haus Labs, alongside her prior responsibilities of creative direction and product development.

Background: Ryan Lally has been promoted to chief brand communications officer at Ralph Lauren Corp. Formerly SVP of global public relations and brand communications, Lally will continue to build on the company’s global comms strategy in this newly created role, while overseeing talent partnerships, events and more. Lally has been with the company for more than two decades, and will continue to report to David Lauren, chief branding and innovation officer.

Background: Alexis Hoopes, formerly global fashion VP at Ebay, has joined The RealReal as chief merchandising officer. At Ebay, she led the company’s $10 billion global fashion business for two-plus years, including the expansion of its Authenticity Guarantee program to new categories, price points and markets, strengthening trust among buyers and sellers. Hoopes will now lead The RealReal’s merchandising strategy, focusing on its luxury assortment and personalized product discovery — as the platform further advances its AI capabilities and unlocks growth opportunities.

Company comments: “Alexis is a proven leader who brings a rare combination of luxury merchandising expertise, global marketplace experience and operational discipline,” Rati Sahi Levesque, president and CEO of The RealReal, said in a statement. “As we build on our leadership in luxury resale, her ability to connect exceptional merchandise with evolving consumer demand will be instrumental in accelerating growth.”

Background: Hector Muelas joined LVMH in 2015 as global VP of content and creative, after working for Apple. Between 2017 and 2019, he was chief brand officer of LVMH-owned luggage brand Rimowa under chief executive Alexandre Arnault. Muelas then returned to Apple as global group creative director in 2019, a role he held until 2021. He returned to LVMH in 2023 as Tiffany & Co.’s global chief brand and creative officer, reuniting with Alexandre Arnault.

He has now been named Louis Vuitton chief brand creative officer, a newly created position reporting to Louis Vuitton deputy CEO Damien Bertrand.

Company comments: “Hector will define and steer our creative storytelling across all touchpoints, thereby ensuring strong overall image consistency. Leading creative and content execution, he will oversee all brand campaigns, with the art buying team led by Magena Chansarel and the content factory team led by Carole Fuchs joining his organization. In close collaboration with our business units, regions, and creative talents, Hector will further elevate our brand desirability, ensuring the house continues to set the benchmark in cultural resonance, creative boldness, and emotional connection with our clients worldwide,” Bertrand said in an internal announcement.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky, who most recently exited the board at Chanel, but remains president of Chanel SAS and fashion, is now co-chair of The Fashion Pact. A non-profit organization, The Fashion Pact is a coalition of CEOs from more than 150 companies representing a third of the global fashion industry by volume. Pavlovsky will work alongside Inditex CEO Óscar García Maceiras and climate campaigner Paul Polman to build on the work of the pact in creating a net-zero fashion industry. (Chanel is among the coalition’s founding signatories back in 2019.)

Company comments: “As we look ahead to 2027, our focus is increasingly on translating collective ambition into implementation, and scaling solutions across the industry. Bruno’s appointment marks an important step in this journey, bringing valuable leadership and perspective as we work to strengthen collaboration across regions, business models and supply chains,” The Fashion Pact wrote on LinkedIn.

Background: Bruno Pavlovsky joined Chanel in 1990 and became a board member in 2018, a duty he will now step down from. Since 2022, he has also been president of the Fédération de la Haute Couture et de la Mode. Pavlovsky remains president of Chanel SAS and of the house’s fashion activities.

Company comments: “This latest move marks the completion of the board’s evolution toward a composition of independent directors, bringing diverse external expertise and perspectives, while retaining executive representation through the global executive chair and global CEO. Bruno Pavlovsky remains fully committed to his role as president of Chanel’s fashion activities and president of Chanel SAS,” Chanel said in a statement.

Background: Zankov has appointed Jack Tobin, founder of luxury brand development consultancy Jack Tobin Agency, as CEO and business partner of Zankov, formalizing a partnership that has developed since Tobin began consulting for the brand two years ago. Since beginning its partnership with Jack Tobin Agency, Zankov has increased its international business more than tenfold and doubled its global stockist network.

Company comments: “Zankov is at an incredibly exciting stage in its growth. I have always envisioned having a partner who could join me in shaping the next chapter of the brand — someone who shares my ambition to build an enduring business while staying true to the creative vision that has always defined Zankov. Jack is the ideal partner to take this next step with, and I’m excited about what we can build together,” says Henry Zankov, founder and creative director.

Background: Net-a-Porter (NAP) has appointed Devina Foley as Americas president to oversee the retailer’s US and Canada strategy. With more than 20 years of experience across retail, merchandising and e-commerce, Foley will help strengthen NAP’s market positioning as it settles into a new era under LuxExperience Group. She has held senior leadership roles at Bandier, Rockets of Awesome and Gilt, following earlier positions at Loft and Gap Inc. Based in New York, Foley will report to NAP CEO Heather Kaminetsky.

Company comments: “Devina brings an impressive breadth of experience and a proven track record of driving growth and leading businesses through transformation,” Kaminetsky said in a statement. “Her leadership and expertise will be invaluable as we continue to grow Net-a-Porter’s US business.”

Background: LVMH has promoted Clara Boissonnas, formerly women’s leather goods product director at Louis Vuitton, to CEO of Pucci. Boissonnas joined Louis Vuitton in 2002 as a product manager, before exiting four years later. After a decade working across Lanvin and Byredo, she returned to LV where she helped shape the maison’s coveted leather goods business. At Pucci, Boissonnas will strengthen the brand’s distinctive creative identity, desirability, and international reach, while reporting to Pietro Beccari, chair and CEO of the LVMH Fashion Group. As for Saar Debrouwere, who has led Pucci since 2022, her future role will be announced in due course, according to the group.

Company comments: “Clara has made a significant contribution to Louis Vuitton through her deep product expertise, strong creative sensibility, and unwavering commitment to excellence. Her ability to combine creative ambition with a clear understanding of the business makes her ideally suited to lead Pucci into its next chapter,” Beccari said in a statement.

Background: Yanina Novitskaya, who has spent the last 19 years at Cartier, most recently as CEO of South East Asia and Oceania, is the next chief executive of Richemont-owned Delvaux. Delvaux, the world’s oldest fine leather goods house, was founded in Brussels in 1829. In its next chapter, Novitskaya succeeds Jean-Marc Loubier, who returned to lead the brand after its acquisition in 2021, and will report to Richemont fashion and accessories CEO Philippe Fortunado.

Company comments: “Yanina’s strong knowledge of the luxury industry will be instrumental in leading Delvaux into its next chapter, strengthening its distinctive positioning and continuing to drive product desirability and international growth,” Fortunato said in a statement.

Background: Marc Jacobs has appointed John Wattiker as CMO to lead the brand’s global marketing strategy. Wattiker joins the brand after almost 15 years at Hearst Magazines working in the company’s advertising business, where he most recently held the role of VP of fashion and luxury. Prior to Hearst, he worked in the banking sector. At Marc Jacobs, Wattiker will oversee efforts to strengthen brand positioning, deepen consumer engagement and further expand the recently acquired brand’s global reach and relevance under new owner WHP Global.

Company comments: “John brings deep experience across luxury, fashion and media, with a clear understanding of how to build brands and engage consumers,” Marc Jacobs CEO Eric Marechalle said in a statement. “He pairs creative instinct with strategic and commercial discipline and brings an extensive network of relationships built over the course of his career. I am confident he will be a great addition to our leadership team as we grow Marc Jacobs globally.”

Background: Chanel has appointed a creative makeup director, Lucia Pieroni. Previously, Pieroni was creative director of makeup at Shiseido-owned Clé de Peau Beauté (2006-2019), which led to a series of partnerships with photographers and designers where Pieroni helped shape beauty direction for fashion shows, editorials, and campaigns. At Chanel, she will work alongside the makeup creation studio reporting to Simona Cattaneo, president of fragrance and beauty.

Company comments: “Lucia possesses an extraordinary instinct for beauty. She perceives the individuality in every face and understands with precision how to reveal it, creating makeup that feels intuitive and expressive, while always celebrating singularity. Her artistic vision and unique savoir-faire will make this collaboration a decisive new chapter for Chanel Makeup,” Cattaneo said in a statement.

Background: Alistair McCallum, formerly global communications VP at Burberry, has been appointed chief marketing officer of Givenchy. McCallum arrives with international comms experience at fellow LVMH house Fendi, and before that, at Alexander McQueen, where he worked with now-Givenchy creative director Sarah Burton. He will report to brand CEO Amandine Ohayon.

Company comments: “The arrival of Alistair McCallum [...] on our executive committee brings recognized expertise in the luxury and fashion worlds to support our international ambition and teams worldwide,” Ohayon said in a statement.

Background: LVMH-owned jewelry brand Repossi has appointed Matthieu Soudan as managing director. The hire comes as the brand’s former CEO Anne de Vergeron returns to her management responsibilities at the LVMH group level. Soudan has been in the LVMH ecosystem for nine years, the majority of which were spent as general manager of Tag Heuer before moving to Bvlgari in 2025. At Repossi, he will lead the brand into its next phase within the world of contemporary high jewelry, while strengthening its positioning and global reach.

Company comments: “I am delighted to entrust the leadership of Repossi to Matthieu Soudan as we open a new chapter in the development of this distinctive maison. At Tag Heuer and more recently at Bvlgari, he has demonstrated a strong strategic vision, together with the ability to execute strategies that support operational excellence and the desirability of our maisons,” Stéphane Bianchi, group managing director and CEO of LVMH Watches & Jewelry, said in a statement.

Background: Capri has appointed Catherine So as the company’s chief legal and sustainability officer. So joins from Tiffany & Co., where she most recently served as senior vice president and general counsel, where she oversaw legal, compliance, intellectual property, litigation, governance and brand protection. She spent 15 years at Tiffany across various roles.

Company comments: “We are pleased to welcome Catherine to Capri Holdings. She is a highly respected legal leader with extensive experience with helping develop global luxury brands and executive teams through periods of transformation and growth,” CEO John D. Idol said in a statement. “Her expertise, leadership, and strategic perspective will be invaluable as we continue to strengthen our business and position our brands for long-term success.”

Background: Poshmark has made a string of executive hires. Creative consultant Jamie Hunter, who worked as a buyer and fashion director at Bergdorf Goodman, has been appointed fashion and creative director of the California-based resale company. This new role signals Poshmark’s ambition to become an authority in the fashion resale space, by bringing its curation, styling and creative direction in-house, informed by Hunter’s two-plus decades in the industry.

Other new hires include: Yoshitaka Matsuzawa as SVP of seller and community experience, leading product development across consumer experiences and AI; Kishore Kumar Mohan (formerly The RealReal) as engineering SVP; Lesley Clifford as VP of merchandising, also a new role supporting a more strategic approach to assortment and brand relationships; and Beth Newman (formerly Canada Goose) as PR and communications director.

Company comments: “We’ve been deliberate about bringing in leaders who add deep expertise in their respective fields and fresh perspectives to Poshmark. With experience spanning fashion, technology and retail, they’re strengthening our leadership team and helping us sharpen our fashion point of view,” chief revenue officer Elizabeth von der Goltz said in a statement.

Background: Stephan Sturm has decided to step down as chair and member of the supervisory board of Hugo Boss, following discussions between the brand and its now-largest shareholder Frasers Group. The Mike Ashley-owned business upped its stake in the German brand in mid-August, from 30.28%% to 47.89%; the rising share comes on the heels of Frasers’s June takeover bid of £1.72 billion, which the Hugo Boss board deemed “inadequate” and urged shareholders to reject.

Now the largest shareholder of the Hugo Boss business, Frasers Group is edging closer to expanding to its portfolio further, following the acquisition of UK department store Harvey Nichols last month. Sturm will continue to serve as chair until a successor has been elected.

Company comments: “On behalf of the supervisory board, I would like to thank Stephan Sturm for his leadership, commitment, and dedication to Hugo Boss. We respect his decision and will work closely with him to ensure a smooth transition,” deputy chair Sinan Piskin said in a statement.

Background: Space NK has named Emma Simpson-Scott as CEO, succeeding Andy Lightfoot, who is stepping down after a decade heading the beauty retailer. Following a period of significant growth and transformation, including its recent acquisition by Ulta Beauty, Simpson-Scott will now lead the business as it matures further. Previously, the executive spent seven and a half years as CMO and 10 years at Space NK altogether.

Company comments: “Under Andy’s leadership, Space NK achieved significant growth, strengthened its position as a market-leading beauty retailer, and successfully transitioned into the Ulta Beauty family,” Kecia Steelman, president CEO of parent company Ulta Beauty, said in a statement. “Emma is a highly respected retail leader who brings deep customer insight, retail expertise and a passion for building exceptional teams. I look forward to our continued work together as she leads Space NK into the next chapter of growth.”

Background: Southern Californian brand St. John has named former co-creative director of Kenzo Humberto Leon as creative director. Beyond Kenzo, Leon co-founded fashion concept store Opening Ceremony in 2002 and is best known for his distinctive multidisciplinary approach to design. At St. John, Leon will oversee the knitwear brand’s image, design, and overall creative direction.

Company comments: “Humberto brings a rare instinct for honoring our history while making it feel entirely new. He understands that true luxury lives in how clothing makes people feel, which is the very spirit Marie Gray built this house on. Together, we’re introducing St. John to a new generation who may not have felt it was made for them until now,” CEO Mandy West said in a statement.

Background: Richemont has appointed Anton Rupert as non-executive co-deputy chair of the board. Rupert, the son of Richemont chair Johann Rupert, has served as a non-executive director on Richemont’s board since 2017. He served as director of Watchfinder from July 2018 until December 2019. Since January 2021, he has served on the advisory board of Asia Partners Fund LP I, a regional Southeast Asia private equity fund focused on growth-stage technology-based opportunities. Following the meeting of Richemont’s board of directors on September 8, Richemont announced his appointment as non-executive co-deputy chair of the board of directors. He will serve alongside Bram Schot, who was appointed non-executive deputy chair in 2024 and who will continue in his role.

Company comments: “This appointment is an important step in the board’s long-term succession planning,” Richemont chairman Johann Rupert said in a statement. “Richemont’s strength has always rested on the continuity that comes from close family involvement, on rigorous governance, and on an unwavering commitment to creativity and craftsmanship. Having Anton and Bram serve together as non-executive co-deputy chairmen ensures that each of these foundations is given the attention it deserves: Anton will continue to safeguard the creative and product priorities that define our maisons, while Bram will ensure that our governance remains of the highest standard.”

Background: James Kelly has been named CEO of Theory, after joining the brand in 2022 as CFO and later as global co-chief operating officer. As global CEO of both Theory and Helmut Lang, Kelly will oversee both brands’ headquarters functions, commercial operations, and global growth initiatives. Before joining Theory, Kelly helped scale Uniqlo’s US expansion. He succeeds Dinesh Tandon, who will transition into the co-chief operating officer role, as well as returning to his role as CEO of Theory China.

Company comments: “James has been an instrumental leader for Theory over the past several years, bringing strategic vision, operational excellence and a deep understanding of our business,” said Kazumi Yanai, chairman of Theory. “As James assumes the role of global CEO and Dinesh focuses his leadership on one of our most important markets, we are further expanding our global organization and positioning Theory for continued success around the world.”

Background: Charlotte Fournet, the niece of Kering chair François-Henri Pinault, has been named CEO of jewelry maison Pomellato, succeeding Kering Italia president Sabina Belli. Fournet joined Saint Laurent in 2014 before moving to Gucci in 2019 and then Bottega Veneta in 2020, where she climbed the merchandising ladder to become director just over three years ago. Krizia Cucurachi, who joined Dodo in 2024 as global product and brand director, has been promoted to CEO. Prior to joining the brand, she spent more than a decade at Swarovski across several senior leadership positions. Both will report to Kering Jewelry CEO Jean-Marc Duplaix, based in Milan.

Company comments: “Jewelry is a strategic growth pillar for Kering. Pomellato and Dodo are two highly distinctive houses with strong identities and tremendous potential. Charlotte’s extensive experience across several Kering houses and Krizia’s strong track record in brand-building and transformation make them ideally positioned to lead the next phase of growth for Pomellato and Dodo,” Duplaix said in a statement.

Background: Sabina Belli, who joined Kering as CEO of Pomellato in 2015, has been named president of Kering Italia. Before joining the French luxury group, Belli held senior marketing and executive roles at WPP, L’Oréal Luxe and LVMH, spanning the likes of Christian Dior Parfums, Moët Hennessy, Veuve Clicquot, and Bvlgari. Since this April, she has also led Kering Accademia per le Eccellenze, a Kering initiative dedicated to preserving and promoting Italian craftsmanship, alongside serving on the directors board of the Kering Foundation. In her new role, Belli will report directly to CEO Luca de Meo, based in Milan.

Company comments: “Italy occupies a unique place in Kering’s history, identity, and future. Its creativity, craftsmanship, and industrial excellence are at the heart of our houses and the long-term vitality of the luxury industry,” de Meo said in a statement. “Sabina brings a deep understanding of the Italian luxury ecosystem and a strong ability to build partnerships across business, education and public institutions.”

Background: Kristin Bauer, who spent three years as chief supply chain officer for sneaker retailer Foot Locker, will join Converse as chief operating officer. As parent company Nike works to revive its Converse business, following consecutive quarters of slow sales, it is rebuilding a leadership structure to help propel growth. Bauer will report to Nike COO Venky Alagirisamy.

Company comments: “We are excited to welcome Kristin and look forward to the perspective she will bring as we continue to build momentum for the brand,” Nike said in a statement.

Background: Jane Ewing has been named chief commercial officer and executive vice president of Nike, reporting directly to CEO Elliott Hill. She joins after a 14-year tenure at Walmart, most recently serving as interim CEO for Sam’s Club China. She also previously held senior leadership roles at Diageo. In her new role, Ewing will lead Nike’s global marketplace organization, including Sales and Nike Direct.

Company’s comments: “Jane’s experience, leadership and global perspective will help us continue this work and accelerate growth across Nike Direct and wholesale. Her role is vital to creating even stronger connections between brand, product and marketplace while serving athletes* and consumers around the world,” Hill said in a statement.

Background: The British Fashion Council (BFC) has announced that David Pemsel is stepping down as chair after four years in the position and 10 years on the executive board. During his time as chair, the BFC achieved record revenue figures (£14 million in FY2024/25), raised £7.2 million through the BFC Foundation and secured a multi-million-pound investment from the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport. Pemsel also appointed Laura Weir as BFC CEO in early 2025. A successor will be announced in September.

Company comments: “David has been an exceptional chair and an unwavering champion of British fashion. His leadership has helped strengthen the British Fashion Council as an organization, creating the stability, governance and long-term foundations that enable us to deliver our ambitions for the industry,” Weir said in a statement.

Background: Alexandre Oulès has been named chief operating officer for the LVMH beauty division, reporting to Véronique Courtois, president and CEO of Parfums Christian Dior and of the LVMH Group’s beauty division. According to the internal announcement, his new role will “oversee manufacturing, supply chain, and purchasing across the beauty division, driving stronger convergence between maisons across all three functions”. Oulès joins from Balenciaga, where he was appointed COO in October 2023. He previously held roles at L’Oréal, Guerlain, Celine and Moët Hennessy.

Company’s comment: “I am delighted to welcome back Alexandre, whose pursuit of operational excellence is widely recognized. His knowledge of the group and the specificities of the beauty world will strongly contribute to the overall efficiency of our operations,” Courtois said.

Background: Maya Dukes, who previously worked at Macy’s as head of graphic design (2001-2007), will return to the retailer as executive creative director. Dukes has more than two decades of experience leading creative strategy for some of the world’s best-known consumer brands, including her most recent role leasing global creative at Delta Airlines. At Macy’s, Dukes will report to CMO Sharon Otterman, overseeing the company’s creative and storytelling to bring the Macy’s brand back to life and help propel its Bold New Chapter strategy.

Company comments: “I am excited to welcome Maya back to Macy’s. Her experience translating brand strategy into compelling storytelling, elevating the customer experience and modernizing the creative process will be critical as we strengthen Macy’s for the future,” Otterman said in a statement.

Background: Skims has appointed its first-ever chief design officer, Erin Magee, best known for her time at Supreme, where she spent over 20 years. Most recently she held the role of chief creative officer, under which she led the brand’s creative vision, design, product development, and product strategy across apparel, accessories, collaborations, and special projects. Skims has also promoted Kim Schraub, who has been on board since Skims’s founding, to chief brand officer from her previous role as creative director. In her new role, Schraub will balance creative and commercial. Prior to joining Skims, Schraub worked at Abercrombie, Victoria’s Secret Pink and Yeezy.

Company comments: “Erin brings an unparalleled creative vision and a proven ability to build brands that transcend fashion and become cultural touchstones,” CEO and co-founder Jens Grede said in a statement. “Her eye for design, her deep understanding of product and her instinct for what resonates make her exactly the right person to lead Skims into its next era. We’re incredibly excited to welcome her to the team.”

“Kim has been with us since before Skims existed. She helped turn an idea into a brand that people genuinely love,” Kim Kardashian, Skims chief creative officer and co-founder, said in a statement. “Her creative instincts have helped shape everything about how Skims shows up in the world, and this promotion is a reflection of the enormous impact she has had, and the trust Jens and I have in her vision. I can’t wait to see where she takes us next.”

Background: Vuori has appointed Carey Collins Krug as CMO. She joins from Abercrombie & Fitch, where she spent the last seven years, four of which she held the CMO role. Prior to Abercrombie, Collins Krug held top marketing positions at David Yurman, Ralph Lauren and Donna Karan. At Vuori, she will lead the brand’s cross-channel marketing initiatives, and focus on global expansion.

Company comments: “Carey brings the kind of brand-building, consumer engagement and cross-functional marketing leadership that will be instrumental as Vuori enters its next chapter of growth,” Joe Kudla, founder and CEO of Vuori, said in a statement. “Her experience helping global lifestyle brands sharpen their storytelling and build deeper connections with consumers aligns closely with where we’re headed as we continue to scale.”

Background: Rains has appointed Tom Bettinson as CEO, succeeding co-founder Daniel Brix Hesselager, who will transition into a business development role after leading the company for a year and a half. Since the initiatives core to Brix Hesselager’s transformation plan, in particular retail development, have been implemented, the focus will now shift to driving commercial success through these investments. Bettinson first joined Rains in 2017, helping to establish the brand’s UK business, before stepping away and rejoining as CSO, with responsibility for all company sales channels, in 2025.

Company comments: “I stepped into the CEO role to lead a fundamental transformation of our concept and organization. It was an extensive undertaking that required swift decision-making. Today, the foundation is in place, and the time is right to pass the baton,” Brix Hesselager said in a statement. “The priority now is ensuring excellence in execution and driving commercial success across all areas of the business. Tom is the right person to lead that next phase.”

Background: Pandora has appointed André Branch as president of North America, one of the Danish jewelry brand’s largest growth markets. Branch brings more than 25 years of experience across global consumer, beauty and lifestyle brands, most recently having served as CEO at Ariana Grande’s R.e.m. Beauty. At Pandora, he will lead the business’s next phase of regional growth, focusing specifically on enhancing customer relevance and brand appeal. Branch is succeeding Luciano Rodembusch, who departed the company in February.

Company comments: “André is a highly accomplished commercial leader with a strong track record of driving growth across global consumer businesses. His ability to combine strategic clarity with disciplined execution makes him exactly the right person to lead our North America business and drive the next phase of growth in the region,” chief commercial officer Massimo Basei said in a statement.

Background: Skims has hired Jasmine Sevan as vice president of communications. With nearly two decades of experience, Sevan will play a key role in advancing Skims’s global communication efforts, further strengthening its position at the intersection of fashion, culture, and innovation. She most recently served as global communications and brand partnerships director at Victoria Beckham, where she led the comms strategy during a period of significant growth, spurred by the brand’s Paris Fashion Week debut, collaborations with Mango and Gap, and the global launch of Netflix documentary, Victoria Beckham. At Skims, Sevan will report to chief communications officer Tracy Nguyen.

Company comments: “Jasmine is an exceptional communications leader with a sharp strategic mindset and a deep understanding of how brands shape culture,” Nguyen said in a statement. “Her experience building reputation for fashion’s most-respected brands, alongside her relationships across media, fashion and entertainment, makes her an incredible addition to Skims.”

Background: Birgit Kretschmer will succeed Harm Ohlmeyer as chief financial officer of Adidas. Kretschmer spent 25 years of her career at the sportswear giant, following a six-year tenure as CFO of German fast fashion company C&A. Harm, who helped with the appointment of Kretschmer as his successor, will stay close to Adidas, ensuring a smooth leadership transition.

Company comments: “I am extremely happy that we have signed Birgit to be the successor of Harm. She knows the industry, she knows Adidas, and she has added the knowledge of cost discipline working as the CFO of a vertical retailer like C&A. I really look forward to welcoming her back on our team,” CEO Bjørn Gulden said in the company’s half-year earnings release.

Background: John Schlifske has exited the Kohl’s board after nearly 15 years of service, stepping down as chair to enter retirement. In his place, Wendy Arlin, who has been a director since 2023, will take on the chair role. Arlin has more than three decades of finance and consumer brand experience.

Company comments: “With deep financial and retail expertise, Wendy provides valuable perspective to both the board and the management team. She has been a valued voice and a natural leader in the boardroom since joining, and I look forward to working with her in this new capacity,” said Michael J. Bender, Kohl’s CEO and board director, in a statement.

Background: Whoop, the wearable fitness tech brand, has named Kyle Leahy as chief commercial officer. She will oversee the company’s commercial operations as it continues to scale across international markets and new channels, specifically its healthcare go-to-market strategy. Leahy comes from Glossier, where she transformed the beauty brand from a direct-to-consumer business into a global omnichannel company, bringing it to profitability during her three-year tenure as CEO.

Company comments: “Kyle has a proven track record of leading strong brands through rapid growth. She knows how to expand premium distribution and build the right partnerships without losing what makes a brand special. That experience will be critical as we bring Whoop to more people around the world,” founder and CEO Will Ahmed said in a statement.

Background: Skims has promoted Tracy Nguyen, formerly executive VP of communications and entertainment, as chief communications officer. Nguyen, who has been at Skims since 2024, will continue to lead global communications for the intimates brand, as well as collaborations and cultural activations across entertainment, sports, and brand partnerships. Most notably, the executive was key in building the partnership between Skims and Nike last year, and was subsequently appointed co-general manager of the venture — a role she will continue in alongside.

Company comments: “From her time as a trusted advisor across my entire brand portfolio — when Skims was just an idea — to joining Skims in a formal executive capacity more than two years ago, Tracy has been an incredible partner and leader. She understands the brand at its core — how to protect it, grow it, and put it in front of the right audiences at the right moments,” said Kim Kardashian, Skims chief creative officer and co-founder, in a statement.

Background: Manolo Blahnik has appointed former Chloé executive Kimberly Mimnaugh as managing director of Americas. Beyond her most recent role as VP of North America retail at Chloé, Mimnaugh’s luxury commercial experience spans various leadership positions at the likes of Brunello Cucinelli, and Theory and Helmut Lang. At Manolo Blahnik, she will deliver the commercial strategy for the brand’s New York-based subsidiary, across retail, wholesale and e-commerce.

Company comments: “Kimberly brings an exceptional combination of luxury retail expertise and commercial leadership. Her proven ability to accelerate direct-to-consumer growth while maintaining a strong wholesale business makes her ideally placed to lead this next phase of our growth in the Americas. I look forward to working closely with her,” CEO Kristina Blahnik said in a statement.

Background: John Smedley, the British knitwear brand that’s been in operation for more than 240 years, has revamped its executive line-up. Jess McGuire-Dudley, managing director since April 2025, has been named CEO, while Bryan Jackson is returning to the company as senior independent director, after retiring last year following 11 years as chair. New recruits include COO Brian Lancaster and CFO Stuart Pannell.

Company comments: “Today, we announce the appointment of a strengthened executive leadership team that combines deep industry expertise, operational excellence, and a shared commitment to securing the long-term future of John Smedley. With ambitious plans to strengthen John Smedley’s position as one of Britain’s most-respected luxury manufacturing brands, this C-suite will take the company into its next phase of growth,” McGuire-Dudley said in a statement shared with Vogue Business.

Background: Yann Musquin has been appointed managing director of LVMH fragrance brands, reporting to Véronique Courtois, president and CEO of Parfums Christian Dior and the LVMH beauty division. Musquin’s appointment comes after Romain Spitzer, who led LVMH fragrance brands for 10 years, was named CEO of Kering-owned house Bottega Veneta.

Musquin joined Parfums Christian Dior in 2008, where he was eventually appointed international fragrance marketing director in 2013, overseeing the creation of the Sauvage fragrance, as well as the development of Miss Dior and the Collection Privée Christian Dior. From 2021, he was fragrance and beauty director at Louis Vuitton, before becoming chief brand officer for Givenchy Parfums and Beauty in December 2024.

In this new role, Musquin will lead the strategic vision for LVMH fragrance brands, with the mission to strengthen the desirability of Givenchy Parfums and Kenzo Parfums, as well as develop the portfolio with new fragrance and beauty expressions.

Company comments: “I had the opportunity to work extensively with Yann on fragrance development at the Parfums Christian Dior. I am convinced that his remarkable expertise in fragrances and the beauty world, his sense of excellence, and his creative vision will make it possible to strengthen the desirability of our Givenchy Parfums and Kenzo Parfums. Yann has all the qualities to pursue the development of our portfolio with ambition and success,” Courtois said in a statement.

Background: Hélène de Tissot has been named global chief financial officer of Chanel, following the retirement of Philippe Blondiaux earlier this month.
