Company comments: “As we drive our bold ‘Beauty Reimagined’ vision, Brian’s deep expertise and fresh perspectives will be pivotal in executing the biggest technology and operational transformation in our company’s history,” said ELC CEO Stéphane de la Faverie in a statement. “Brian’s experience in modernising infrastructure, building resilient and sustainable platforms, and advancing AI-driven capabilities will be critical as we accelerate our evolution into a more agile and consumer-focused organisation.”

Background: Acne Studios has appointed Brune Buonomano as new global CMO. In her new role, she will join the executive committee and report to Acne Studios CEO Mattias Magnusson, while working closely with Jonny Johansson, co-founder and creative director of Acne Studios. Buonomano joins from Mazarine Group, where she served as executive vice president for four years. Prior to that, she spent 14 years within the Havas Group, where she assumed increasing responsibilities until she became co-CEO of BETC Etoile Rouge and publisher of Mastermind Magazine, which she co-founded with Marie-Amélie Sauvé.

Company comments: “I am pleased to welcome Brune as a key member of our executive management team. Brune brings tremendous experience and joins at an exciting time for Acne Studios, as we are taking the company to the next level. I am confident of her capacity to help build the next part of our journey and to keep sharpening our brand voice,” says Magnusson.

Background: Ulta Beauty has appointed Lauren Brindley as chief merchandising and digital officer. Brindley succeeds Monica Arnaudo, who will retire in June. In her new role, Brindley will be responsible for Ulta Beauty’s merchandising, e-commerce, wellness and marketplace strategies, while leading the company’s assortment brand-building strategy. Brindley brings over 20 years of global beauty and retail expertise to the retailer, having previously served as chief executive officer of Revolution Beauty for two years. Prior to that, she held senior leadership roles at Walgreens and Boots UK.

Company comments: “Providing our guests with the best beauty and wellness assortment while building strong, strategic partnerships with our brands is critical to Ulta Beauty’s future growth,” said Kecia Steelman, Ulta Beauty’s president and CEO, in a statement. “I’m confident Lauren is the right person to fuel our continued success. She is a proven, strategic leader with deep industry expertise, a global perspective and a passion for beauty that aligns with our vision for the future.”

Background: After exiting Loewe in March, Jonathan Anderson will succeed Kim Jones (who stepped down in January) at Dior Men. The Northern Irish designer created his namesake brand in 2008, of which LVMH took a minority stake in 2013. At Loewe, the house became one of luxury’s hottest fashion brands under his tenure. And with Dior impacted by the luxury downturn and global turmoil as of late, Anderson will be charged with blending his conceptual and clean design codes with the Dior DNA to give the megabrand a boost. His first show for Dior Men will be on 27 June.

Background: Moda Operandi has appointed April Hennig to the newly created role of president. Formerly Moda’s chief merchandising and marketing officer, Hennig will lead the company’s revenue-driving and brand-building functions, including private client sales, digital marketing, creative and merchandising. In the new role, Hennig will unite these teams with the goal of achieving "enhanced brand desirability, deepened client relationships and accelerated growth", the company says. She will continue to report to CEO Jim Gold.

Company comments: “In [Hennig’s] new role, she will be responsible for all consumer-facing aspects of Moda’s business: product curation, sales and marketing. The change will allow us to even more effectively serve our clients and brand partners as we continue our journey as the most special luxury e-commerce destination in America,” Gold said.

Background: After Jean Paul Gaultier retired from the runway in 2020, his Puig-owned house initiated a rotating designer model, in which a guest talent created each couture collection. Now, the brand is changing strategy, tapping Duran Lantink as creative director to lead both couture and ready-to-wear. The Dutch designer is to put his own brand — which saw him become a recipient of the Andam Special Prize in 2023 and the LVMH Prize’s Karl Lagerfeld Award in 2024 — on pause. Lantink’s first ready-to-wear collection for the house will be for SS26.

Company comments: “I see in him the energy, audacity and playful spirit through fashion that I had at the beginning of my own journey: the new enfant terrible of fashion,” Gaultier said.

Background: Shiseido has appointed Alberto Noé as interim CEO of the Americas region to replace Ron Gee, who resigned 14 April for undisclosed reasons. In his new role, Noé will oversee both the EMEA and Americas regions until a permanent successor for Gee is found. Noé brings over a decade of experience at Shiseido EMEA, and previously served as managing director of Lancôme Italy. His background also includes leadership roles at Chanel, where he was commercial director, and at LVMH as sales director for Dior.

Background: On 11 April, Mytheresa received its last regulatory clearance (from the European Commission) to acquire Yoox Net-a-Porter. Ahead of the planned 23 April closing, the company announced a new senior leadership team, composed of many standing Mytheresa executives that will now assume their same titles at the group level. CEO Michael Kliger will now be group CEO and managing director (and will continue as CEO of the Mytheresa business “for now”); Heather Kaminetsky, now Mytheresa North America president, will be CEO of Net-a-Porter; and Tony Bateman, founding partner of Mr Porter, will be appointed CEO of Mr Porter.

Company comments: “We have selected our future management team at store, brand and group level to bring together the most experienced and capable leaders for each role. All these outstanding leaders share a passion for customers, the willingness to drive change and a deep understanding of their business areas. This thoughtfully selected team draws on Mytheresa’s established management strengths, the experience of strong leaders from the YNAP organization, and is further enhanced by highly accomplished external hires,” Kliger said.

Background: Kering Beauté has tapped Nathalie Berger-Duquene to succeed Sarah Rotheram, who departed the position in October 2024. Berger-Duquene most recently held the position as Balmain Beauty’s global general brand manager at Estée Lauder Companies. The incoming CEO has been charged with spearheading the next development phase for the fragrance brand.

Company comments: “In her role, Nathalie Berger-Duquene will lead the House of Creed in a new stage of its development and growth with the support of Creed and Kering Beauté’s global teams,” the company said.

Background: Most recently chief design officer for Savage X Fenty, Adam Selman is the first designer to be appointed to the executive creative director role at Victoria’s Secret. In his new role, Selman will oversee creative, public relations, the brand’s styling and fashion team, and copy, according to the brand. He will report to Victoria’s Secret CEO Hillary Super until a new CMO is appointed to oversee the designer.

Company comments: “I am excited to welcome Adam to our team. He is a true visionary, operating at the crossroads of fashion and culture, always attuned to today’s consumer. His creative insight, cultural understanding and brand-building expertise are exactly what our brands need as we enter this next stage of innovation and growth,” Super said.

Background: The Italian house hires Ramon Ros to succeed Pierre-Emmanuel Angeloglou, the latter of whom was appointed deputy CEO of Christian Dior Couture last month. A promotion from within, Ros was most recently Louis Vuitton president and CEO of Mainland China. He will join at a time of transition for Fendi, following the departure of artistic director Kim Jones, announced in October.

Company comments: “Ramon’s deep expertise in luxury retail and clienteling, coupled with his passion for product excellence and collaborative leadership, will enable him to elevate the Roman maison to new heights, preserving Fendi’s unique history and commitment to artisanal craftsmanship,” LVMH said.

Background: Part of the ongoing LVMH reshuffle, Charlotte Coupé joins from Louis Vuitton, where she currently serves as business unit director of men’s ready-to-wear. Following the announcement that former CEO Sylvain Blanc will be departing the brand, Coupé will report to Sidney Toledano, senior advisor to LVMH group chairman and CEO Bernard Arnault. The appointment comes as Kenzo is fine-tuning its strategy, returning to the womenswear schedule and hiring design director Joshua Bullen.

Background: H&M Group-owned fashion chain & Other Stories has named British designer Jonathan Saunders as its first-ever chief creative officer. Saunders was previously chief creative oﬃcer at Diane von Furstenberg and creative director of Pollini, and has consulted for brands such as Calvin Klein, Tiffany, Chloé, Louis Vuitton, Alexander McQueen, Pucci and Marc Jacobs, alongside leading his eponymous line.

Company comments: “Jonathan brings a refined blend of creativity and passion to & Other Stories and will play a key role in taking the brand into the next phase. His engagement and creative leadership, combined with a deep understanding of contemporary fashion, will be instrumental as we move forward,” said Lina Söderqvist, managing director of & Other Stories.

Background: Victoria Beckham has appointed Sybille Darricarrère Lunel as CEO. Lunel was most recently global business unit director of leather goods at Christian Dior Couture, where she oversaw the global product assortment across five collections per year, working closely with creative, production, sales, retail and communications teams. Prior to this, she was general merchandise and buying director at Galeries Lafayette. At Victoria Beckham, Lunel will take over from chairman Ralph Toledano, who has been acting CEO since Marie Leblanc stepped down in October 2024.

Company comments: “I look forward to having a strong, creative, smart woman with an entrepreneurial mindset and energy by my side,” said Victoria Beckham, founder and creative director. “I look forward to leading with Sybille and having her knowledge and respect for product and her experience in the industry to help us go to the next level.”

Background: Jean-Christophe Babin joined LVMH in 2000 as CEO of Tag Heuer, which he led for 12 years, and has been CEO of Bvlgari since 2013. As of 1 April, he will be CEO of LVMH Watches — succeeding Frédéric Arnault, who has been appointed CEO of Loro Piana — alongside maintaining his current responsibilities at Bvlgari.

Company comments: “Under the leadership of Frédéric Arnault, the Watches division has undertaken a significant transformation, including the implementation of operational synergies between the group’s watchmaking maisons, and substantial work on the positioning and challenges of each of them. I thank Frédéric and am pleased to see this dynamic continue with the appointment of Jean-Christophe, who will leverage his entrepreneurial spirit, energy and exceptional leadership qualities to serve the sustainable and ambitious growth of the division,” said Stéphane Bianchi, LVMH group managing director, in a statement.

Background: Francesca Amfitheatrof is exiting Louis Vuitton after seven years as artistic director of jewellery and watches. The designer was born in Japan, before growing up in New York, Rome and then London. In 2013, she became Tiffany’s design director, launching iconic lines such as the Tiffany T and Hardwear. She joined Louis Vuitton in 2018, where she has been behind the success of LV Volt, the maison’s unisex line. For the time being, the house will continue designing and conceiving its jewellery and high jewellery collections internally.

Company comments: “After a successful collaboration of seven years on the creation of jewellery and high jewellery collections, Louis Vuitton and Francesca Amfitheatrof have mutually decided to separate ways. With her remarkable talent and limitless creativity, Amfitheatrof has undoubtedly left an indelible impression on the legacy of jewellery at Louis Vuitton,” the company said.

Background: Portuguese national Miguel Castro Freitas is to succeed Casey Cadwallader as creative director of Mugler. Little known to the industry, Castro Freitas graduated from Central Saint Martins in 2004, only to be handpicked soon after by John Galliano to work at Dior. He has been head of tailoring at Christian Dior, led by Raf Simons, head of womenswear at Dries Van Noten and creative director of Sportmax. His debut for the L’Oréal-owned brand will take place in September, during the high-stake Spring/Summer 2026 season.

Company comments: “Having worked under some of the industry’s most prolific designers, Miguel boasts an incredible talent in tailoring, combined with a vision that is all his own. His love and knowledge of Mugler’s couture codes and heritage will be a limitless source of storytelling and help propel the house into the future,” said Adrian Corsin, L’Oréal managing director.

Background: The founders and former creative directors of Proenza Schouler — the cool girl New York label launched in 2002 — have been appointed creative directors of Loewe. The goal for Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez, each Parsons School of Design graduates, is to honour the codes of the LVMH house through the lenses of their cultural histories and personal aesthetics. The duo announced their departure from Proenza Schouler in January, remaining both shareholders and board members.

Company comments: “Jack and Lazaro’s vision and creativity are a perfect match for the codes of the house that we have built,” said Loewe CEO Pascale Lepoivre.

Background: After an 11-year run — and “exceptional growth” — the Northern Irish designer is exiting the Spanish luxury house, following a revered Autumn/Winter 2025 co-ed presentation. Jonathan Anderson was appointed creative director of Loewe in September 2013, after his namesake brand caught the attention of LVMH execs. Anderson took Loewe from a small luxury brand that few knew how to pronounce to one of the buzziest labels in fashion. He maintained the house’s focus on craftsmanship, bringing strong cultural references, from canonical literature and music to hyperrealism. Alongside successful products like the Puzzle bag, Anderson built a Loewe universe.

Company comments: “What he has contributed to Loewe goes beyond creativity. He has built a rich and eclectic world with strong foundations in craft which will enable the house to thrive long after his departure,” Sidney Toledano, adviser to LVMH chairman and CEO Bernard Arnault, said.

Background: As Gucci’s next creative lead, Demna will be tasked with reviving its sense of identity while reapplying his own design language to the storied Italian house and turn around revenues. It is likely he will look to bring a renewed global outlook as only the second non-Italian to lead design at the brand, after Tom Ford. His approach has so far paid off, with previous creative success at Balenciaga owing to the subversively streetwise and witty aesthetic he first enunciated with Vetements in 2014.

Company comments: “His creative power is exactly what Gucci needs,” said Kering chairman and CEO François-Henri Pinault.

Background: After a decade-long run, the Georgian designer is leaving the Spanish house he joined in October 2015, shortly after Vetements (the label he founded with his brother) showed at Paris Fashion Week for the first time. In the last decade, Demna brought Balenciaga to the forefront of the industry by consistently pushing the boundaries of fashion’s playbook. His last show for the Kering-owned house will be during couture in July 2025.

Background: Dario Vitale, 41, is widely seen as one of the most exciting and innovative upcomers in the Milan fashion scene. He graduated from Istituto Marangoni in 2006, working first at DSquared2 for a year and then at Bottega Veneta under Tomas Maier. He joined Miu Miu in 2010, where he worked his way up the ladder to become design director of ready-to-wear and head of image. He departed Prada’s sister house in January to fill the shoes of Donatella Versace, now chief brand ambassador.

Company comments: “Championing the next generation of designers has always been important to me. I am thrilled that Dario Vitale will be joining us, and excited to see Versace through new eyes,” said Versace.

Background: The news comes seven years after the Versace family sold its controlling interest in Versace, alongside a 20 per cent slice owned by Blackstone, to US group Capri for €1.83 billion. As part of the deal, Donatella stayed on under contract as Versace’s chief creative officer to lead collection design and represent the house more broadly. When founding designer Gianni was murdered on the steps of his Miami Beach house in July 1997, Donatella stepped up to lead design. Her title will now change to chief brand ambassador.

Background: The 29-year-old son of luxury titan Bernard Arnault joins the Italian brand, known for its fine cashmere, at a strong time for the house, which has become a poster child for the quiet luxury trend. It marks a strategic shift for Frédéric Arnault, one from hard luxury to fashion, which is LVMH’s core business. He became CEO of Tag Heuer in 2020, and in January 2024, was appointed CEO of LVMH Watches overlooking Tag Heuer, Hublot and Zenith. He will report to LVMH Italy chairman Toni Belloni.

Background: Simone Bellotti moves to Jil Sander, whose creative director post was left vacant following the departure of Luke and Lucie Meier last month, after being quietly recruited to Bally’s design team in October 2022. He became design director in May 2023, debuting at Milan Fashion Week Spring/Summer 2024 and creating well-received collections. Prior to Bally, Bellotti spent 16 years in the Gucci design studio under Frida Giannini and Alessandro Michele.

Company comments: “Simone embarks on this journey with extensive experience and a distinct talent. Over the time spent together, we shared the strategic vision and mission for Jil Sander, the values of innovation and sophistication that make it an iconic and unique brand,” said Renzo Rosso, chairman of OTB Group.

Background: The Chinese-owned house promotes former design director Louise Trotter’s second in command, after Trotter exited in January to take the creative helm of Bottega Veneta. Mark Thomas, who graduated from Central Saint Martins in 2001, is a seasoned designer. He joined Carven in 2023 as senior designer, following stints at Givenchy, Joseph and Helmut Lang, the latter of which as creative director from 2017 to 2019.

Background: Sustainability changemaker Matteo Ward has joined Inside Out (IO) as CEO of its fashion, textiles and home vertical. IO is the latest venture by environmental advocate and entrepreneur Suzy Amis Cameron, who is married to the filmmaker James Cameron. Pitched as a “wayfinding collective” designed to “deliver revolutionary solutions to the world’s most urgent challenges”, the holding company has six verticals, covering research and technology, food, education, media, wellness, and fashion, textiles and home. IO had acquired Ward’s consulting agency Wråd, which previously collaborated with Ferragamo and Polimoda, among others, driving sustainable transformations in fashion. In addition to developing its own brands, IO is investing in sustainability leaders, including regenerative merino wool brand Sheep Inc and New Zealand-based innovation company Rubisco.

Background: Sarah Benady brings a wealth of experience in expanding French brands internationally. Her most recent role was as president of Celine North America. Her CV also includes stints at The Kooples, overseeing its European business and then leading the brand in North America; Ba&sh, as its North America CEO; and French department store Printemps, assisting its chief merchandising officer. In her new position, Benady will work alongside founder and designer Simon Porte Jacquemus to establish the label as a “global high-end luxury maison”, the company said in a statement. Jacquemus has been without a CEO since Bastien Daguzan vacated in December 2023.

Background: The end of the couple’s seven-year tenure helming the house comes just after their Autumn/Winter 2025 show. The Meiers came on board following the exit of Rodolfo Paglialunga in 2017. Alongside shaping a freshly precise iteration of abstracted minimalism, the Meiers’s by-current-standards lengthy tenure at Jil Sander established them as the only married co-creative directors in luxury fashion.

Background: Fernando Fernandez will succeed Hein Schumacher in the CEO role, as the former chief executive steps down after a two-year tenure. Fernandez, currently CFO and executive director, has been in the company for more than 37 years, notably leading the group’s fast-growing beauty and well-being division, which includes Dermalogica, Paula’s Choice and K18. Following disappointing earnings results, the focus will be on building a future-fit portfolio with an attractive growth footprint.

Company comments: “Having worked with Fernando closely over the last 14 months, the board is very confident in his ability to lead a high-performing management team, realise the benefits of the Growth Action Plan with urgency, and deliver the shareholder value that the company’s potential demands,” said Unilever chairman Ian Meakins.

Background: Silvia Onofri was brand president of VF Corp-owned outerwear brand Napapijri between January 2023 and January 2025, following a six-year stint at Bvlgari and 15 years at Bally where she eventually rose to chief commercial officer of global wholesale. One of Onofri’s tasks will be to maintain the momentum and desirability of the house built during the tenure of previous CEO Benedetta Petruzzo, who left to join Christian Dior Couture as managing director in October.

Background: Kelly Mahoney served as senior vice president of customer and growth marketing in 2024 before she was appointed CMO. Previously, Mahoney held various marketing and strategy leadership roles at Ulta Beauty for 10 years. She shaped the brand’s personalisation efforts, including leveraging data to strengthen Ulta’s loyalty program, and was responsible for scaling the transformation of real-time, data-led multi-channel marketing communications.

Company comments: “Under Kelly’s stewardship, our industry-leading loyalty program, Ulta Beauty Rewards, grew to more than 44 million members, and within less than a month of serving as interim CMO, Kelly led the company’s first Super Bowl activation. We know Kelly will be a valued member of our executive team and a continued champion for keeping our guests at the centre of all we do,” the company said.

Background: Joël Hazan started his career at management consultancy firm Boston Consulting Group in 2005, rising to become a partner and managing director in 2015, and leading the fashion and luxury practice at the Paris office. At Kering, Hazan will report to Francesca Bellettini, deputy CEO in charge of brand development, and will succeed Mélanie Flouquet.

Company comments: “Appointing Joël will strengthen the operational support Kering provides to its houses, enabling them to gain efficiency and drive Kering’s business development ambitions forward,” the company said.

Background: Mélanie Flouquet was Kering chief strategy officer from 2021 to February 2025. Previously, she worked at JP Morgan for 20 years, where she was managing director leading luxury goods equity research. She will now report to deputy CEO and COO Jean-Marc Duplaix.

Company comments: “This newly created position aims to further strengthen Kering’s governance and risk management globally, enhance the integration of its regional activities and promote cross-functional collaboration,” the company said.

Background: Ali Goldstein joined L’Oréal’s US arm in 2001, filling leadership roles across L’Oréal Paris, Maybelline and Garnier before serving as SVP of strategy and business development for the consumer products division. In this role, Goldstein was responsible for identifying new business opportunities, including acquisitions and helping to develop the division’s stateside growth plan. Since 2019, Goldstein has served as US president of L’Oréal Paris.

Company comments: “Ali Goldstein’s unmatched knowledge of the industry and the American beauty market, her sensitivity to spotting emerging trends and scouting new business opportunities, and her decades-long experience of building powerful brands and setting them on a course for growth make her the perfect candidate to lead our company’s brand acquisition strategy into the future,” said L’Oréal North America president David Greenberg in a statement.

Background: After two years, Sabato De Sarno is exiting Gucci amid ongoing brand struggles. The brand’s Autumn/Winter 2025 show at Milan Fashion Week on 25 February will be presented by the Gucci design studio. Appointed to replace Alessandro Michele, De Sarno had previously held positions at Valentino (where he spent 13 years, working his way up to fashion director, overseeing the men’s and women’s ready-to-wear collections), at Dolce & Gabbana (as head designer of women’s knitwear and jersey collections) and Prada (as an assistant pattern-maker for the womenswear collections).

Company comments: “I would like to express my deep gratitude to Sabato for his passion and dedication to Gucci. I sincerely appreciate how he honoured Gucci’s craftsmanship and heritage with such commitment,” said Gucci CEO Stefano Cantino.

Background: Serge Brunschwig was CEO of Fendi from March 2018 to May 2024. He joined LVMH in 19995, holding various roles at Louis Vuitton and Sephora in Asia and France before becoming CEO of Céline in 2006, chief operating officer of Dior Couture in 2008 and chairman and CEO of Dior Homme in 2015.

Company comments: “We are delighted to welcome Serge Brunschwig to our Group. In his role as CEO of Jil Sander, Serge will aim to further elevate the positioning of this brand with invaluable potential, carefully and strategically guiding its growth trajectory. Thanks to his experience and international vision, he will also contribute to defining an even more ambitious strategic path for OTB,” said Ubaldo Minelli, OTB Group CEO.

Background: Marco Gobbetti was appointed in January 2022 from Burberry to steer a turnaround at Ferragamo. He appointed Fashion East graduate Maximilian Davis in March 2022. Gobbetti’s departure was a mutual agreement, according to the statement. Following the decision, Ferragamo has immediately started the process for selecting a new CEO to “continue the activities of brand renewal and heritage enhancement in order to strengthen brand evolution”, the statement says.

Company comments: “I would like to thank Marco Gobbetti, who in recent years has set up and developed a significant brand renewal and evolution activity, as well as significant product innovation and brand positioning, while also carrying out important work on the organisational evolution of the company and the group, which is the basis for continuing the renewal strategy,” said Ferragamo chairman Leonardo Ferragamo in a statement.

Background: Melanie Grant will exit the Responsible Jewellery Council (RJC) after two years at the helm, during which she oversaw an increase in membership to 2,000 companies, an overhaul of the organisation’s standards framework, and the introduction of a Lab Grown Materials standard. Grant will continue to support interim executive director John Hall in a consultant role, while working towards the publication of Phaidon’s The Jewellery Book later this year. Hall has worked at the RJC since its inception in 2005.

Company comments: “It is with mixed emotions that we announce Mel’s transition from her role at the RJC,” president and CEO Dave Meleski said in a statement. “While I am sorry for her to step down, I am thankful for all that she has accomplished in her two years as executive director of the organisation, and how she has transformed it positively into a much better place today than when she arrived.”

Background: Lauren Edelman joined Victoria Beckham Beauty as chief marketing officer in 2023 before being promoted to CEO. Edelman has 17 years of experience in luxury beauty and fragrance including tenures at L’Oréal, Chanel and Rose Inc.

Background: Jueptner joined ELC in 2009 as SVP of strategy, new business development and transformation initiatives before being promoted to group president of international in 2022. Background: Hachuel joins from Pangaia, where he spent four years and was most recently chief strategy officer, leading market expansion, operational efficiency and business transformation after a career in investment banking. There’s no denim without Demi. At tonight’s 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards in New York City, Demi Moore stepped out in a tongue-in-cheek GapStudio look that redefined the meaning of denim-on-denim.

#6695. What Exactly Was Barry Keoghan’s Skin-Lifting Treatment?

Even during his busy filming schedule for the upcoming quartet of Beatles biopics, Barry Keoghan manages to find time for self-care. Just last week, an Instagram video by skincare practitioner Nilam Holmes showed him undergoing his second XERF treatment at her UK-based clinic Dermaspa. The non-invasive treatment uses radio frequency to support collagen production and improve skin firmness without risking any fat loss on the face. According to its website, results last around 12 to 18 months, with pricing around $6,000 for two sessions (or about $3,300 for one).

“Barry is filming a big project at the moment with a very intense schedule, so he hasn’t been able to get in much and he can’t have any downtime,” Holmes tells GQ, referring to the recovery period more invasive procedures require. “That’s why I chose XERF for him. It gives a firmer rested look to his face without interrupting his work.”

According to Holmes, XERF is popular because people say it offers a “non-surgical facelift,” but she says the results are not that dramatic. The best candidates for XERF are people who want “subtle, natural-looking results” and have “mild laxity,” which is skin that’s only slightly loose or saggy.

She tells us that Keoghan has been a client of hers for “a while now” and that she’ll tailor his treatments based on what his skin needs. For example, if he’s feeling tired from filming, she might do some RF skin tightening—another form of radio frequency for addressing sagging skin—or lymphatic drainage. If his face is “being troubled from makeup” she’ll do a mild laser with a deep-cleaning HydraFacial. She says Keoghan manages to come in every four to six weeks for appointments during which she’ll offer Skinpen Microneedling—a treatment that reduces the appearance of fine lines, acne scars, and uneven skin texture.

“Once a year we’ll do a more intensive skin-tightening treatment such as Ultraformer III HIFU"— a non-invasive ultrasound device for skin tightening—“or Morpheus8”—a tool that combines microneedling with radio frequency—“which do involve some downtime,” she adds.

Keoghan has been pretty tight-lipped about those Beatles biopics he’s starring in. But in recent years, the 34-year-old Oscar-nominated actor has been open about other aspects of his life like growing up in foster care—which resonated with him while he was making the movie Lemonade—and being bullied online for his appearance. In an interview with SiriusXM in March this year, Keoghan talked about the “abuse” he receives online about his looks and how it makes him “not want to go outside.”

In Holmes’ Instagram post, Keoghan voices over: “I feel better about myself; I look better.” From Holmes’ perspective, the actor’s trips to her clinic are simply about taking caring of his skin.

“Looking after your skin isn’t about changing who you are—it’s part of looking after yourself, in the same way people look after their health, fitness and well-being,” Holmes says. “When it comes from that place, it’s a really positive thing.”

She says a lot of her clients want to enhance their features. In the past, she says it used to be mostly younger women. Nowadays, she’s seeing “more inquiries from young men with the rise of ‘looksmaxxing.’”

#6694. Nearly 6 Million Bodum French Presses Are Being Recalled After Dozens Of Burn Injuries

What to know before your next cup of coffee.

Before you break out your beans and get brewing your next morning cup of coffee, listen up. A popular French press coffee maker has just been recalled for breaking and causing serious burn injuries. Here’s what we know.

Numerous Bodum 8-cup and 12-cup French press coffee makers are being recalled nationwide. Affected models include Bistro, Brazil, Caffettiera, Chambord, Crema, Java, Jesper, and Kenya French press machines, all with replaceable glass carafes. The recall affects about 5.9 million machines.

These machines have been sold for over half a century, from 1974 through October 2026. Retailers including Target, Walmart, and Amazon sold the affected coffee makers for anywhere between $15 and $65.

According to the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, the carafe can break unexpectedly during use if the glass is damaged or cracked—including if a metal spoon is used to stir the coffee—posing a risk of severe burn injuries. To date, Bodum USA has identified 70 reports of carafes breaking during use, 48 of which involved burns.

Consumers with the affected Bodum products should stop using metal spoons or other utensils to stir their coffee within the carafe. Owners of the affected French Press models can contact the company to receive a plastic Bodum stirring spoon and a warning label reminding them not to use cracked or damaged carafes or metal spoons.

#6692. Peptides Are About to Flood the Market. And Bro Science Is Coming for Us All

This past February, Health and Human Services secretary and MAHA Final Boss Robert F. Kennedy Jr. made it known during an interview with Joe Rogan that he intended to direct the FDA to lessen restrictions on a handful of peptides that had previously been banned under the Biden administration. The peptides in question, which included influencer favorites BPC-157 and TB-500 (collectively dubbed the “Wolverine stack” for their reported regenerative properties) had been placed on the FDA’s “do not compound” list, effectively barring pharmacies from providing them to patients, for reasons including serious safety concerns and a general lack of comprehensive human trials. No new research had emerged to prompt RFK Jr.’s announcement. Rather, the HHS head, a self-proclaimed “big fan” of peptides, believed the drugs should never have been banned in the first place—a decision that, in his view, was responsible for the subsequent explosion of a thriving black market for peptides online. So, for the past eight months, healthcare professionals have been waiting with baited breath for the other shoe to drop.

And then this past Wednesday hit with a thud.

In a seemingly unilateral decision—one that flies in the face of FDA scientists who warned earlier this year of the potential, largely unknown implications of effectively releasing scantily researched injectables into the wild—RFK announced that patients (or anyone with a prescription) would now have access to six of these previously outlawed peptides through a loophole-like policy called “enforcement discretion.”

Internet-famous peptides like BPC-157 and TB-500 might be the future, but right now they’re a shot in the dark.

To explain exactly what that means, I called up Edgar J. Asebey, a life sciences regulatory and transactional attorney and partner at the Frier Levitt law firm who leads the FDA Practice Group. “I always tell people I speak three languages: English, Spanish, and FDA,” he says. “Enforcement discretion means that the FDA will not enforce a certain regulation. And in this case, it's the prohibition against compounding these six peptides. That's what it boils down to.”

Enforcement discretion is typically considered a break-in-case-of-emergency avenue for freeing up availability of certain drugs when warranted, Asebey says. “For example, when the GLP-1s were in shortage, pharmacies could lawfully compound exact copies of Ozempic and Wegovy.” In other words, the six peptides in question—BPC-157, TB-500, MOTS-c, Semax, KPV, and Epitalon—are still categorically unapproved by the FDA for human use, but Kennedy is going to allow pharmacies to dispense them as if they were, until further notice.

While this may seem outrageous, not everybody is outraged. For one, obviously, peptides are big business. (Market research firm Grand View Research valued the global peptide industry at over 140 billion in 2025, with North America accounting for more than 60% of that revenue.) Aside from that, however, one of Kennedy’s stated motivations is to reduce people’s incentive to procure peptides from regulation-skirting med spas and the dark corners of the internet, where substances like BPC-157 can be ordered to your door with the same ease as buying paper towels on Amazon. Since July, the Alliance for Safe Online Pharmacies (ASOP Global) has tracked nearly 21,000 peptide listings across more than 300 websites, including upwards of 8,800 listings for BPC-157 alone. As you might imagine, quality and safety present serious concerns to anyone choosing to go that route—that is, beyond the potential risks of using these peptides even in their purest forms—hence the burgeoning cottage industry of peptide purity trackers and testing services.

“My view is simple,” says Meena Verma, MD, MPH, a board-certified internist and nephrologist, and founder of Blue Coast Longevity in Newport Beach, CA. “People are already using these peptides, and there is an urgent need for harm reduction. Allowing licensed pharmacies to compound them under physician guidance means patients can now have an accountable channel with assurance of safety.”

But how this policy change plays out may not be quite that simple. Whereas purveyors of these six peptides—whether operating online or in person—were previously identifiable as unlawful simply by virtue of offering the unapproved drugs, Kennedy's mandate to usher these peptides into the broader health marketplace muddies the waters, making it harder for consumers to tell which providers are legit. "The online market is already flush with illegal actors who now can more easily hide amongst the masses with limited risk of getting caught,” reads a statement that ASOP Global released within hours of Kennedy’s announcement on Wednesday. “Without enhanced and consistent new enforcement of the market, today’s policy will allow criminals to hide amongst the newly compliant.”

Kennedy’s plan notes that compounding pharmacies will be subject to specific safety criteria, like requiring that the peptides are manufactured in an FDA-registered facility, but as The New York Times has pointed out, “the step basically only requires a manufacturer to notify the agency of its address.”

When you consider the scale of the peptide market alongside the reality of what the FDA is actually capable of policing with its post-DOGE workforce—following the laying off of 3,500 workers—it begs the question of whether the criteria laid out in Kennedy’s plan will even matter at all.

"For one, if you're going to have guardrails, you're going to need to enforce them,” says Leigh Verbois, PhD, ASOP's global board chair and the former director of the FDA’s Office of Drug Security, Integrity, and Response. “There needs to be resources to actually take action, full stop. And two, the organizations that are intended to utilize those guardrails may not even look at them. There are too many [compounding pharmacies] to be able to enforce against."

But I’d argue there’s something far more dangerous, and more consequential, than the possibility that this latest decision might inadvertently feed the back-alley peptide market rather than curtail it. After all, not everyone is out there looking for peptides. (I know I’m certainly not.) But we all need to go to the doctor at some point—something that could now conceivably land you on the receiving end of a prescription for a drug that has never even been researched in a human being.

“To classify this as safe would just be irresponsible,” says Motisola Lewis, MD, an Internal Medicine physician and the founder of Lewis Medical NY. “If you have a cancer patient—say, a woman who just had breast cancer—and she wants to fix her knee that just got injured, and she ends up getting an injection of BPC-157. This is known to promote tissue growth. This is known to promote vascularization. We don't know what effect it has on a patient who has had cancer. Does it promote cancer growth? We don't know.”

Peptides are blurring the line between supplements and prescription drugs.

The inescapable irony here is that not long ago it was the MAHA movement that was encouraging people to be skeptical of mainstream medical providers, to do your own research before just allowing your doctor to jab you with a COVID-19 vaccine. And now, by injecting these six potentially harmful peptides into mainstream medicine, where they will be readily available to physicians with varying degrees of familiarity with the substances themselves and the politics surrounding them, the administration has gone ahead and given the rest of us a very real reason to do our own research. Sure, this only applies to peptides at the moment, but a precedent has been set. And you can no longer afford not to pay attention. None of us can.

“When patients walk into their physician's office, or talk to a telehealth provider, they have an assumption that there will be a positive outcome—that the patient is seeking and that the physician is intending to meet,” says Dr. Verbois. “But without any of the quality, safety, or efficacy, it's completely the wild, wild west. If anyone in my family, in need of a drug for treatment, were to ask me if they should go down a path of utilizing a peptide of this sort, my response to them would be, ‘Never. Instead, seek out a treatment for that disease that's been shown to be safe and effective. These have not been, and you are putting yourself in harm's way.’”

#6691. Winter Is Coming—It’s Time to Embrace the Personality Coat

We’re in that part of fall when personality jackets get their short but sweet moment in the spotlight. For a few glorious weeks, we get to pull out those lightweight statement jackets that are so lovingly tucked into our closets—in all their various patterns, colors, and fabrications—wearing them with little underneath. Enjoy this bright and brief shining moment—the time of puffers and the Uniqlo heattech is imminent. Sure, the first wear of a tailored cashmere coat is a jolt of electricity to the wardrobe, but soon enough, it’ll start to feel rote.

Recently, celebrities have been all-in on personality-filled coats that refuse to trade weather preparedness for standout silhouettes, unexpected colors, and funky patterns. In short: cold weather months don’t automatically demand blacks, grays, and camels.

There is perhaps no greater proponent of the statement coat than Jennifer Lawrence. Judging by the roster of outerwear she’s worn over the past month, the actor shows no fear of bold colors or patterns: In early October, she bundled up in a green jacquard Dries Van Noten puffer jacket patterned with delicate orange flowers. At the end of the month, she left the house in a sweeping velvet coat from Colleen Allen. If the duster’s celadon hue wasn’t already a standout, the austere Victorian silhouette made it a true eye-catcher.

But even a neutral color can still make for a punchy piece of outerwear. Dakota Johnson and Celine Dion have both hopped aboard team texture: Johnson celebrated her birthday in a calf-length black leather Nour Hammour coat with a slinky faux-fur trim. Dion, meanwhile, recently greeted fans outside her Paris hotel in an impossibly fluffy Max Mara teddy coat, which she wore cinched at the waist.

So, for anyone still unprepared for the impending freezing temperatures, consider following Jennifer Lawrence, Dakota Johnson, and Celine Dion’s lead and adding a personality coat to your winter wardrobe.

#6690. Reckoning With Borat, 20 Years Later

Last month, I sat in a packed-to-the-gills movie theater to experience the latest release from a controversial comedian whose work regularly blurs the line between docu-reality and narrative fiction. I am, of course, referring to Ali G: Who Iz I?—the cinematic return of Sacha Baron Cohen’s once-and-still-somewhat-beloved durag-doffing titular character.

Before the film was unceremoniously dumped on Prime Video last week, I managed to snag a ticket to the only New York City screening that wasn’t totally sold-out, booking a seat—last row, tucked in an alcove of the theater—with the intention of isolated note-taking and (gasp!) the occasional phone-glance should the movie prove tedious. The recliners next to me were eventually claimed by a gentleman decked in a very Ali G-esque skull cap and wraparounds, who unleashed a deafening “BOOYAKASHA!” after Nicole Kidman’s AMC intro.

Cohen’s brand of confrontational cringe comedy continues to attract a level of interest, thanks in part to a certain mustached-and-mankini’d Kazakh journalist. The cultural explosion that was Borat! Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan (has any movie title so padded the word count?) turns 20 years old this week, and it remains a curious artifact of the 2000s: impossibly dated and slightly better than you might remember, even as its creator’s talent has slowly and unmistakably eroded.

If you were just old enough to purchase a ticket to an R-rated movie in 2006, Borat felt like a truly out-of-nowhere phenomenon in terms of mass impact. But the character, armed with little more than a shabby suit and an aggressive cheer, emerged from Cohen’s cult favorite Da Ali G Show, which ran for one season on BBC’s Channel 4 in 2000 before making the leap to HBO in 2003. Alongside Ali G and the gay Austrian fashion correspondent Brüno, Borat Sagdiyev was just one of the many personalities Cohen regularly deployed in the thorny thickets of gotcha-mentary, trading in culturally oblivious and antisemitic observations supposedly inherited from his Kazakh homeland, often to the shock and dismay of his unsuspecting subjects.

These fool-me-once hijinks weren’t necessarily groundbreaking, even for HBO’s then-provocative late-night programming. Several years prior, The Chris Rock Show engaged in similar man-on-the-street shenanigans (once, he polled residents of NYC’s notoriously hate-crime-prone Howard Beach region about renaming a street after Tupac Shakur). But segments in which Ali G addressed Buzz Aldrin as Buzz Lightyear, or the one where Borat led a bar full of Arizonans in a rousing chorus of “Throw the Jew Down the Well,” were practically reverse-engineered for virality in the internet’s pre-social-media infancy, and the appeal of Cohen’s approach—how far will he go, and will ordinary folk follow him?—was easy to understand, regardless of the visceral discomfort it may have generated.

Straying from the sketch-based format of Da Ali G Show, Borat embraced a loose narrative structure, with its titular inquirer setting out for America to make a documentary on the country’s social peccadilloes with the intent of eventually romancing Pamela Anderson. If you want to get highfalutin about it, the plot itself situates Borat within the legacy of films about Europeans attempting to understand America—a small-but-fascinating subgenre that includes Paul Verhoeven’s fairytale-cum-nightmare Showgirls, the post-hippie pessimism of Michaelangelo Antonioni’s Zabriskie Point, and Kristoffer Borgli’s social-mores rom-dramedy The Drama.

Don’t get it twisted, though: Borat was and still is best enjoyed as a showcase of physical comedy and inflammatory non sequiturs. It’s no less funny in 2026 to watch a grown man wash his face in a toilet bowl, or gesture toward a tortoise while sincerely asking, “What type of dog is this?” The scene in which an etiquette coach attempts to guide Borat through the intricacies of comic timing is itself an excellent study in comic timing; the notorious full-frontal hotel chase sequence between Borat and his producer Azamat (portrayed by steadily-working character actor Ken Davitian) is a marvel for its sheer escalation alone. This stuff killed in a massive Northern New Jersey movie theater when I was 19, and it still kills from the confines of my couch 20 years on.

Unlike much of Cohen’s subsequent work, Borat is not an explicitly political film. Nonetheless, a good deal of its “GREAT SUCCESS!”—$262 million in box receipts off an $18 million budget, with a Best Actor Golden Globe for Cohen himself—is undoubtedly owed to a different sort of comic timing. The film came out in the throes of George W. Bush’s second presidential term, with the US mired in two wars abroad and a hell of its own making. Americans were thirsty for easy targets to shoulder the blame and, if possible, provide some cheap laughs in the process.

Their thirst was quenched in the form of Borat’s many unsuspecting subjects. Some of this was low-hanging fruit: Borat telling a group of feminists to smile more, or acting like a literal bull in a china shop amidst Confederate memorabilia. But the film’s more sensational material depicted rough corners of the American psyche long hidden in plain sight. Most memorably, Borat encounters a group of rowdy frat boys who huff about white pride and express dismay at the abolishment of slavery before engaging in a viewing of Anderson’s infamous leaked sex tape with ex-husband Tommy Lee.

Not everyone was displeased at their portrayal, though. Joe and Miriam Behar, the Jewish couple who offered Borat and Azamat room and board, were good-natured in a 2006 interview with the Boston Globe. For her part, Miriam shrugged off Borat’s naked antisemitism. “To me it's an anti-Muslim movie, not anti-Jewish, because Kazakhstan is mostly Muslim,” she offered.

Behar’s observation underlines the casual bigotry that otherwise stains Borat. The film’s portrayal of Kazakh culture is undoubtedly offensive, and provoked mixed reactions from the country’s government for years to come. For what it’s worth, Cohen pushes back—intentionally or not—on anti-Muslim sentiments during the film’s rodeo sequence, in which Borat tells a particularly racist attendee that he is indeed “not Muslim.”

But given the post-9/11 climate into which Borat was launched, the implications of a foreign correspondent from a majority-Muslim country espousing antisemitic and misogynistic viewpoints are crystal-clear, and Cohen himself seems too smart to sincerely profess a lack of awareness as to how this might be received. It doesn’t help that his subsequent projects resulted in exponential escalations of offense: 2012’s more narratively-focused The Dictator spared no quarter when it came to stereotypes of Arab culture, while the astoundingly homophobic Brüno, from 2009, was loaded with gags about anal sex and resulted in an out-of-court settlement with a Palestinian grocer who was falsely credited as a former terrorist in the film itself.

After 2016’s box-office bomb Grimsby, which is most notable for the allegations of on-set sexual harassment co-star Rebel Wilson later brought toward Cohen, his work went in a more explicitly political direction. There was his 2018 docu-satire series Who Is America?—two episodes of which featured writing and directing contributions from Nathan Fielder—and 2020’s Borat Subsequent Moviefilm, a second-verse-same-as-the-first sequel which earned several Oscar nominations and brought a truly bizarre “October surprise” to that year’s presidential election involving actress Maria Bakalova, Rudy Giuliani, and the former New York City Mayor’s pants zipper.

Both of those films were more explicitly message-y than they were riotously funny. Cohen’s latest, Ali G: Who Iz I?, is neither, carrying the all-too-familiar stink of a comedian insisting that their capacity to offend amounts to protected speech. At 55, Cohen is clearly not as willing to submit himself to the ragdoll physics he once deployed; in its place is an often-sullen-looking Ali G, his dreads now gray, weighing the merits of cultural appropriation and sparring with a DEI coordinator about the origins of the durag. The entire affair is belabored and depressing.

It made me think of the Who Is America? character Dr. Nira Cain-N'Degeocello, a send-up of Rachel Dolezal-flavored liberals in the form of a Berkeley professor who dons dashikis and keffiyehs. Early in the film, he rages against Ali G’s culturally appropriative ways to a majority-Black community meeting in Oakland. “We don’t care!,” shouts one participant. In hindsight, it’s as much an expression of exhaustion with the dictates of capital-D discourse as it is a referendum on Cohen’s confrontational method, which now yields far less interesting insights about the national psyche than it did when Borat arrived on American soil in 2006.

#6687. Jude Bellingham Stripped to His Skivvies for Calvin Klein’s Latest Campaign

Last week, Calvin Klein dropped a hint of their next underwear campaign star via Instagram. The clip featured a guy gliding his fingers from his boxers up to his chest. Very suggestive. Very sexy. Instagram, obviously, went wild. A teaser of a teaser, you might say.

Now, the New York label has revealed all. The model in question? Jude Bellingham.

Shot by Oliver Hadlee Pearch on a hot Madrid day, the campaign features Bellingham posing against a clean white background—all the better to keep the focus squarely on the England international. In the exclusive photo above (don’t say we don’t spoil you), Bellingham is sporting CK’s Icon Cotton Stretch Boxer Slim.

Bellingham wears the rest of the Icon Cotton Stretch collection (and nothing else) throughout the campaign, which includes the new Stretch Shine Trunk with a shiny Infinity Bond logo waistband, the Boxer Brief, Low Rise Trunk and Hip Brief. In one shot, he’s pictured doing his goal celebration, which means the image may pop into your head the next time he scores on the pitch.

Maybe it’s obvious from the campaign, but the 23-year-old took to the role of model very naturally. He attributes his ease in front of the camera to the underwear.

“I really enjoyed working on this campaign,” Bellingham says via email. “I liked the idea of ‘the icon underneath’—that confidence starts with feeling comfortable in yourself. Calvin Klein is such an iconic brand, so it was great to bring that idea to life in my own way.”

Over the years, CK has linked up with its fair share of footballers. In 2023, the label shot Liverpool captain Virgil Van Dijk. That same year, Tottenham’s Son Heung-Min stripped to his skivvies as well. And at the end of 2025, it was Bellingham’s Real Madrid and England teammate Trent Alexander-Arnold’s turn. Maybe Bellingham went to him for advice—not that it looks like he needed it. Clearly, the guy knows how to nail the shot.

#6685. 9 Best Scalp Shampoos for Your Scalp to Help Dryness, Flakiness, and Sensitivity

By now, we know that scalp care is haircare. As excepted, then, the days I let my routine slip and I don’t tend to my scalp are when my hair will look dull, dry, flaky, and overall just “meh.” Before I reach for a serum or some sort of scalp mask, I look to the one product that really is the foundation of my hair routine: a good scalp shampoo

Over time, I’ve learned that picking a shampoo for your scalp really depends on what you’re looking to treat. Is your scalp super oily? Are you dealing with dandruff? Have you gone too product heavy and need a detox? Or perhaps you’re scalp has been close to one too many hot tool, and could use some soothing ASAP? For every scalp concern, we tapped the experts to break down the best shampoos for the scalp that they’d actually recommend. Read on below and get ready to click *add to cart.*

What do dermatologists recommend for scalp?

Dermatologists always recommend a good shampoo for the scalp to give it a thorough cleanse. But which one depends on your specific needs and how well your skin will tolerate certain ingredients. “I wouldn't choose a shampoo simply because it says, ‘sulfate-free,’” adds Dr. King. “The important question is whether the overall surfactant system effectively cleans without irritating your particular scalp.”

“Shampoos with effective surfactants are best for cleaning the scalp,” says Dr. King. Some of those surfactants she says to look for include sulfates like sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) and sodium laureth sulfate (SLES), but you can look for gentler ones like sodium methyl cocoyl taurate.

Dr. Erickson says that if you’re dealing with a dry scalp, you’ll want to skip harsher surfactants like sulfates, and fragrance to minimize irritation. Instead, look for hydrating, barrier repairing ingredients like ceramides, niacinamide, glycerin, and panthenol to pair with gentle surfactants or exfoliators.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to scalp shampoos, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, lather, and the hair-care concerns they address. #6683. Why El Clasico Is the Best Grudge Match in All of Sports

Last Saturday, before the biggest grudge match in international soccer, Spanish police officers decked out in riot gear surrounded my Barcelona hotel. Blue lights bounced from the sun-stained stone of the alley as kids scrambled away in the distance. In the skirmish, one had lost a single ASICS sneaker that sat idly in the road until, sometime between night and the light of day, someone snatched it up for themselves. You often hear of the way heated football rivalries and cup finals bring out a kind of mob mentality among fans. The match, however, wasn’t set to kick off for another 24 hours.

Three days prior I’d landed in Barcelona to attend FC Barcelona versus Real Madrid, better known as El Clásico, for which Tyler the Creator’s GOLF brand had partnered with Spotify on Barcelona’s gameday kits. If you care about football in the slightest you know about El Clásico, though it’s worth knowing about even if you don’t.

Since 1902—the year of Real Madrid’s founding, and three years after that of FC Barcelona—the two biggest football clubs in Spain have clashed in a rivalry match dubbed El Clásico (the face-off now happens twice a season, plus various tournament play that varies in schedule year to year). Before last week’s installment, the match had been played 264 times over 122 years. In most high-stakes football rivalries, one club holds a historical edge: Arsenal has a handy 20 to 30 wins over Tottenham Hotspur in the North London Derby, depending on when you start keeping track, while Manchester United edges out Liverpool in total wins. But heading into the first El Clásico of the 2026-27 La Liga season, Barcelona and Real Madrid stood deadlocked with 106 wins each.

American sports rivalries are often the result of proximity, with most pitting divisional neighbors and crosstown rivals against one another, with the exception of teams that share a bitter history of championship bouts (like the Lakers and the Celtics). But if we’re being honest, not even Yankees-Red Sox holds a candle to El Clásico. Apart from both competing in the upper echelon of La Liga’s clubs, FC Barcelona and Real Madrid’s rivalry has stewed in over a century of political turmoil between the Catalan capital and the city that houses the Spanish throne. During the 20th century as Spain looked to enforce a uniform identity across the nation, Catalonia sought to maintain its independence from the crown and, crucially, its right to speak Catalan rather than Spanish. Francisco Franco’s dictatorship brought more enmity, as Madrid became the proxy club for a centralized Spain while Barcelona came to represent Catalonia’s Republican Left. During the Franco years, when both the language and the flag of Catalan were banned, Barcelona’s Camp Nou stadium became a safe haven for the free expression of Catalan identity. Meanwhile, Franco’s foreign minister Fernando Maria de Castiella declared Real Madrid “the best embassy we’ve ever had.” The wounds of that era have hardly subsided: while the war may be over, as recently as 2017 the Catalan people voted on whether or not they’d remain a part of Spain (the vote was declared illegal by the Spanish government, and there was police intervention at polling stations).

Today, the clubs are recognized as polar opposites in every sense, from politics to style of play: Real Madrid stands for conservatism and a unified Spain, while Barcelona remains the club of the rebellious Left. Madrid takes an Evil Empire approach to roster construction, buying up the most exciting free agents on the market for record-breaking fees. (This century alone they’ve rostered Cristiano Ronaldo, David Beckham, and Zinedine Zidane, and the club currently boasts a striker line that includes Jude Bellingham, Kylian Mbappé, and Vinicius Jr.) Barcelona, on the other hand, has the most acclaimed and successful youth academy in all of football. The school, La Masia, has promoted a singular theory of football for decades, prioritizing position play and a dominant possession game perfected by FC Barcelona veterans like Lionel Messi, Xavi, Pep Guardiola, and Andrés Iniesta. When Spain won the World Cup this summer, they did so with eight former students of La Masia on the pitch (one of whom, Marc Cucarella, currently plays for Real Madrid).

To this day, the rivalry is characterized by an unmistakable hostility. In my four days in Barcelona, I didn’t see one person wearing Real Madrid’s crest, though the souvenir shops lining La Rambla were well-stocked with the club’s bootleg gear. At one point, I walked past a wall scrawled with graffiti: “SPANISH GO HOME.” When we finally got to the match, most Madrid fans were sequestered to a supporter section in the upper deck surrounded by protective plexiglass.

“This is the biggest match in club football,” explained Joel Jaggar, a British transplant who’s lived in Barcelona for a decade. Jaggar runs Real Vintage Football, a rare jersey boutique in El Raval (just outside of the city’s Gothic Quarter) that was unsurprisingly overwhelmed with visitors all weekend. He’d stocked up on at least a hundred Messi jerseys, all of which were gone by the time they closed on Friday. “A lot of people come to Barcelona specifically for this game,” he shared. “Big fans, sure, but also people who want to experience the game for the sake of the experience.” Globally, he argued, the word “Barcelona” is as closely associated with the club as it is the city. “You can’t say the same for Madrid,” he quipped.

Jaggar and I met the morning after a swell of student-organized protests regarding the city’s cost-of-living crisis boiled over into vandalism and looting near the neighborhood that houses his store. There was even suspicion El Clásico would have to be postponed or cancelled altogether. Come morning though, those anxieties had faded–as is so often the case, football continued uninterrupted.

Even with capacity capped at around 62,000 during ongoing renovations, Camp Nou is something to behold. Ahead of kickoff, supporters lifted color-coordinated pieces of poster nestled into each seat,forming a massive, stadium-wide tifo in the colors of the club and, in our section, the Catalonian flag. Fireworks exploded, and El Clásico began.

But much of the match’s first half was mired in tension, as Barcelona dominated possession but failed to score. The crowd finally began to pop when Madrid nabbed their first goal, then properly exploded when Barca tied it up in the second half. When Mbappé scored his second goal of the evening at ‘87 minutes after a beautiful assist from Bellingham, he vaulted over to the gate of the Barcelona supporters’ section, taunting them as trash thrown from the crowd rained over him. Madrid held on, gaining the tiniest of advantages in the El Clásico win count: 107 to their rivals’ 106.

As we walked out of Camp Nou, which will hold a whopping 105,000 spectators when its renovation is complete, I thought about the sort of sporting events that tend to grace bucket lists: Super Bowls and World Cup Finals and World Series games. So often the point is the spectacle of a season or tournament ending—the big trophy, the championship ring, the confetti and fireworks. El Clásico is different. There’s no trophy at the end, no ultimate resolution. Like the ideological divide for which it’s become a proxy, El Clásico is in a constant state of ebb and flow. Each time Barcelona and Real Madrid take the pitch, there’s no decisive victory so much as another brick laid in the foundation of football’s greatest rivalry. These clubs have come to blows 265 times. But as long as there are football stadiums in Barcelona and Madrid, El Clásico will endure as a conduit for the enduring rancor between the country's two biggest cities.

#6682. Keke Palmer Unearths a Rare Bob Mackie at the 2026 CFDA Awards

As the host of tonight’s 2026 CFDA Awards in New York City, one imagines that Keke Palmer felt a certain pressure to deliver us a major fashion moment. The annual awards ceremony, after all, is all about celebrating American style and design. And the good news is, Palmer certainly did not disappoint on that front.

The star went archival this evening—as she is wont to do—hitting the red carpet in a one-of-a-kind (and incredibly rare) Bob Mackie piece from the 1970s. The dress has a particularly noteworthy history: The strappy, shimmery-gold gown was originally custom-made for actor and singer Raquel Welch, which she wore to perform “I’m a Woman” alongside Cher on The Cher Show back in 1975. (You’ve all seen the clip.)

Turns out, the iconic piece of pop culture was sourced from the professional vintage dealer Timeless Vixen—a celebrity favorite that Sabrina Carpenter and Kylie Jenner also use for their extremely rare red carpet pulls. “When Keke’s styling team reached out looking for something special by Bob Mackie, this piece immediately came to mind,” says Lauren Lepire, owner of Timeless Vixen. “I’ve always adored his work, and with his recent passing, it’s especially meaningful to see Keke bring such an iconic design back into the spotlight.”

Fashion lost Mackie back in September, and the late designer—known for his impeccable, expressive glitz—was responsible for dressing everyone from Cher to Carol Burnett. On Palmer, his signature glamorous aesthetic shone just as brightly and served as proof that a classic Bob Mackie will never go out of style—and, in fact, only gets more and more in-demand.

#6681. Snickers Apple Salad

Candy in salad might seem contradictory, but this Snickers apple salad is here to prove it can be done. Chopped apples are tossed with Snickers in a creamy vanilla dressing and drizzled with caramel for a cool and sweet dessert that will surprise and delight everyone at bonfire night. Trust me—it’s a Midwest classic for a reason.

What People Are Saying:“Childhood favorite! ❤️” - NanaManda2025

Start by making a salt water bath for the apples. In a big bowl, stir together water and salt in a bowl until the salt is dissolved. Keep the bowl nearby while you cut the apples into 1/2″ pieces, adding the apples to the salt bath as soon as they’re cut—this will stop them from browning. When all the apples have been cut and fully submerged in the water, drain the apples and transfer about one-eighth of them to a small container—these will be for topping the salad. Cover and refrigerate them until you’re ready to serve the salad.

In a large bowl, whisk together the milk and pudding mix until thickened (this won’t take longer than a minute). Use a flexible rubber spatula to gently fold in the Cool Whip.

Then fold in the remaining apples and most of the chopped Snickers until incorporated.

Transfer the salad to a serving bowl and chill in the refrigerator until it’s cold—1 hour should be just fine. When you’re ready to serve, top with the remaining apples and chopped Snickers, and drizzle with caramel sauce.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

While you can technically keep Snickers apple salad up to 3 days in the refrigerator, it’s really best the day it’s made. The longer it sits, the looser it gets. By day 3, it’s basically Snickers apple soup.
