#6680. Cottage Cheese Meatballs and More Recipes We Made This Week

It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

Call me a kindergartener, but lately my favorite sweet is a big crunchy-chewy cereal treat. Thank goodness my fellow Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewczyk developed BA’s Best Rice Krispies Treats, complete with browned butter and unmelted mini marshmallows stirred in along with the melty sugar glue. I sometimes like to play and add a little drizzle of tahini or toasted nuts into the mix; but honestly nothing hits quite like a classic RKT. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

Remember the TikTok cucumber guy? He’s doing a collaboration with Chipotle now. What a time to be alive! To celebrate, I mandolined my stash of Persians, drizzled them with toasted sesame oil, seasoned them with salt and MSG and sriracha, dolloped them with mayo, then shook the hell out of them. The easiest, most satisfying way to eat a side salad. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO and cooking

The thing I miss most about living in a house instead of my city apartment is the ability to grill. I would grill at every meal if I could! But this week I made deputy food editor Hana Asbrink’s Gochujang Yogurt Chicken, and my craving for char was sated. She calls on you to broil, not bake, your chicken thighs which allow for the sugars in the gochujang to caramelize then burn to crispy perfection. Plus, this made enough for my household of two to enjoy the leftovers for two desk lunches. A definite win in my book. —Carly Westerfield, manager audience strategy

I did not plan to make an apple pie this week. I had plans to make salmon bowls, breakfast burritos, but no apple pie. Nevertheless, by some strange confluence of events that I still don’t quite understand, I found myself standing in front of an egg-washed, double-crusted, towering apple pie, crimping the edges of the dough. I followed the recipe for BA’s Best Apple Pie which has a rather long list of ingredients, and some steps that might seem unfamiliar to pie-heads, but in the end it’s worth the fuss. —Sam Stone, senior editor

My coworkers have jumped on the cottage cheese bandwagon and are sneaking the ingredient into everything: smoothies, lasagna, meatballs! I have fallen for every iteration. Keep ’em coming. But the meatballs? Now those are very special. Mixing the ground beef with cottage cheese seasons them with salty tang from the inside out. It also stretches the recipe, which means more meatballs (yay!). I ate them throughout the week with tangles of noodles, tucked into a sub for lunch, and mixed into a bracing salad. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

Though I am a vegetarian chili gal myself, I just made a batch of pumpkin chili for a care package for a meat loving loved one. It has ground beef, two types of beans (I threw in lentils too), and instead of the typical tomato backdrop, a can of pumpkin purée for a glowing hue and squashy depth. I almost always double a soup recipe—more yield, barely more work—and I’m glad I did. Now I have a few extra containers in the freezer that’ll come in handy for a cold night down the road. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Also for the care package, I made a giant batch of Chickpea Saag. With frozen spinach and canned chickpeas, this recipe makes the most of ingredients I almost always have around. With rice, Greek yogurt, and lime wedges, it’s a cozy meal in its own right. But I like to sprinkle some feta on top just to gild the lily. —E.L.

I love hosting, but at the end of a long week, I need to maximize flavor and minimize dishes. That’s why I love this Spiced Red Rice Chicken recipe from Eden Eats. It allowed me to have everything prepped before guests arrived, so I could enjoy the hang and not fuss about timing. After seasoning chicken thighs generously with salt and letting them rest for 30 minutes, I seared them, set aside, and sautéed onions, garlic in all the flavor left over (I skipped the red pepper for one of my guests). I added additional spices and tomato paste and toasted the rice. I added chicken broth, placed the chicken back in skin side up, and tossed in some knobs of butter so the rice would crisp up nicely. Into the oven at 425 for 30 minutes, and it was yummy and convenient, not to mention a definite crowd-pleaser—and my dishwasher was happy! —Abi Lieff, assistant to the editor in chief

I’m not much of a pasta person. (I know, gasp!) But when fellow Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser first developed her Smashed Broccoli Pasta—a recipe that combines over a pound of broccoli with less than one pound of pasta—my heart opened up to the idea of making it for dinner. Her technique is genius, smashing broccoli into verdant rubble that burrows its way into tubular pasta. With not much more (just red pepper, garlic, and anchovies if you’re feeling frisky), you get a veggie-loaded, fiber-packed pasta in no time. Rebecca, thank you. Perhaps I will become a pasta convert. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor

A fried fish sandwich has no season. Also, I’m currently in Tennessee, where it’s hit 90° this week, so it’s basically still summer. I used my colleague Shilpa Uskokovic’s excellent Fritto Misto batter to coat some flounder. After frying, I slid a couple small fillets into top-split hot dog buns with juicy slices of tomato and a quick tartar sauce. It was pure summer satisfaction, even this deep into October. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO and cooking

The days when my husband and I both commute are, to put it lightly, b-a-n-a-n-a-s. That’s when my deep freezer fulfills its destiny. Case in point: this superlative basil pesto, thawed overnight, tossed with hot rigatoni, plus frozen peas thrown in with the pasta for the last few minutes of boiling. It is nourishing and feels purposeful, even if it took less than 10 minutes of effort. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

Andy Baraghani’s Honey-Chipotle Shrimp Tacos are one of my most-made recipes of all time. Last week I decided to change things up and eat the shrimp over some homemade Mexican rice and beans instead of wrapping them in a tortilla. The shrimp are so easy to make (just toss in a two-ingredient marinade and pan-fry) that I ended up cooking fresh batches for lunch on the following days to pair with the leftover rice and beans. The canned chipotles in adobo lend a smoky complexity, and I love how the honey helps the shrimp take on just enough char. A luxurious WFH lunch if there ever was one! —Alaina Chou, commerce writer

Soup on a weeknight? It’s a foreign concept to me. If I’m making soup, I’m committing hours to the cause. But this week I couldn’t quell my craving for a sippable bowl, so I scoured the archive for a quick hit and landed on this Curried Lentil, Tomato, and Coconut Soup. Red lentils break down and create a substantial body, while golden Japanese S&B curry powder adds a mellow earthy kick. After mixing in crushed tomatoes and coconut milk, I went rogue and followed up with a couple dashes of fish sauce for extra umami. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

The ever adaptable rotisserie chicken is one of my favorite emergency dinners. When crunched for time, I’ll grab one on my way home and transform the bird into something unrecognizable. Most recently, I used it to make Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser’s Nuoc Cham Chicken Salad. The pulled meat is tossed with the quickest mayo-lime dressing, then stuffed into lettuce leaves. I like to finish the cups with sliced cucumber, fried shallots, and a flurry of fresh herbs. Don’t bother bringing out plates. I eat this with my hands straight from the platter like nachos. —Carly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy

Whenever I want something more for breakfast, but I don’t want to work for it, it’s a Dutch baby all the way. Heat a skillet with butter, dump a couple of always-on-hand ingredients—eggs, flour, milk, sugar—into a blender, and 20 minutes later, it isn’t breakfast: It’s brunch. Last weekend I tossed the reserved browned butter from Epi’s Take It Easy Dutch Baby into a bowl of sliced Italian plums. I added a glug of maple syrup and a pinch of salt, then let the fruit soak in the flavors while I fiddled over my coffee. Puffed bébé out of the oven, the plums and all their juices went on top, and I sat down to enjoy my morning. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, cooking and SEO

I make lentil soup pretty frequently once the “feels like” temperature dips below 50 degrees. And I was just about to mince up my mirepoix when I stumbled upon senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic’s Soy-Braised Black Lentils. The promise of salty, tender-but-toothsome legumes on a bed of rice was good enough to shake up my routine. I hauled out my rice cooker, set it to steam, and started a dead-simple simmer of a pack of shiny black Beluga lentils with glugs of soy sauce and thin slices of garlic. Once the liquid was mostly gone, I stirred in glossy agave nectar plus added sugar until they formed a loose, syrupy glaze. We ate half the pot tucked into sheets of toasted seaweed snack along with generous spoonfuls of rice. The next morning, the rest was eaten with crusty bread and fried eggs. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor

Ever since I started working at BA, I’ve seen this single recipe for Bolognese top the charts time and time again. An oldie but a baddie, it’s received over 500 comments that would taunt me on a daily basis, with one overall glaring thesis: Make this! Now! So I decided to hunker down, put on a killer album (Once in a Lifetime), and get comfortable in the kitchen. Yes, this Bolognese takes time—cough cough, three hours—but so do all good things. For those who need immediate gratification, your kitchen will be awash in the savory, primal smells of browned beef and pancetta in just 10 minutes. After adding a good amount of liquid from wine, stock, and milk (in stages), then stirring, dancing, and stirring, it was finally time to serve my meaty sauce tangled with fat pappardelle and a charitable shower of Parmesan. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

When I saw a bunch of bright-eyed leeks at the farmers market from my favorite vendor, I knew just what to do with them: my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s cheesy baked pasta. It was one of those love-at-first-sight recipes for me in the Test Kitchen—somehow minimalist and dramatic at the same time. Save this one for a chilly night when you’re having friends over. The sauce uses a cup of white wine, so there’s most of a bottle left to enjoy with dinner. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director

I’ve been making a lot of solo dinners lately, and nine times out of ten that means I’m cooking an omelet. My version with fried shallot, apple, and Fontina cheese is a go-to—I wrote all about it for our series, Me, Myself, and Dinner—but if I haven’t gone grocery shopping, I’ll just cobble together fun stuff from my fridge. Some recent wins: chopped kimchi and yellow cheddar; spinach, feta, and dill; black beans, avocado, and salsa macha. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor

This week I did something I haven’t done in years. I roasted a chicken. And it was revelatory. Not fussy. Easy! Rewarding. Inspired by the method in Kitty Cowles’s cookbook, I sprinkled the bird with salt and let it hang out in the fridge for a few hours. Then I rubbed it with olive oil, threw some lemon and garlic in the cavity, and roasted it as high as my oven would go, convection on. While the chicken was resting, its skin a golden crackle, I deglazed the pan juices with white wine, and let those simmer into a tangy gravy. Served with a salad, it was the coziest supper, even romantic if you ignore my toddler cooing. The next day, the carcass simmered in a pot of water with onion and ginger for a broth I’ll sip for days. The surplus meat has morphed into a rice bowl, towering sandwich, day care lunch box, 3 p.m. snack. And the joy from it all? Incalculable. —E.L.

I’m always on the hunt for a protein-rich, not-too-finicky dinner that I can pull together in a blip. It’s gotta taste good because I’ll probably cook it for five consecutive days, at which point I will tire of it and resume my hunt anew. Like sands through the hourglass, these are the recipes of our lives. This week I settled on customizable Soy-Glazed Salmon Bowls. Cook the salmon in that salty-sweet soy and honey sauce, throw it atop rice, and add whatever vegetables you have. This time, I went with shreddy carrots and cukes, plus some of those crispy sheets of nori that I used to scoop up bite after bite. —Sam Stone, senior editor

My very talented colleague Shilpa Uskokovic forever changed the way I cook ground chicken. She mixes the chicken with baking soda—yes, baking soda—for clusters of bouncy nubbins. Now, anytime a recipe calls for ground meat, I use this hack. This week’s victim: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps. It has a sweet, fiery sauce made from sriracha, brown sugar, soy, and fish sauce that deliberately clings to the juicy meat. I piled the chicken into butter lettuce with a squeeze of lime, and a handful of torn mint for freshness. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking

And it has precious little to do with how much you spend. They say what goes around comes around, and when the occasion comes to buy her something special, there's not better time to return a little of the favor. To that end, we've rounded up the best gifts for mom, from modest indulgences to proper splurges, all chosen with an eye toward good taste, a little surprise, and the small triumph of getting it just right.

Still stumped? We'd suggest perusing the rest of our gift guides and signing up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more gift ideas worth your money.

I have an AYR sweater in this very fabric, and I've been wearing the hell out of it lately. It's extraordinarily soft, with a bouncy, bouclé-like texture that you really have to feel to appreciate. The High has all that going for it, plus a cropped fit and a prim, high-set collar.

No. 04 Bois de Balincourt has long drawn comparisons to Le Labo's Santal 33, only at a considerably friendlier price and without the burdern of its own ubiquity. Warm sandalwood and cedar, with earthy vetiver and a little spice—a perfect year-round candle.

I'm a coffee drinker through and through, but I'd consider switching allegiances to tea if it meant getting to use this teapot from Balmuda. Just looking at the thing feels therapeutic.

This insulated Dutch oven tote from Staub and Clare V. is just the thing for the potluck monarch arriving with a cassoulet in tow. A highly specific gifting proposition, admittedly, but an excellent one nonetheless.

Inspired by the pleated designs of Issey Miyake, Wooj's Kinoko lamp has a pretty mushroom silhouette and a softly ribbed shade. A charming little thing for that neglected corner that could use some illumination.

There are plenty of newfangled brands making cute, colorful homewares these days, but long live Marimekko. These towels caught my eye for their classic brick pattern, rendered in a perfect shade of red, with all the pedigree of Finnish design behind them.

Apple's new entry-level laptop might be marketed to students, but it's also a very good laptop for anyone who just needs to do regular laptop things. Brooklyn-based designer Virginia Sin made a name for herself with porcelain versions of disposable paper plates, and her talent for making everyday objects feel a little more special extends beyond the dinner table. Case in point: this little number, which would look mighty fine on mom's desk.

If mom's recently been promoted to grandmother, I know you've been thinking about getting her a digital picture frame, and yes, you absolutely should. But not just any digital picture frame: the Aura is the one to beat, and only the best will do when it comes to showing off the new bundle.

Never underestimate the restorative powers of a little targeted heat. Ostrichpillow's new Embrace is a clever upgrade to the humble heating pad, with a wearable design, three heat settings, and up to three hours of cordless warmth.

#6678. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)

#6675. The Truth About ‘Natural Flavors’ On Food Labels Might Surprise You

The word “natural” comes with a few caveats.

I consider myself a pretty diligent ingredient-label reader. But there’s one phrase I see constantly that, until recently, I hadn’t given much thought to: “natural flavors.”

It’s printed on everything from flavored drinks to packaged snacks, and it sounds pretty straightforward. You’d probably assume that if something contains natural flavors, those flavors come directly from the foods they’re supposed to taste like. After all, that’s what natural suggests—except the actual definition is much broader than you might expect.

According to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), natural flavors can come from a surprisingly long list of sources, including fruits, vegetables, spices, herbs, dairy products, meat, seafood, and even certain fermentation products. And while those ingredients must come from qualifying sources, turning them into flavorings can be far more involved than simply squeezing juice from a fruit.

So what exactly does “natural flavors” mean, and how much does that label actually tell us about what’s in our food? Here’s what you should know.

The FDA’s definition of natural flavors focuses on where the flavoring comes from, not necessarily the food it’s supposed to taste like. Under federal regulations, natural flavors can include essential oils, extracts, distillates, and substances produced through roasting, heating, or enzymatic processing. They can originate from everything from fruit and vegetable juices to herbs, roots, bark, and fermentation products.

That means seeing “natural flavors” on a strawberry-flavored product doesn’t automatically mean the added flavoring came from strawberries.

Specific FDA rules govern how manufacturers describe flavors on the front of packages, particularly when a product’s recognizable flavor comes from sources other than the named food. But the generic ingredient-list declaration alone doesn’t identify the original source. In other words, the word “natural” doesn’t necessarily tell you what you’re tasting.

The FDA generally requires food manufacturers to list ingredients in descending order by weight. But flavorings are one category that can be declared collectively rather than listing every individual flavoring substance.

Under federal regulations, qualifying ingredients can simply appear as “natural flavor” or “natural flavors” on a product’s ingredient list. So manufacturers can use any combination of flavorings without disclosing the specific ones in your food.

There are exceptions, particularly for major food allergens, but the rule helps explain why the ingredient list doesn’t always provide a complete breakdown of a product’s flavor formulation.

The word “natural” tends to sound reassuring, especially when it’s printed on a product alongside claims about ingredients or quality. But it doesn’t automatically tell you anything about that food’s nutritional value.

According to the FDA, food ingredients must meet the same safety standard whether they’re naturally or artificially derived. The agency has also explained that its longstanding policy concerning the broader term “natural” on food labels was not intended to establish any particular nutritional or health benefit.

So while natural and artificial flavors differ in how they’re sourced, that distinction alone doesn’t establish that one is healthier, more nutritious, or safer than the other. And that feels like a pretty important distinction when you’re trying to make sense of the grocery aisle.

Another distinction worth knowing is that “natural” and “organic” don’t mean the same thing. The USDA has additional requirements for flavorings used in certified organic foods. Under federal organic regulations, manufacturers can use nonsynthetic flavors when organic flavors aren’t commercially available.

Those flavorings must come from organic or nonsynthetic sources and cannot be produced using synthetic solvents, synthetic carrier systems, or artificial preservatives. Those are additional restrictions beyond simply meeting the FDA’s definition of natural flavoring.

So while a conventional food and an organic food might both list natural flavors, that doesn’t necessarily mean the flavorings were produced under identical requirements.

The biggest takeaway is that natural flavors aren’t necessarily something to avoid. They’re just a lot less specific than many may assume. The label tells you that the flavoring meets the FDA’s definition of natural, but it doesn’t necessarily identify the ingredient it came from, explain how it was processed, or reveal every flavoring component. It also doesn’t automatically make the product healthier than something containing artificial flavors.

If you’re curious about what you’re eating, it helps to look beyond those two words. Check the full ingredient list, pay attention to how the product describes its flavor on the front of the package, and contact the manufacturer if you need more specific information about a flavoring’s source.

Ultimately, the most surprising thing about natural flavors is just how little those two words actually reveal.

#6674. What Writing a Book About JFK Jr. Taught Me About Personal Style

John F. Kennedy Jr. wasn’t the first guy to ride a bike wearing a suit. Likewise, the presidential scion and People’s 1988 Sexiest Man Alive didn’t invent the backward Kangol cap, the pinstriped suit, or wearing a waistcoat with jeans—he just did it better than pretty much anybody else. That’s a big part of why he was one of the most photographed men on the planet in the 1990s, and why he remains a menswear moodboard staple today, nearly 30 years after his untimely death. Still, no matter how hard you try, and no matter how closely you hew to the source material, all attempts to replicate JFK Jr.’s style are destined to leave you looking like a runner-up in a Washington Square Park lookalike contest.

Ask anyone who encountered John-John in his prime—which, in my experience, is virtually everyone who lived in Manhattan in the 1990s—and the first thing they’ll mention is his magnetism, his charm, and the fact that, against all odds, he was actually better-looking in person. I know this because, having recently written a book about JFK Jr.’s style, I’ve spent a good part of the last year poring over photos, reading biographies, speaking to people who knew him, and otherwise immersing myself in his world. Among the conclusions I’ve come to is that you probably won’t look as cool as JFK Jr. did wearing rollerblades, but there are a few style moves you can borrow from his playbook without resorting to full Kennedy cosplay.

JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was built on four pillars: tailoring, preppy basics, workwear, and sportswear. But it was the idiosyncratic way he combined them (i.e., a backward baseball cap with a suit, a polo neck sweater under a tweed blazer, hiking boots with tailored trousers) that resulted in some of his most memorable looks. Surprisingly, while the combination of straight-leg jeans, a button-up dress shirt, and a blazer has become shorthand for JFK Jr.’s style, I’ve never seen any evidence of him wearing it. In fact, he seldom wore jeans at all (some speculate his mother thought they looked shabby, while others told me that jeans didn’t complement his active lifestyle). That said, plenty of other ’90s style icons, from Ralph Lauren to Jerry Seinfeld, rocked this particular look, and it’s a pretty easy one to pull off. As with everything about JFK Jr.’s style, it’s not about lifting these combinations wholesale, but understanding the precise balance of contrast that makes them work.

One of the most consistent elements of JFK Jr.’s style was his love of discordant accessories, from his collection of flat caps to his ever-present wallet chain to his Oakley Eye Jacket shades. Some of these were practical—he was so prone to misplacing his wallet and keys that he needed to chain them to his pants—but others reflected his love of color (funky knit caps), his enthusiasm for skiing (fleece headbands), and his passion for travel (various hats picked up on trips to India and Thailand). Some accessories will suit you better than others, but if you have a personal connection to it, all the better. And most importantly, limit yourself to one standout add-on per outfit.

Speaking of accessories: JFK Jr. was a dedicated scarf guy, and he’d pair one with everything from joggers and sneakers to his best navy blue suit. Rather than draping a scarf loosely around his neck, he tended to tie it in either a dressy overhand or classic Parisian knot, both of which lend a more formal look. He also loved wearing a thick scarf as outerwear, throwing it over a sweatshirt on a chilly day instead of a coat, often paired with a knit cap. For best results, don’t pick a scarf that matches the rest of your outfit too closely.

Among the most surprising things I discovered about JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was his watch collection. I wasn’t able to uncover any evidence of him wearing the long-lost Rolex Daytona given to him by Aristotle Onassis (a watch that, if ever found, would give Paul Newman a run for his money), but I did identify an unusually wide range of other pieces in his collection, from a Victorinox Swiss Army field watch to a Swatch chronograph to a vintage Rolex Oyster Perpetual. This is of a piece with everything else we know about JFK Jr.: he wasn’t bound by any single style, brand, or price point, and got just as much enjoyment out of a cheap quartz watch as a luxury mechanical one.

As a rich kid raised on the Upper East Side, JFK Jr.’s closet included plenty of blazers, chinos, and polos. He was a gym rat who loved playing sports, so he also had a lot of sweats, tees, and sneakers. He was a downtown socialite, so he owned a lot of nice suits and tuxes, too. He also had an enviable collection of graphic tees from NYC institutions like the Russian & Turkish Baths in the East Village and the New York Athletic Club, as well as some commemorating events like the 1984 NYC Fresh Festival, a seminal moment in hip-hop history. What stands out to me—and what I believe makes his style so distinctive—is that JFK Jr.’s wardrobe was an authentic reflection of who he was, where he came from, and what he loved. This might be the most important style lesson any of us can learn from him: Great personal style is less about clothes than wearing them in a way that expresses your individuality.

#6673. Schmaltzy Chicken and Stuffing Skillet

While you might think of instant stuffing as a once-a-year darling that makes an annual appearance like Punxsutawney Phil, this recipe is a case study of why this product should be put to use throughout the year. (Boxes of the dried mix can be found near the breadcrumbs any month.) Here, it’s called into action to prop up skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs in a bed of savory stuffing that’s bolstered by aromatics and sweet-tart dried cranberries. Starting with a cold pan ensures even rendering of the chicken fat and crispy skin. The lot gets baked together, allowing the savory drippings from the chicken to soak into the stuffing. Serve with a side of cranberry sauce, a fresh salad, or all by itself for a one-pan dinner that recalls Thanksgiving any night of the week.

More delicious skillet dinners this way: Chicken Thighs With Spiced Couscous and Carrots; Ruffled Mushroom Pot Pie; and One-Skillet Chicken Pot Pie.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Season 2 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (about 4 medium) on both sides with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Pour 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil into a cold large stainless-steel skillet and swirl to coat bottom of pan. Arrange chicken, skin side down, in pan and place over medium-high heat. Cook undisturbed, rotating pan around on burner often to promote even browning, until skin is browned and chicken releases easily from pan, 7–10 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet or large plate and arrange skin side up.

Combine 1 large onion, finely chopped, 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, and 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan and cook over medium-high heat, stirring often, until onion is softened and just starting to turn golden, 8–12 minutes. Add one 6-oz. box instant stuffing mix, ½ cup unsweetened dried cranberries, and 1¼ cups water, then finely grate in zest from 1 lemon and set lemon aside. Mix until stuffing is hydrated. Remove pan from heat and push stuffing to sides to create wells for chicken to rest in. Nestle thighs, skin side up, into stuffing. Transfer pan to oven and bake until chicken is cooked through and top of stuffing is golden brown and crisp, 45–55 minutes.

Top chicken and stuffing with more dried cranberries and reserved celery leaves. Cut reserved lemon into wedges and serve alongside for squeezing over.

#6672. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6670. Apple Cinnamon Bread

Sorry, banana bread, there’s a new quick bread coming for the crown. Bursting with chunks of cinnamon apples, this easy bread is a MAJOR hit come fall. Gone apple picking? It's the perfect baking project to use up some of those goodies. Don't worry, you'll still have enough for apple pie, too. Our secret weapon? Orange juice! This loaf is perfectly balanced, not too sweet, and tender and fluffy. It pairs well with a cup of tea or coffee, but you can also totally eat it by itself as a festive midday snack.

What People Are Saying:"This is a ridiculously delicious recipe! Really might be the best sweet loaf I've ever had/made." -GoldPin

"Wonderful recipe making it today for the third time!" -GreenSnow

Start by preheating your oven to 350° and lining a 9x5-inch loaf pan with parchment paper. Now you are ready to make your apple mixture! First, core and slice your apples into chunks, about 1 inch in thickness. In a large bowl, stir together chopped apples, lemon juice, brown sugar, and cinnamon until your apples are evenly coated in the sugar and spice mixture. Set this bowl aside, and get started on your batter.

In another large bowl, using a hand mixer, cream together butter and sugar until light and fluffy—about 2-5 minutes. Scrape the sides of the bowl continually to ensure everything is evenly combined. Then, add in your eggs and vanilla and beat until smooth. In a separate bowl, whisk together flour and baking powder. Then add this dry mixture to your butter mixture, keeping your mixing on low. Be careful not to over mix, which will result in an overly dense cake! Add in your orange juice and mix until just combined.

Now that your batter is done, scoop half of it into a greased loaf pan, spreading it out with a butter knife or the back of a spoon. Then spoon in half the apple mixture. Top this with the remaining batter, then press in the remaining apples on top.

Now your loaf is ready for the oven! Bake until your loaf is golden and a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake comes out clean, about 1 hour and 15 minutes. Let cool completely. Enjoy!

This apple cinnamon bread can be stored, covered, at room temperature for 3 to 4 days. You can also wrap it tightly in plastic wrap, then wrap it with foil or place it in a freezer-safe zip-top bag, and freeze for up to 3 months.

#6669. 14 Best Work Jackets for Men 2026, According to GQ Editors

For better or worse, the best work jackets for men are no longer associated with garages, factory floors, and loading docks. Instead, as the likes of Paul Mescal and Austin Butler (who told GQ he wore his for a year straight) continue to fly their flag, a great work jacket has become every guy's fastest route to semi-rugged heartthrob style.

Honestly, they make looking good almost too easy. First, they inject your fits with casual, weekend tough-guy energy. (This, to be clear, is a plus.) Second, they flatter you in all the right places, framing your shoulders and neatening up your waistline whether you’re pairing them with jeans or the kinds of wide, puddling trousers we've long been yapping about.

Better still, you don’t have to spend a fortune. The classics from Dickies and Carhartt are as dependable as ever, and even the independent designer options are within reach of your budget—this is a cotton-forward option, after all. Here are 14 of our favorites, all of which will only look better after a few years (and a few scuffs) of real wear.

The Carhartt Detroit work jacket is the classic for a reason. It’s been around for more than 70 years—not quite as old as blue jeans or cowboy boots, but easily in the upper echelon of American fashion’s great exports. So much so that today, luxury brands are riffing on it, even selling pre-distressed, washed-down versions at triple the price. (And yes, this is also the work jacket that Austin Butler told us he wears.)

Cut to the waist, and built from thick, stiff canvas with three perfectly placed front pockets, the Detroit is an Eisenhower-style silhouette (during WWII, the then-Army General overhauled U.S. military dress and introduced the cropped, boxy jacket to American forces). Its insulated blanket lining and corduroy collar also make it one of the few true year-round, toasty work jackets out there. Simply put, this is a real piece of clothing for real life. (Though if it's not fancy enough for you, there’s always the street-ready, slimmer, unlined Carhartt WIP version.)

Just like Dickies' iconic 874 work pants, the brand's insulated Eisenhower jacket (there he is again) is a hard-wearing, warm, wallet-friendly piece of gear that fits incredibly well. Nearly as old as the Detroit Jacket above, it doesn’t always get the same respect. But maybe that's just because it flies a little more under the radar, with its logo patch tucked discreetly near the hem. Decades in, it remains a low-key, low-cost icon—less shouty than its Carhartt cousin, but every bit as authentic.

Wallace & Barnes, J.Crew's workwear line, is back with tough fabrics, heritage details, and a big hit of #menswear-era nostalgia—and this wool-lined work jacket shows exactly why folks missed it so much. It has all of the heartthrob-coded details you probably had in mind when you decided to look for a jacket like this: Corduroy collar, zippered chest pocket, slightly cropped fit. But it isn't just good-looking. It also has a wool-blend blanket lining, for superior warmth to help you enjoy it even if the depths of winter. And that, if cost-per-wear logic still applies, makes it more than worth its slightly higher price point.

Welcome to the world of truly warm fabrics, and actually glove-friendly pockets. Filson’s been mastering cold-weather gear since your great-great-grandfather was in short pants, and this work jacket continues that legacy. Based on the brand’s original 1914 Cruiser, it’s cut from 24-ounce Mackinaw wool — a tightly woven twill that truly blocks wind, sheds rain, and stays warm even when wet. Without being mean, it’s built to outlast even you. Pricey? Sure. But it’s the kind of thing your kids will remember you by (and fight for) someday.

Buck Mason’s archive is full to bursting with vintage pieces from decades past, which explains why its collections are filled with absolute bangers these days. Here the brand has taken a mid-century work jacket and remade it, tweaking the fit to make it a touch more relaxed, and using a soft Italian doeskin cotton fabric that’s more plush than anything a worksite would have issued back in the day. There's even more to love in the details: Shoulder pleats for easy movement, real horn buttons on the chest pockets, and a dressy point collar.

For Lo-heads, Polo Ralph Lauren's hard-wearing zipper jackets are the stuff of legend. And while you might have grown up with an inherited cotton example from your dad, in the last decade of so, Polo has been pushing its ‘Bi-Swing’ polyester and/or nylon takes instead. That's fine, but some of us aren't so willing to trade in the soft, rugged comfort of a full-cotton jacket. That's where the rarer Bayport Poplin jacket comes in. A work jacket with no delusions, it’s not stealing the working man’s valor — it knows exactly what it is. It’s Ralph Lauren, and it knows you’re working hard at hardly working. But it's also strong enough to handle whatever activities you throw at it, leisure or otherwise.

Sure, Copenhagen's Mfpen has its silhouettes dialed, but don't overlook its fabrications. Here, it’s a dense wool-blend with a multi-tonal yarn construction. Textured, substantive, perfect.

While most waxed cotton jackets lean more country estate than work site, Tom Beckbe's high-quality range include a few closer, more modern fits. Perfect for those looking for a work jacket that's also waterproof.

A designer-adjacent example for the fashion crowd, this piece from South Korea's FrizmWORKS doesn't just look good, it feels good too, thanks to that soft leather collar that's just buttery once it's flipped up.

Stan Ray is part of what you might call the big three of American workwear, alongside Dickies and Carhartt). The Texas-born brand’s aptly named Roughneck Jacket delivers exactly what you’d expect. It’s tough, practical, and built for wear. Ribbed cuffs keep the cold out, while the washed-out hue delivers a perfectly broken-in look from day one.

This jacket from New York's Corridor—made from a hefty cotton-blend twill—is a more colorful take on the work jacket, and bound to give any fall fit a lift.

Just as the Polo jacket above is an RL icon, so is this faithfully-recreated nautical deck jacket from Ralph's RRL line. It's restocked every fall, it sells out every fall.

A key feature of all work jackets is their shorter length, but for those of us who want to make sure ours hits right at the belt, look no further than Abercrombie’s entry.

A leading Parisian purveyor of vintage garms, BRUT has recently moved into making its own stuff, all rooted in the archival vintage styles they obsess over. The results are, how you say, on point.

These days, work jackets seem to have an undeniable stranglehold on the imagination of guys who spend all day staring at their keyboards. (There’s a political element to this, of course. Whether or not you act in solidarity with your fellow laborers under capitalism, a work jacket allows you to look the part of the everyman.) But also, they’re just a great jacket for busy lives! There’s a generally accommodating cut that doesn’t restrict your movement, plenty of pockets, and hardy materials that can easily handle a snag, or sudden shower.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6668. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

This year’s honorees are a varied and buzzy cohort: Anthony Vaccarello was named International Designer of the Year for his decade of work at Saint Laurent; Gap Inc. will receive the Innovation Award presented by Amazon Fashion and presented by Demi Moore; Tory Burch will receive the Positive Change Award; photographers Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin have been selected as this year’s Geoffrey Beene Lifetime Achievement Award recipients; Linda Fargo will take home the Founder’s Award in honor of Eleanor Lambert; Eva Chen will accept the Media Award in honor of Eugenia Sheppard; the Isabel Toledo Board of Directors’ Tribute will be presented to Susan Cianciolo; and the Fashion Icon Award will be presented to architect Peter Marino.

#6666. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6665. The Halloween Candy That Matches Your Zodiac Sign, According To An Astrologer

Whether you fully commit to spooky season or prefer to keep things low-key, you can’t truly celebrate Halloween without enjoying some candy. Different sweets have cultivated fierce brand loyalties. But the key to finding your favorite Halloween candy may be hiding among the stars.

We consulted astrologer and author Lisa Stardust to find which candy best reflects each zodiac sign's personality. From old-school chocolates to wild, wacky treats, her choices span the full sweet spectrum.

Aries is defined by its bold and ambitious approach to life. Stardust describes the cardinal fire sign as “passionate, electrifying, and intense.” But Aries can also be a bit impulsive. “You never know what you’re going to get next based on their emotions,” she adds.

In honor of Aries’ fiery spirit, Stardust chooses Hot Tamales as the candy that best reflects the sign. With its vibrant red hue, intense spice, and unapologetic cinnamon-forward flavor, there’s no better sweet to symbolize the sign.

Compared to Aries' bold energy, Taurus is decidedly more practical. The earth sign is known for being stable, dependable, and guided by logic over emotion. While Taurus may resist change, the sign also has good taste and knows its way around the finer things in life.

And what candy represents that tried-and-true energy better than a classic bar of Hershey’s milk chocolate? “They’re both iconic and never go out of style,” Stardust explains. “Their tastes might be simple, but they’re always decadent and indulgent.”

Gemini is the astrological embodiment of street smarts. The air sign is very astute, with the uncanny ability to read a room and adapt accordingly. This perceptiveness translates to strong social skills and the ability to elevate the mood of any room.

The candy that best reflects this energy is, unsurprisingly, Smarties. “Geminis are intellectual, and they have a little bit of zest to them,” explains Stardust. “They’re sugary and sweet but also a little messy.”

The cardinal water sign is not shy about expressing emotions. Cancers are best described as the teddy bears of the zodiac: sensitive, empathetic, and the embodiment of comfort. Those with Cancer in their chart are prone to shielding others from their complex emotions, but make no mistake—there are a lot of feelings.

A candy that matches Cancer’s mushy inner self is Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups. “They are very protective on the outside, but they're tender on the inside,” Stardust says.

Leo can’t help but be the life of the party. The fire sign is very extroverted, with a personality so big it verges on theatrical. Stardust describes Leos as “fun and flamboyant,” even if they sometimes get on other people’s nerves.

In her opinion, the sweets that represent Leo best are Twizzlers. Stardust notes that you “can have a lot of fun eating them,” whether it’s peeling them apart or biting off the ends to use as a straw. If it involves playing with your food, it’s perfect for Leo.

Virgos are Type A to their cores. The earth sign has a precise attention to detail and is always looking to solve problems. But the constant focus on logic and perfection often obscures a deep well of emotions.

“There’s more to them than you may think, and there’s definitely another flavor to them on the inside, because they’re ruled by Mercury,” Stardust explains. The candy that best mirrors this energy is a York Peppermint Patty. The seemingly simple chocolate exterior hides a sweet, sharp minty center (if that’s not Virgo, I don’t know what is).

Libra is represented by scales, which reflects the air sign’s desire for fairness and justice. The empathetic and compassionate Libra tends to consider all points of view to make the most measured decisions that’ll make everyone happy. (But sometimes, that may mean not making a decision at all.)

Libra’s balanced approach to life is why Stardust chooses Twix as their ideal candy. Left Twix or right Twix? Thankfully, Libra doesn’t have to choose. “They’re a package deal,” Stardust says. So whether they want to enjoy both or share with someone else, Libras are Twix’s target audience.

Scorpios embody the phrase, “looks like they could kill you, is a cinnamon roll.” The water sign is often misunderstood. While undoubtedly intense, Scorpio’s dark, almost brooding exterior hides a lot of emotional complexity.

The sign shares a lot of characteristics with one candy in particular: Sour Patch Kids. “They have a really deep personality to them; they’re sweet with a sharp, tangy bite.” And, like the multicolored gummy treats, Scorpio is the true manifestation of “sour, sweet, gone.”

Sagittarius is seemingly always on a journey—whether it be physical, emotional, or spiritual. The fire sign is known as an explorer, with lofty aspirations and an aversion to playing it safe.

This energy is exactly why Stardust chooses 3 Musketeers as the quintessential Sagittarius sweet. “The namesake is adventurous, and it speaks for itself,” she explains.

When you need someone reliable, responsible, and grounded, you can’t go wrong with a Capricorn. This pragmatic, logical earth sign is incredibly goal-oriented and has the Type A personality to make it happen.

How many licks does it take to get to the center of a Tootsie Pop? Capricorn may be the only sign in the zodiac that’s disciplined enough to find out, which is why Stardust chooses the lollipop as their ideal candy. “It’s a classic, just like Capricorn,” she says. “They’re traditional, steady, strong, and you have to have patience to eat them.”

Aquarius marches to the beat of its own drummer. The air sign loves to be a contrarian and will unapologetically take the road less traveled. Nothing is too unique or too strange for Aquarius.

And what candy matches that energy better than a bag of Pop Rocks? “They’re unexpected and veer from the norm of traditional candy,” Stardust explains. They’re shocking, surprising, and delightful in their own special way—just like Aquarius loves to be.

Pisces always seems to have its head in the clouds. The water sign has a dreamy, romantic approach to life and has an extremely vivid imagination. “They feel all the feels,” Stardust explains.

Pisces needs a candy that can keep up mentally and emotionally, which is why she chooses Skittles as their ideal sweet. “It’s all about the rainbow and the imagination,” Stardust says. “They get to taste the rainbow and all of the sensations in every bite.”

#6664. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

AI companies know they are being held hostage by each other, and that they need to take action to self-regulate before they suffer major reputational and legal consequences. There is a blueprint on how they can do it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The largest artificial intelligence (AI) firms increasingly understand that they are hostages of one another. If one firm pushes ahead recklessly, others may feel compelled to follow. If one deploys a dangerous model without adequate safeguards, others may see it as a green light to do the same.

The debate over AI has centered on what governments should do to regulate this frontier technology. That remains essential. But a more immediate question is emerging: Can the companies building these powerful systems take action independently before they lose credibility and suffer legal consequences?

That question no longer looks theoretical and is being recognized as an urgent challenge. We've already seen AI firms lose control of their models — for example, in Australia, a rogue AI hacked a government healthcare website. If we are not careful, it's only a matter of time before one of these incidents causes large-scale, real-world harm, like shutting down an electricity grid or municipal water system, or a mass misdiagnosis in a health system. If this trend continues, the entire industry could become tarnished.

But there is a blueprint for self-regulation in a risky business: the nuclear industry, which has built up layers of oversight, controls and self-scrutiny over decades.

Frontier AI may require something similar: private regulation among competitors that do not trust one another but have a mutual interest in preventing outcomes that could damage them all. This does not appeal to the better angels of human nature — it's self-preservation for the industry itself.

There is a historical precedent for this kind of arrangement. The nuclear sector did not become safe because every actor suddenly became benevolent. It became safer through a layered system of peer scrutiny, technical standards, information-sharing and external oversight. International organizations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), which was established in 1957, emerged to coordinate monitoring and verification, while national regulators and industry bodies gradually built professional norms around catastrophic risk.

The result was not perfect safety, as the Chernobyl disaster in 1986 clearly attests. But nuclear governance architecture is designed around the recognition that in high-risk technological systems, one actor's failure can become everyone's problem. This was seen following Chernobyl: global nuclear safety increased significantly after the disaster, with upgrades to reactor designs, improved training and international monitoring networks.

In the aftermath of the Chernobyl disaster, safety and regulation in the global nuclear industry increased.

And this movement to self-regulation also occurred in the U.S. nuclear sector, following the Three-Mile Island nuclear accident near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, in 1979. The reactor suffered a partial meltdown after a relatively minor cooling malfunction. Investigations later revealed design flaws in instruments and alarms, along with inadequate emergency response training, were the root cause of the incident.

The event nearly killed the nuclear energy industry in the U.S., causing public support to fall from a record high of 69% in 1977 to 46%t in 1979. The entire industry suffered because of failures at one facility. In response, the U.S. nuclear industry established the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations (INPO) in December 1979 to improve operational safety.

The analogy to AI should not be overstated. Nuclear materials are easier to count than algorithms, and nuclear facilities are harder to hide than model weights. The outcomes of a catastrophic AI blunder are also less existential, although its use in weapon systems is not without risk. In September, an AI hallucination almost led to the U.S. intercepting a Chinese ship suspected of carrying nuclear material to Iran.

Yet the comparison remains useful because the core governance problem is similar. In both cases, competitors operate in an environment where the downside risk of unchecked rivalry is borne by society while the upside is private gain for these firms. The challenge is to create institutions that make restraint the rational default — even when no actor fully trusts the others, and the inner workings of the industry are not readily visible to outsiders.

For AI, that could mean reciprocal evaluation of frontier models before deployment, secure mechanisms for sharing safety information, agreed red lines around certain capabilities, and independent third parties empowered to audit compliance. Such mechanisms would not replace government regulation. They would instead serve as an intermediate layer: stronger than voluntary ethics statements but more adaptive and technically informed than legislation alone can often be in fast-moving domains. The state would act as a background enforcer.

AI governance is often discussed as if the only choices were laissez-faire innovation or heavy-handed state control. History suggests a third path.

AI executives appear willing to look for solutions too, with Elon Musk recently suggesting a peer-review system before advanced model release, and Demis Hassabis, co-founder and chair of Google DeepMind, putting forward a framework for an AI Standards Body, similar to the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority.

Skeptics will object, with reason, that industry-led governance can become cartel behavior or public-relations theater. Companies may use "safety" language to entrench incumbency, slow rivals or deflect binding regulation. Those are real dangers. The lesson from nuclear history is not that private coordination works automatically. It is that private coordination works only when nested inside a broader system of transparency, verification and public authority. Without those elements, private regulation becomes little more than trust-me rhetoric.

Still, dismissing private regulation altogether would be a mistake. Governments do not yet possess the technical capacity, speed or international alignment needed to oversee frontier AI on their own. And if the leading labs already see themselves as bound together by shared exposure to catastrophic risk, that recognition can become the basis for institutional design. The question is how to turn mutual fear into durable rules.

That is where the nuclear analogy is most powerful. It reminds us that industries facing existential hazards do not need perfect trust in order to cooperate. They need mechanisms that make cooperation preferable to defection. In practice, that means inspections, peer review, incident reporting, professional norms and a state-backed enforcement perimeter. AI governance is often discussed as if the only choices were laissez-faire innovation or heavy-handed state control. History suggests a third path: structured private coordination under public shadow.

The real opportunity, then, is not to celebrate the newfound (apparent) prudence of technology executives, it is to recognize what their comments reveal. When even fierce rivals begin to argue for mutual scrutiny, they are admitting that competition alone cannot govern the frontier. That admission should be treated not as reassurance but as evidence that the risk has become collective.

The policy task now is to build institutions that fit that reality. Governments should push for mandatory reporting, independent evaluation and legal backstops. But they should also encourage enforceable forms of peer oversight among the handful of firms whose systems may shape the trajectory of the technology. Frontier AI is becoming an industry in which the leading actors are hostages of one another. The nuclear age showed that such conditions can produce serious governance. The hope is that AI firms learn that lesson before they learn the cost of ignoring it at the peril of the public at large.

Opinion on Live Science gives you insight on the most important issues in science that affect you and the world around you today, written by experts and leading scientists in their field.

Akhil Bhardwaj is an Associate Professor of Strategy and Organization at the University of Bath, UK. He studies extreme events, which range from organizational disasters to radical innovation. Akhil is interested in the epistemological problem of understanding the underlying dynamics that lead up to these events. He also studies how thinking can be improved as well as the implications of AI adoption in the context of strategic management, entrepreneurship, and high-risk systems. His work is philosophically grounded in pragmatism. Prior to joining academia, Akhil has worked as an engineer and manager at CAT., Inc and consulted as a SOX compliance analyst in the U.S.

#6662. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6661. Failproof Homestyle Chicken Kari

This recipe is inspired by the garam masala my mother used to make back in India. Just a pinch adds incredible depth and flavor to both meat and vegetable dishes—it’s the secret ingredient that often leaves my guests wondering why my Indian food tastes so exceptional. And now you can use it too! This version perfectly balances the warming notes of cloves and nutmeg, and it’s the one I return to time and time again. If you prefer a sweeter blend, add more cinnamon and fennel seeds; if you want a spicier kick, increase the black pepper and cloves.

In a small bowl, toss 12 dried bay leaves, 12 whole cloves, 5 black cardamom pods, 4 whole star anise pods, three 3" (7.5-cm) cinnamon sticks, 1 whole nutmeg, 3 Tbsp. coriander seeds, 3 Tbsp. whole mace fronds, 2 Tbsp. cumin seeds, 1 Tbsp. black peppercorns, and 2 tsp. white poppy seeds to combine.

Heat a medium dry skillet over low heat until hot. Add the spice mixture and toast until slightly fragrant, about 45 seconds. Transfer back to the bowl and let cool.

Transfer the whole nutmeg to a mortar and break into smaller pieces with a pestle (this is just to make it easier to grind, so don’t worry about being too precise!). Repeat with the cinnamon. Tear the bay leaves into smaller pieces. Transfer all of the spices to a spice grinder and grind into a fine powder (it will be slightly warm when you remove the lid). Transfer to an airtight container (do not cover yet) and let cool completely. Then close the lid.

Do Ahead: Garam masala can be made 1 month ahead. Cover and store in a cool, dark place.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

In a small pan over medium-high heat, warm 2 Tbsp. peanut oil or any vegetable oil or avocado oil until it shimmers. Add 1 tsp. cumin seeds and cook until fragrant and they start to turn brown, about 1 minute. Be careful not to let the seeds burn or they will taste bitter. Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Serve immediately or let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

To a mortar and pestle or food processor, add one 2" (5-cm) piece fresh ginger, chopped, 4 garlic cloves, peeled, and 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, chopped, and pound or pulse into a chunky paste. To a medium bowl, add 2 lb. (910 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, excess fat trimmed, cut into 2" [5-cm] pieces, along with the ginger-garlic paste and 1 tsp. fine sea salt and toss to combine. Cover and place in the refrigerator to marinate for a minimum of 1 hour or overnight.

In a medium heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-low heat, warm ⅓ cup (80 ml) vegetable oil or avocado oil, then add 1 tsp. cumin seeds, ½ tsp. black mustard seeds, ½ tsp. black peppercorns, 5 whole cloves, 1 fresh or dried bay leaf, 1 star anise, and one 3" [7.5-cm] cinnamon stick, broken into small pieces, and lightly toast and until fragrant, about 1 minute. Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Add ½ cup (120 ml) water and mix again. Cover and cook until the chicken is cooked through and tender, 30 minutes, stirring halfway through.

Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

Do Ahead: Store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 1 month.
