#6660. Roxie Nafousi’s 5 Biggest Business Lessons From Closing Her Fragrance Brand

Roxie Nafousi knows a thing or two about turning an audience into a business. The self-development coach and manifestation author has sold two million books since 2022, all the while building a lucrative ecosystem spanning an app, workshops and other products like journals and affirmation cards all centered on personal development. Translating that community into a successful consumer brand, however, proved a different challenge.

With Alia, her fragrance line, Nafousi set out to create something that could extend beyond her own personal brand. “I genuinely believed that we could create a major international fragrance brand,” she says over Zoom. “I hoped it would expand beyond fragrance into candles and incense. I thought the sky was the limit, and I felt so full of hope and excitement.”

The reality was a little more complicated: production delays, disagreements with a business partner and a resulting larger-than-expected financial commitment (£300,000 in total, against an originally expected £50,000 investment) all put pressure on the business. And while a high-profile launch that included celebrity events and retail placements seemed promising, delayed inventory and lackluster sales compounded the challenges. A cease-and-desist letter from a global brand ultimately brought the venture to a close, which Nafousi announced earlier this week on her personal Instagram.

Speaking to Vogue Business exclusively in the days after, Nafousi says a big part of the struggle was comparing online narratives of success with her own journey. “Social media is full of stories about people who create a brand and sell out overnight. There’s so much of that, and not nearly enough of the reality that it’s really hard and sometimes things don’t work out,” she says. “I really want people to make sure they understand what they’re getting into.”

“During the first few months [of launching Alia], when sales were trickling in and things weren’t really happening, I felt ashamed,” Nafousi adds. “I thought, ‘Oh my God, I’m irrelevant. I was so stupid to think I could make this work.’ I was comparing myself with these amazing brands, so it took me time to realize that not succeeding in my fragrance business wasn’t a failure. It was an amazing lesson.”

Here, Nafousi reveals her five biggest business lessons off the back of the brand.

The rise of the creator-founder has fueled a popular narrative whereby building a social media following is a natural precursor to building a consumer business. Big online followings can theoretically bypass some of the traditional barriers to launching a brand, from customer acquisition to building trust, but appetite for someone’s content or recommendations does not necessarily translate into demand for an entirely different category.

“It’s absolutely not a given that you can have an audience for one thing and expect them to transfer easily over to another,” Nafousi says. “Attention is not the same as demand. So many people confuse the number of followers they have with the number of people who actually want to spend their own money on something they create.”

In Alia’s case, Nafousi believed there was a natural connection between the fragrance brand and the world she built around self-development and empowerment, with scent offering another way for women to embody different parts of themselves. Its debut Alter Ego collection featured fragrances named Main Character, Power House and Scene Stealer, reflecting the themes that had become central to Nafousi’s personal brand across her Manifest and Confidence books.

“I did think that, because the messages were aligned, it would make sense,” she says. “I talk about empowerment and becoming the best version of yourself, and to me, Alia was just an extension of that. I definitely thought my audience would understand it.”

In hindsight, Nafousi believes more market and consumer research could have established whether fragrance was the right category in the first place. “People’s money is precious, and the way they spend it is changing. You need to do the research into what they actually want from you. What’s missing from their lives? What do they need? And just because you love something doesn’t mean someone else will,” she says. “I’d probably challenge myself more.”

Initially expected to invest £50,000 in Alia through a 50-50 partnership, Nafousi unfortunately found herself having to buy out her business partner when the relationship became strained. Her initial investment effectively doubled, while costs continued to mount as she took on additional responsibilities within the business. Nafousi found herself having to recruit additional support, bringing unexpected recruitment fees and a new salary into the equation alongside lawyers and accountants.

“The money and investment required were far greater than I’d imagined. There just seemed to be bills coming out of nowhere. I remember getting a bill for £70,000 in January this year, and I couldn’t understand where it had come from. It was production costs,” she says. The financial pressure then extended to decisions around how much inventory to commit to. For Nafousi, having sold two million copies of her book, 12,000 starting units felt relatively modest by comparison, but surplus stock and resulting production delays quickly became an issue.

“That was a big mistake, ordering far too much stock at the beginning,” she says. There were also problems with the timing of production: the perfumes arrived late, missing the initial momentum. “I really wouldn’t do it alone. I’d find the right partner, someone I’d gone through some shit with first. I’d really ask them how they deal with conflict and get to know their communication style, to make sure we could handle things together as a team.”

“For me, the most interesting thing was that we had all the ingredients you’d expect to work,” Nafousi says. “We had incredible press and huge events attended by so many wonderful celebrities, influencers and other people. All the ingredients were there for a great launch that should have translated into sales.”

Yet generating attention is only part of the challenge. With consumers becoming more selective about their spending and competition for visibility intensifying, brands face growing costs to acquire customers. “In general, we’re seeing that consumers are much more mindful of their spending,” Nafousi says. “It takes a lot more to acquire a customer than it used to. There’s so much competition, and consumers are bombarded with things. You can’t simply post something on your Stories or your feed and say, ‘Guys, I’ve got this thing,’ and expect that to be enough anymore.”

The unpredictability of organic reach can also lead to brands spending heavily on content and imagery without necessarily engaging a meaningful audience. For founders, this makes it important to diversify their marketing efforts rather than relying on social media alone, testing different ways to reach and engage potential customers. “The algorithm fucks us all, really. I might have spent so much money on social media and having someone create beautiful imagery for Alia, but nobody’s seeing it. Maybe 100 people are seeing it.”

Nafousi also found that some of the launch strategies commonly used by similar brands — such as gifting products to influencers — generated visibility without necessarily prompting purchases. What proved more effective was a direct appeal to her own community. Nafousi invited followers who genuinely wanted to try Alia to receive the product in exchange for sharing their thoughts. The resulting user-generated content, often from those with relatively small audiences, performed better than traditional gifting.

In-person activations also helped bridge the gap between awareness and purchase. At her Manifest Live show, a pop-up store allowed attendees to smell the fragrance and interact with the product, an experience she says performed particularly well.

For many emerging brands, securing a retail partnership can feel like a major milestone. “Having spoken to a lot of other founders, I’ve heard the same thing repeatedly. They get so excited about getting into retail that they don’t realize how much money they then have to spend to maintain their position and earn their place on the shelves,” she says. Retailers want to see that brands are generating sales, Nafousi explains, yet driving those conversions can require more spending on marketing and in-store visibility.

Early on, Alia supplied Lookfantastic with around 3,000 specially made 10ml fragrances for its advent calendar — assuming it would influence the decisions of further retailers and consumers to buy into the brand. While the initiative put the product into thousands of consumers’ hands, it didn’t directly drive sales. “I was so excited, because it was right at the beginning of the journey. We were getting the product into the hands of around 3,000 people, which was really fun,” Nafousi says. “But it was also quite a big expense.”

There were exceptions. Violet Grey, the US beauty retailer known for its tightly curated selection, performed particularly well for Alia. Nafousi believes the retailer’s niche positioning and trusted relationship with its customers helped the brand connect with the right audience. The value of a retail partnership, therefore, depends not simply on the number of doors a brand enters, but on whether the retailer’s customer base and positioning align with the product.

For founders, persistence is often celebrated, but knowing when to stop investing in a business can be just as important as having the conviction to start one.

Although production delays and packaging issues created friction in the early stages, Nafousi saw them as common setbacks. “At that point, I thought, ‘You know what? Every founder has these issues,’ so I wasn’t particularly worried about it,” she says. The bigger concern came when sales failed to gain traction. “I wanted to close it down when we launched. I think we made about two sales in the first week. The following week, there were no sales. Then, there was one sale. It was so deflating.”

Still, discovery sets were yet to launch and a forthcoming Space NK listing offered another opportunity to build momentum. Nafousi continued experimenting with sampling and brand activations, but soon realized that greater investment in advertising and awareness was needed. “I just thought, ‘God, I don’t know if I’m ready to invest even more money when I don’t know whether it’s going to work,’” she explains.

Nafousi was also approached by potential investors midway through the journey, but turned them down to keep her autonomy. “If I wanted to say, ‘You know what? I’m going to close this down,’ I didn’t want to lose that freedom,” she says. Ultimately, the decision to close Alia was made for her when she received a cease-and-desist letter from another brand operating under a similar name, giving her until December 31 to sell all remaining stock. Although she could have rebranded to continue trading, Nafousi saw it as a sign that it was time to move on. “I genuinely believe I manifested it in some way. I think it was a gift from the universe.”

Now, she is viewing the experience as one of growth. “The way I see it is that every entrepreneur will have something along their journey that doesn’t work out the way they hoped,” she says.

In her confidence book, one of the central tenets is learning to do hard things. “It’s not about feeling like you’re able to do everything or that you’re amazing at everything. A big part of confidence is knowing that even when things go wrong, you can handle it. That’s the resilience part. It’s knowing that I’m going to be able to cope with whatever comes my way, and I feel that now more than ever.”

#6659. Instant Pot Mac & Cheese

Instant Pot meals are THE hack to make dinner prep and clean-up a walk in the park. If it’s one of those nights when you can’t be bothered to pull out all the pots and pans for an elaborate meal but still want a tasty dinner, this recipe is for you. Mac and cheese is already the ultimate comfort food, but this recipe makes it practically effortless. Just toss everything into the pot, let the Instant Pot work its magic, and get ready for a big bowl of cheesy goodness. Before you know it, you'll have the cheesiest mac and cheese on your hands, perfect for a satisfying weeknight dinner or an easy, last-minute BBQ side.

Start by grabbing your Instant Pot or any other pressure cooker. Pour in the water, then add the macaroni, butter, mustard, paprika, and a teaspoon of salt. Secure the lid, set it to Manual on High Pressure, and let it cook for 4 minutes. Once it’s done, quickly release the pressure according to your machine’s instructions. When the pressure has fully released, go ahead and open the lid.

Stir in cheddar, Fontina, milk, and Parmesan until melted and combined.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

If you have any leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for around 3-4 days.

#6658. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

Gigantopithecus was the largest primate that ever lived. What would have happened when human ancestors encountered it?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At nearly 10 feet (3 meters) tall and around 500 pounds (230 kilograms), Gigantopithecus was the largest primate that ever lived.

Foraging across the dense tropical forests of Southeast Asia between 2 million and 200,000 years ago, the giant ape may have shared the habitat with new arrivals — hominins such as Homo erectus. (Hominins are members of the group that includes modern humans, their ancestors and closely related species, after the evolutionary split from great apes.)

Despite their immense size Gigantopithecus mainly consumed plants and is closely related to modern-day orangutans.

So what would have happened when Gigantopithecus encountered these human ancestors?

Experts suggested a variety of possible scenarios, including that Gigantopithecus and human ancestors didn't encounter each other at all.

It's "very difficult to say with any certainty, as we have no direct evidence documenting interactions between Gigantopithecus and human ancestors," Renaud Joannes-Boyau, director of higher-degree research training at Southern Cross University in Australia and an archaeologist who has conducted extensive research into human evolution, told Live Science in an email.

What would have happened if hominins encountered Gigantopithecus?

"That said, if we look at the broader pattern of human evolution, our lineage [Homo] has consistently behaved as an apex predator," Joannes-Boyau said. "Humans and our ancestors have shown a remarkable tendency to explore, exploit and, at times, eliminate large animals that shared their environment. I think it is reasonable to imagine that those interactions may have involved a mixture of indifference, curiosity and violence, depending on the circumstances."

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

Friedemann Schrenk, a professor of paleobiology at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz in Germany, thinks Gigantopithecus would have likely tried to avoid humans. "Humans were and are the most aggressive primates ever on earth using tools and weapons and were probably encroaching on Gigantopithecus habitats," he told Live Science in an email. Homo erectus made use of hand axes and possibly hafted spears.

Schrenk envisions the hypothetical interactions as similar to those between modern-day humans and orangutans, which has resulted in humans encroaching on orangutan habitats and the apes' populations declining. "After all, Gigantopithecus was a gigantic orangutan," he said, noting that if there was hostility in a direct encounter, early humans would have been the aggressors.

Yet it's also possible that Gigantopithecus and hominins lived in different environments in Southeast Asia, which would have minimized the number of interactions they had, said Hervé Bocherens, a professor of biogeology at the University of Tübingen in Germany.

Fossilized Gigantopithecus jawbones suggest that the giant ape's diet was plant-based.

The "carbon stable isotopic ratios measured on some teeth of both taxa suggest a different habitat, closed forests for Gigantopithecus and open savannah for Homo erectus," Bocherens told Live Science in an email. However, because of limited data, "we cannot exclude that some hominins were also present in more forested environments," he added. Grinding patterns in their teeth suggest that Gigantopithecus' diet was essentially plant-based and may have included bamboo.

In a 2024 study, scientists investigated the demise of Gigantopithecus and found no evidence that hominins contributed to Gigantopithecus' extinction. Instead, they determined that the main cause was environmental change that resulted in a reduction in the forested environment where Gigantopithecus lived and foraged. In fact, hominins and Gigantopithecus may not have encountered each other at all, Yingqi Zhang, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and first author of the paper, told Live Science in an email.

We can only imagine what hominins would have thought when they glimpsed these gigantic creatures. It’s not clear how hominins and Gigantopithecus would have interacted, if they ever did, said Frido Welker, a professor of biomolecular paleoanthropology at the University of Copenhagen. He thinks they would have avoided each other but they may have "been in awe when they did happen to run into each other."

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6656. Chicken Pozole Verde

This chicken pozole verde recipe puts a whole bird to work, making a fragrant broth and plenty of tender shredded meat in one go. Roasted tomatillos and a mix of green chiles give the Mexican stew its tang and heat; a final swirl of cilantro purée adds fresh flavor and turns the whole pot brilliantly green.

The tomatillos and peppers roast while the chicken simmers. Toasting the canned hominy—a tip from Test Kitchen alum Rick Martinez—gives it a flavor “almost like a corn nut.” But if that’s one step too many, skip it—the stew will still be awesome.

Set out red onion, cilantro, dried oregano, and lime wedges, and let everyone load up their own bowl. Add avocado for creaminess, or shredded cabbage, sliced radishes, and crushed tortilla chips for crunch.

Canned white or golden hominy works here. These plump, chewy corn kernels give the stew its hearty texture. Dried hominy needs to be cooked separately before adding it to the pot.

Mexican oregano is a different herb from Mediterranean oregano, with floral, citrusy notes and a hint of anise. We prefer it in this pozole, but regular dried oregano works too.

No. The whole chicken simmers in water with onion, garlic, and spices to make the broth. Before adding the shredded chicken and cilantro purée, taste the broth and season with salt and pepper.

Can I make pozole verde ahead or freeze it?

Yes. Cook the chicken up to 3 days ahead and refrigerate it in its broth, then finish the recipe when you’re ready to serve. You can also freeze the finished pozole. Take Rick’s advice and stash a quart for your next weeknight dinner emergency.

Heat ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Cook 1 large yellow onion, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, seasoning with kosher salt and stirring occasionally, until very tender, 12–15 minutes. Add 2 tsp. ground coriander, 1 tsp. ground cumin, and ½ tsp. dried oregano, preferably Mexican, and cook, stirring constantly, until very fragrant, about 1 minute.

Place one 3½–4-lb. whole chicken in pot and pour in 12 cups water. Bring to a simmer and cook chicken, uncovered and reducing heat as needed to maintain a very gentle simmer (and turning once or twice if it isn’t completely submerged), until cooked through and legs wiggle easily in their joints, 40–50 minutes.

Meanwhile, preheat oven to 425°. Spread out 4 poblano chiles, 2 Cubanelle peppers or 2 more poblano chiles, 3 serrano chiles, and 1½ lb. tomatillos, husks removed, rinsed, on a large rimmed baking sheet. Roast, tossing once or twice, until chiles and peppers are browned and collapsing and tomatillos are tender, 30–40 minutes. Let cool.

Transfer chicken to a cutting board; set broth in pot aside. Let chicken sit until cool enough to handle. Pull meat from bones and shred into bite-size pieces; discard chicken skin and bones.

Split open chiles and peppers; remove stems and seeds and discard. Remove any skin that can be easily peeled off and discard. Transfer chiles and peppers to a blender and add tomatillos; reserve baking sheet. Blend until smooth. Stir chile purée into reserved broth and bring to a simmer. Reserve blender.

Spread out two 15-oz. cans golden or white hominy, rinsed, in an even layer on reserved baking sheet and roast, tossing halfway through, until very fragrant and hominy around edges of baking sheet are just beginning to brown, 12–18 minutes. Scrape into pot with broth.

Season broth with salt and freshly ground black pepper and simmer, uncovered, until flavors come together and broth is rich tasting, about 20 minutes. Ladle ½ cup broth into reserved blender. Add 2 cups cilantro leaves with tender stems and purée until smooth and very bright green, at least 1 minute. Add chicken to broth and cook until heated through, then stir in cilantro purée. Taste posole and season with more salt if needed.

Divide posole among bowls. Top with ½ small red onion, thinly sliced, and more cilantro leaves and dried oregano. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over.

Do Ahead: Chicken can be cooked 3 days ahead. Let cool in broth; cover and chill.

Editor’s note: This recipe was first published in 2017 as ‘Posole Verde With Chicken’; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more hearty soup recipes from Epicurious →

#6654. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6653. 23 Thanksgiving Bread Recipes: Rolls, Biscuits, and More

Pies get most of the Thanksgiving baking glory. But these Thanksgiving bread recipes make a strong case for saving some oven space for buttery dinner rolls, flaky biscuits, and midnight-sandwich-ready loaves. Think golden sweet potato buns soft enough to nap on, buttermilk cornbread to eat with butter or bake into dressing, and tender sweet loaves to nibble on Thanksgiving morning. Several recipes have make-ahead options too.

There’s no need to overhaul a classic. Adapted from The Fannie Farmer Baking Book, these Parker House rolls have buttery folds, golden tops, and a finish of flaky salt. Bake enough for seconds.

These pillowy rolls get their warm color and gentle sweetness from mashed sweet potato. Bake and freeze them up to a month ahead, then reheat and brush with melted butter before serving.

Butter tucked inside each roll melts as it bakes, crisping the bottom. “If you can imagine a warm dinner roll meeting a flaky croissant, you’re getting closer,” says Hana Asbrink.

Pillowy rolls swirled with sweet-salty pork floss, mayo, scallions, and furikake. Bake and freeze them up to three months ahead, then warm them through while everyone finds a seat.

A tangzhong—a cooked flour-and-milk paste—helps these sour cream and chive rolls stay exceptionally soft. Tear one off to mop up gravy, then save a few for tomorrow’s turkey sandwiches.

Garlic bread, meet buttery dinner roll. Fresh and dried dill work their way into these pillowy buns, which get a generous brushing of garlic butter after baking. Save one for a gravy swipe.

So many layers, you’ll feel like a geologist unearthing them. Claire Saffitz’s biscuits get their height from a cut-and-stack technique. Another reason to love them: You can freeze the unbaked biscuits up to a month ahead.

All the herby goodness of Thanksgiving stuffing, packed into a biscuit: sage, rosemary, fennel seed, and scallions. Save a few for breakfast the next morning, preferably under a generous ladle of leftover gravy.

No rolling pin, no biscuit cutter, no problem. Canned creamed corn keeps these drop biscuits tender, while Calabrian chile honey butter brings a little heat.

For the guest who always takes the biggest piece of garlic bread: flaky buttermilk biscuits loaded with Parmesan and parsley. Freeze them unbaked, then bake straight from frozen when the oven frees up.

Biscuits or cornbread? This cheesy mash-up means you don’t have to choose. Sharp cheddar and fresh sage work their way into flaky, buttery layers that feel right at home on the Thanksgiving table.

Looking to start a fight? Declare a cornbread recipe “best.” This version strikes a balance: a tender crumb, buttermilk tang, and a touch of sweetness. Eat it with butter—or turn it into cornbread dressing.

Cheddar, caramelized corn, and hot honey butter take this cornbread well beyond the usual. Nervous about the flip? “Don’t be afraid of flipping the bread—I promise you can do it,” says former BA food editor Rachel Gurjar.

Pumpkin purée gives this fall-ish rendition of our no-knead focaccia recipe its golden color and gentle sweetness. Finish with rosemary and flaky salt, then tear off a piece for dipping in olive oil. You can bake it a day ahead.

Leave the oven to the turkey. These flaky, skillet-cooked parathas have brown butter and sage tucked between their layers. Parcook them a day ahead, then fry until golden just before dinner.

A garlic knot with centerpiece ambitions. This braided loaf wraps buttery dough around garlic, Parmesan, and parsley, then gets another garlicky brush after baking. Start the dough a day ahead.

Leave the stand mixer where it is. This focaccia asks for a little patience, not much elbow grease, to produce its airy crumb and golden crust. An overnight rise gets you started; garlic butter finishes the job.

Focaccia’s leaf-shaped French cousin deserves a turn in the Thanksgiving bread basket. Green olives, rosemary, and lemon zest bring plenty of flavor. And yes, the dough comes together in one bowl.

In this crusty yeast bread recipe, apple juice replaces water. The apple flavor is subtle, but the appeal of a warm slice with butter is not.

Oats and chia seeds give this gluten-free loaf a dense, chewy crumb. No kneading, shaping, or scoring; just be sure to use the gluten-free oats and oat flour specified in the recipe.

Give Thanksgiving morning the sticky-bun treatment. This pull-apart bread packs tender apples between cinnamon-sugar-coated bites, with tangy cider caramel coating the whole thing. Put on a pot of coffee and let everyone help themselves.

Chocolate or vanilla? Rick Martinez’s conchas give you both, with a two-tone sugar topping over buttery Mexican sweet buns. Another reason to love them: You can bake them up to three days ahead.

Start the holiday with a thick slice of ginger-spiked pumpkin bread and a generous schmear of salted maple butter. You can bake the loaf up to four days ahead, leaving Thanksgiving morning for coffee and slicing—and, uh, all that other prep.

Maple-glazed turkey, garlicky mashed potatoes, pumpkin chiffon pie, and more recipes worthy of your Thanksgiving table.

Like brown-butter brussels sprouts with gochujang, green bean salad with Parmesan dressing, our best-ever mashed potatoes, and more reasons to rebrand the holiday “Sidesgiving.”

From hot toddies to big-batch punch, these festive drinks will get you in the holiday spirit.

Like pumpkin flan de queso, rosemary-pear snacking cake, Amish pecan cream pie, and more.

Stare into the transfixing eye of the "Seagull Nebula" in this newly-released test image from the visionary Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What it is: The head of the sassy Seagull Nebula (IC 2177)Where it is: Between the constellations Monoceros and Canis Major, about 3,700 light-years awayWhen it was shared: Oct. 22, 2026

When a seagull stares you down, scientists recommend that you stare right back at it to keep your dignity (and your french fries) intact.

Two years ago, astronomers at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory put this idea — and their brand-new telescope — to a test of cosmic proportions, aiming an experimental 144-megapixel camera at the menacing blue eye of the Seagull Nebula (IC 2177).

Located about 3,700 light-years from Earth, the Seagull Nebula is a conglomeration of three giant, billowing clouds of irradiated gas. The "head" of the bird, featured in Rubin's image above, is a cloud called Sharpless 2-292. Its pink plumage is made of hydrogen gas, which glows brightly as ionizing radiation flies forth from the young stars at the cloud's center. The bird's blue "feathers" are clouds of dust reflecting the light from young, blue stars nesting elsewhere in the region.

It's unclear who won this stellar stare-down. If the bird appeared to blink, that's only because its eye is really the triple-star system HD 53367, a flickering trio of very young and energetic stars actively shaping the cloud around them.

The Rubin Observatory, meanwhile, had to avert its gaze quickly; this image is just one of about 16,000 exposures taken of the night sky between Oct. 24 and Dec. 11, 2024, according to the National Science Foundation, which co-manages Rubin along with the U.S. Department of Energy. Taken with the aforementioned Commissioning Camera (ComCam), the deep-space photos served as an early test of the observatory's hardware, software and image-processing capabilities.

A comparison of ComCam's field of view (right box) with the LSST Cam's field of view (left box). The relative size of the full moon is shown for scale. LSST Cam, currently in use at the observatory, can see roughly 20 times more than ComCam saw in its test observations.

ComCam's test image is remarkably crisp — but what's even more impressive is that Rubin has since upgraded to a camera with more than 20 times the field of view. The Legacy Survey of Space and Time Camera currently mounted on the observatory's Simonyi Survey Telescope takes 3,200-megapixel images of the night sky every 30 seconds, completing a full scan of the entire southern sky every few nights, Tony Tyson, Rubin's chief scientist, previously told Live Science.

Now that the Legacy Survey of Space and Time has officially begun, Rubin will spend the next 10 years photographing the sky night after night, creating a time-lapse movie of the universe that is expected to reveal millions of cosmic wonders, from exploding supernovas to newfound comets and exoplanets. Perhaps it will even spot another bird.

#6649. New Year’s Pork Roast with Sauerkraut

In our home, we eat pork with sauerkraut for forward progress in the new year, along with 12 grapes for good luck each month ahead. Many years ago, our friend Doug was facing financial difficulties, so we brought this New Year’s dinner to his family. His fortunes turned for the better, and he became such a believer that when we later faced a heartbreaking time, he returned the gesture and brought the same meal to us. I can’t guarantee this pork and sauerkraut will bring good luck, but I can promise a delicious, comforting New Year’s Day dinner. —Bernadette Laganella, Voorhees, New Jersey

#6648. Vietnamese Coffee Martini

You get dessert and a cocktail all in one with this Vietnamese coffee martini, which adds sweetened condensed milk to the classic espresso martini for a rich, frothy sip.

Whipping up a Vietnamese coffee martini after dinner means two things: You don’t have to make dessert, and you aren’t going to sleep anytime soon. This cocktail is next-level sweet and caffeinated, and it makes your regular espresso martini look like child’s play. Sure, this cocktail shares some of the same elements (vodka, coffee liqueur and espresso), but it includes sweetened condensed milk for a rich, luxurious texture, signature caramel sweetness and super-frothy finish.

Vietnamese coffee is typically made with dark-roasted robusta beans, which taste bolder and more chocolatey than the arabica beans in most coffee blends. In traditional preparations, the grounds drip slowly through a small metal filter called a phin, straight into a glass with a layer of sweetened condensed milk waiting at the bottom. Fresh milk was hard to come by and didn’t keep well in Vietnam’s heat, so canned milk became the go-to. It’s almost as thick as syrup and tastes a little like melted caramel. Shaken into a cocktail, it lands somewhere closer to a creamy Baileys espresso martini than a classic one, only richer.

Fill a cocktail shaker three-fourths full with ice. Add the vodka, espresso, sweetened condensed milk and Kahlua. Cover the shaker and shake hard until condensation forms on the outside, 10 to 15 seconds.

Strain the cocktail into a glass and top with the coffee beans. Serve immediately, while the foam is at its fluffiest.

Editor’s Tip: Chill your martini glass or coupe for 10 to 15 minutes before you start mixing. A frosty glass keeps the cocktail colder longer and helps the foam hold its shape.

Enjoy a Vietnamese coffee espresso martini right after you shake it, since the foam starts to deflate as it sits. If you’ve mixed up a little extra, store the unshaken mixture of vodka, coffee, condensed milk and Kahlua in a sealed jar in the refrigerator for up to two days. Give it a good stir, then shake it over fresh ice right before serving to revive the froth.

Making Vietnamese coffee martinis ahead of time is a smart move for hosting. Brew and chill the espresso or cold brew up to a day ahead, then mix the cocktail without ice. Refrigerate the batched cocktail until guests arrive. When it’s go time, shake each drink to order with fresh ice so every glass gets that signature foamy top.

For a dairy-free Vietnamese coffee martini, swap the regular sweetened condensed milk for sweetened condensed coconut milk. You should be able to find it in most grocery stores near the baking aisle. It shakes up just as creamy and sweet, with a subtle toasted coconut flavor that plays beautifully with the coffee. Kahlua is dairy-free, so the rest of the recipe stays the same.

Vietnamese coffee is usually made with robusta beans, which have nearly twice the caffeine of the arabica beans used in most espresso blends. Ounce for ounce, phin-brewed Vietnamese coffee can rival a shot of espresso, which is why it stands up so well to sweet condensed milk.

The foam comes from the oils in freshly brewed coffee, so espresso gives you the most dramatic froth, while cold brew and instant coffee create a slightly thinner layer. The condensed milk helps, too, adding body that traps air bubbles as you shake. Use plenty of ice, shake like you mean it and strain right away into a chilled glass so the foam settles on top in a smooth, creamy cap.

#6647. The Cheesecake Factory Drama, Explained

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered Italy’s looming food shortage.

Well, it’s over. Last Ditch, the bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, that became the center of a tornado of scrutiny, ridicule, discourse, and, er, media coverage a few weeks ago is now closed as it searches for new co-owners, or to sell the bar to new owners. If your memory needs a refresh, the TL;DR is that the bar relaxed its COVID-conscious mask restrictions, and it tore the local community apart.

The Boston Globe covered the drama, and the story quickly went viral. But despite—or perhaps because of—its newfound infamy, the bar couldn’t attract enough clientele to stay open. Could new owners resurrect the beleaguered business?

Also in the discourse this week: Washington, DC residents will be voting on a foie gras ban which has prominent chefs coming out as firmly pro-foie, despite public backlash. José Andrés argues that the American food system also mistreats many other animals—and that we have bigger issues, like child hunger, to address.

Also in today’s Open Tab: why The Cheesecake Factory has made headlines this week, how salmon could decide Alaska’s midterm elections, a delivery platform acquisition for the ages, and a look inside LA’s buzzy Skywalker Grill.

This week the Cheesecake Factory’s name was splashed across headlines in a handful of national magazines and newspapers—a feat that hasn’t happened since…ever? It’s hard to say.

This story starts last weekend, when former president Barack Obama made a joke at a campaign rally in Ohio. “[President Trump’s] got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere,” he said.

Trump himself responded on Monday. “For you to say it’s a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president,” he told reporters. The White House X account followed up with some AI-generated trolling.

Rick McCormack, the chain’s former vice president of design, also weighed in. “I think it’s a little bit sad that the pettiness of politics would create that sound bite, knowing all our challenges going on in the country today,” he said.

Is the Cheesecake Factory designed to look like it was done by an Egypt-obsessed kid with an unrestricted budget and a lot of ambition? Yes. But that’s part of its charm. You need a maximalist setting to match a maximalist menu, a maximalist experience. As I see it, The Cheesecake Factory is designed as it is so that ordering an “all day morning cocktail” (?), or a slice of “Brownie Crunch Choc-o-Lot Cheesecake” suddenly doesn’t seem so crazy. The Cheesecake Factory, as we were reminded again and again this week, is an American institution. So, unfortunately, is a quips-based, sound-byte-heavy political system.

And don’t feel too bad about the beleaguered corporate chain, which operates 200-plus locations. The C-suite is laughing their way to the bank: Stock analysts were quick to point out it is among the highest performing stocks on the market.

A few weeks ago a friend who grew up in Alaska told me nonchalantly that the state’s upcoming primary would be decided by salmon. “It’s the only thing that matters,” he said.. According to a recent feature in the New Yorker, it looks like he was right.

For many Alaskans fishing is both a job and a way to nourish their family. The democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, even settled on the slogan ““Fish, Family, Freedom.” But in recent years, runs of king salmon and chum salmon have collapsed, and don’t seem to be recovering. Experts point to climate change, but activists point to the practice of trawling—a method of fishing that includes pulling an enormous net behind the boat— for pollack which also catches millions of salmon which get killed and discarded by fishermen.

“This is an ecological crisis, a cultural trauma, an economic emergency and a public-health disaster,” reads one op-ed in an Alaskan paper.

Today in sentences that a Victorian tween wouldn’t understand a single word of: Delivery platform DoorDash, most recently in the news for its new fleet of drones, will buy Instacart for $17 billion.

It’s hard to overstate just how enormous this deal will be. Instacart is among America’s dominant platforms for grocery delivery, and DoorDash corners the market on the country's restaurant delivery apparatus.

The size of the acquisition would, under most administrations, attract FTC scrutiny. This is a pretty big consolidation in the field, after all. But the Trump administration has been particularly permissive of giant companies coming together to maximize their joint slay. In this case “joint slay” means market share and monopoly.

Museums must have a buzzy restaurant attached these days, and Los Angeles’s Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is no different. That’s where you’ll find Skywalker Grill, which, despite its monied environs, features a menu that’s surprisingly approachable. As Bon Appétit contributor Khushbu Shah tells us, it’s quickly become one of the city’s hottest tables. She takes us inside the restaurant to break down its surprisingly accessible menu.

#6646. 12 Of Your Favorite Foods That Were Invented By Accident

Sometimes the best things happen when everything goes wrong.

Here at Delish, we’re no strangers to a tasty creation. From our viral Marry Me Chicken to our delectable Dubai Chocolate Brownies, our talented food editors are always experimenting in the kitchen to come up with your next great dish. But not every beloved food comes from hard work and endless testing. Some of our favorites actually owe their existence to happy accidents. Here are 12 foods that we have pure dumb luck to thank for.

Named after the English county where it originated, Worcestershire sauce is the accidental brainchild of John Wheeley Lea and William Henry Perrins. In 1835, a nobleman tasked the two chemists with creating a sauce from a recipe he had brought back from Asia. The duo worked on the sauce, but their client was unenthused, so they stored it in a cellar to languish. Over a year later, they found and tried it again, noting that the aging process made it taste delicious. Two years later, they were selling it.

While ice cream cones are a staple in any ice cream shop today, they weren't always. At the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, a concessionaire named Ernest A. Hamwi sold a Middle Eastern pastry called zalabis, or zalabiyeh. Next to him, an ice cream vendor ran out of serving dishes and, thinking on his feet, Hamwi rolled up his waffle-like pastry into a cone so his neighbor could keep serving ice cream. The result? Clearly a success.

That said, Hamwi isn’t the only man credited with the ice cream cone. Just one year prior, Italo Marchiony received a patent in New York City for a mold used to make edible ice cream cups. Hamwi, however, brought them mass recognition.

While the inventor and origins of the potato chip are contested, one of the most popular stories credits a happy accident at Moon’s Lake House in Saratoga Springs, New York. A very particular customer sent back their order of fried potatoes, asking for thinner slices. Annoyed, the chef (often credited as George Crum) sliced them as thin as he could and fried them extra long—as it turned out, the customer loved them. And now we have our beloved potato chips.

Yogurt has been around for millennia, dating back to around 5,000 B.C. Many accounts credit its discovery to an accident: Milk stored in bags in warm weather was exposed to bacteria, causing it to ferment into yogurt. As it turned out, yogurt became a great way to preserve milk.

If you’ve ever been the victim of killer brain freeze due to chugging a Slurpee, this one’s for you. A man named Omar Knedlik is credited with inventing the drink after a soda fountain broke in his store. He put soda in the freezer to keep it cold, accidentally creating slushy drinks that customers loved. He later used parts from a car air conditioner to build a machine that could recreate the frozen beverages. He named the product ICEE, which 7-Eleven eventually licensed and began selling under a different name exclusively at its stores. And that’s how we got our Slurpee.

Nashville hot chicken has one of the best origin stories of any food. In the 1930s, a man named Thornton Prince was known as quite the ladies’ man. One of the women he was seeing decided to seek revenge after Prince had been out all night. For payback, she loaded his favorite fried chicken recipe with every spicy ingredient she could find in her kitchen. Lo and behold, her plan backfired, as Prince loved the result. He went on to open a fried chicken shop with his brothers, and the rest is history.

You have a forgetful 11-year-old to thank for Popsicles. Back in 1905, Frank Epperson accidentally left a glass of water with powdered soda mix and a stirring stick outside overnight. Come morning, the mixture was frozen, but he popped it out of the glass and enjoyed his creation. He began making these ice pops for his friends, and in 1924, he filed a patent. Up until then, he was calling them Eppsicles, but his children changed the name to Pop’s ‘sicles, and the name stuck.

We have a sanitarium to thank for our favorite breakfast cereal, if you can believe it. Dr. John Harvey Kellogg worked alongside his brother Will at Battle Creek Sanitarium, where he accidentally created what is now known as corn flakes. Kellogg was trying to make a wheat-based dough for his patients. After leaving the dough out overnight by accident, he put it through rollers and found that it produced thin flakes, which the patients ended up loving. He later substituted corn and added sugar to commercialize the product.

Raisins date all the way back to around 2000 B.C. Historians believe ancient Persians and Egyptians discovered grapes that had dried on the vine and realized they could eat them. Wall paintings from that time period show dried fruit being both eaten and used as decor.

While the exact origins of pink lemonade are contested, two popular theories trace its creation back to the circus. In the first story, a teenage circus worker invented the drink after accidentally dropping red cinnamon candies into a vat of lemonade. Rather than toss the batch, he went with the flow and sold the now-pink lemonade.

The other story is a bit more off-putting. One circus worker reportedly ran out of water for the lemonade and used a bucket of dirty water that a performer had just used to wash her pink tights instead. He then sold the resulting beverage as pink lemonade. I really hope the first story is the accurate one.

It’s hard to believe that cheese puffs were initially created for animals, not humans. Animal food manufacturer Flakall Corporation created the cheesy snack we love today in 1935. To make animal feed, the company used a machine that ground corn. During the cleaning process, introducing moist corn into the machine produced airy corn puffs. An employee brought some home and experimented with seasoning them to create a product for humans.

The result was called Korn Kurls, and the company began producing them. The snack became so successful that the company changed its name to help distance itself from its humble beginnings in animal feed.

Now a beloved staple on many a Tex-Mex menu, the chimichanga is younger than you might think. The most common legend credits El Charro Café founder Monica Flin with inventing the fried dish. Apparently, she accidentally dropped a burrito into a deep fryer and started swearing at the mistake. Because children were present, she quickly switched gears and shouted “chimichanga”—which translates to “thingamajig”—instead. The rest, as they say, is history.

In this excerpt from "Killing the Dead," author John Blair looks at how the printed press ramped up tales of vampirism, leading to stories of people eating a supposed vampire's organs and drinking their blood in a bid to avoid the same fate.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the 17th and 18th centuries, the fear of vampires reached extraordinarily heights. People believed corpses could reanimate and wander around, terrorizing villages and spreading disease. They went to extreme lengths to prevent a vampire from rising. Some chopped the deceased person's head off, others placed sickles across their necks. Many were placed face down in their graves. In one grave in Poland, the remains of a boy were found with an iron padlock around his foot.

In this excerpt from "Killing the Dead: Vampire Epidemics from Mesopotamia to the New World" (Princeton University Press, 2025), author and historian John Blair reveals the impact the printed press had on the spread of vampiric lore — and the grizzly purported practice of ingesting the blood and organs of a vampire to prevent other people becoming one.

With the invention of printing, the circulation of European stories about restless corpses moved up several gears. Occasional early references were followed by a clutch of theological and philosophical discussions during c. 1580-1610, and then — from the 1670s — a steadily growing volume of printed academic and historical debate and commentary, reaching a climax in 1732.

Another landmark came in 1746 when the Benedictine scholar Dom Augustin Calmet published his survey of supernatural beings, which was quickly reissued in several editions, including an English one of 1759. This book's section on vampires was the most influential academic work on the subject ever published. Its straightforwardly evidence-based approach was a breath of fresh air after a long series of increasingly derivative works.

It achieved its remarkable popularity because it entered the market at the right point: saturated with so much fragmented and repetitive discussion of "vampires" (still a relatively new word), the reading public wanted a textbook. Calmet inspired a huge progeny of followers and popularisers, bringing the stories to a much wider readership; a good example of the genre is the Histoire des vampires et des spectres malfaisants [History of Vampires and Malevolent Specters] of 1820, a pocketbook that re-packages Calmet for the mass market.

Calmet's book remains the ultimate source of much modern vampire literature in Europe and America, both fi­ctional and supposedly historical, and was transformative in bringing the topic to a wider reading public. There and elsewhere, stories were now frozen on the printed page, where later generations could read them. But they were stories still: not necessarily more reliable, and by no means stable in transmission.

The tangled story of consuming blood from vampire corpses starts in a different and very unexpected place.

The complexity of interactions between learned discourse and popular practice is illustrated by one particularly bizarre and repellant (not to say dangerous) strand in the belief-system. This is the practice of ingesting blood or organs from a supposed vampire corpse, or ashes derived from burning them, as a remedy for vampire-induced illness.

Although not wholly dissimilar from the idea that victims will recover as they watch the smoke rise from burning vampire organs — already known in 11th-century England — its shocking physicality sets it apart. Did people in pre-modern Europe really do this?

A complicating factor is the medicinal use of human blood and bodyparts, in accordance with the theories of the physician, philosopher, and alchemist "Paracelsus" (Theophrastus von Hohenheim, c. 1493–1541). A brilliant experimenter, Paracelsus believed that substances healed through occult 'influences' or 'spirits,' the most powerful being those derived from what they were meant to cure: the human body.

The fact that medicine now rejects these hypotheses should not make us view them patronizingly: in the early modern period, ingesting or anointing with substances from Egyptian mummies or the blood of executed criminals seemed as rational as doing the same with any other substance. These Paracelsian ideas entered popular practice: at a beheading in Vienna in 1668/9, a man ran forward and caught the spouting blood to cure his epilepsy.

An illustration of an execution of a vampire.

The tangled story of consuming blood from vampire corpses starts in a different and very unexpected place. In 1687, a major ethnographical account of parts of West Africa by the Capuchin missionary Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi was published in Bologna. In it, Cavazzi describes magical and medical practices among the Mbundu of Angola, including a method of obtaining vital curative fluid from undecayed corpses:

When they are in a fresh and intact state when unearthed, their heads are cut from their bodies, from which it is said that blood flows out (which may happen through some illusion or deceit). It is collected and made into poultices for the sick, or mixed into their food, which infallibly guarantees health. Thereafter the dead person, having lost his strength, will no longer be able to harass them.

From Angola to Paris: in May 1693, a story appeared in the society magazine Mercure Galant. The author was the courtier and polymath Pierre des Noyers (1607–93), who spent several years in Poland in the entourage of Queen Louise-Marie. Much earlier, in 1639, he had written to a friend about the being known as upior (Ruthenian) or striga (Polish): born with teeth; eating its shroud and then its hands and arms in the coffi­n; causing successive deaths of family members; and extinguished by decapitation and release of pent-up blood.

This story is rather highly coloured (eating the hands and arms is unusual), but it does probably originate in genuine oral accounts of the shroud-chewer belief.

Very different is des Noyers’s account from 1693. Now the striges and upierz have become corpse-hijacking demons: 'It is said that the demon takes this blood from the body of a living person, or from certain animals, and carries it into a dead body; for it is alleged that the demon goes out from this corpse during a certain period, between noon and midnight, after which it returns and stores there the blood that it has gathered.'

They denied cutting out the heart, mixing the blood into flour, and baking cakes with it, but the judges were sceptical and made them swear an oath.

The blood comes out of the mouth, nose, and ears of the corpse, the corpse swims in blood, and it starts to eat its shroud. The demon especially troubles former associates and relatives of the dead 'host,' appearing to them in the guise of parents or friends, and does not leave until all the family members have died in succession. The remedy is to exhume the corpse, which is found soft, flexible, bloated, and red:

When they are found in that state, having the likeness of those who had appeared in dreams, their heads are cut off and their hearts are opened, and a quantity of blood flows out. It is collected and kneaded into flour, which is made into bread, which is a certain remedy to guarantee against such a terrible affliction. After the heads [of the dead people] have been cut off, those whom the Spirit torments at night are no longer troubled by it, and are well thereafter.

This narrative has problems. The idea of the demon using the corpse as a safe-deposit for its hoard of blood seems to be unique; so, probably, is the time-slot between noon and midnight. These read like clerical rationalizations, perhaps fed to des Noyers by some Polish priest and overlaid on his earlier, more authentic observations. But more fundamentally, it seems obvious that des Noyers’s account of Poland shamelessly re-works Cavazzi's account of Angola, published eight years previously.

It might not be quite so simple. An earlier common source, still unidenti­fied, remains possible. The descriptions of mixing blood into food and poultices look remarkably close to Paracelsian ideas, extended from ordinary corpses to undead ones: was even Cavazzi's account distorted by his own medical learning? But in any case des Noyers’s account is a piece of unprincipled plagiarism, worthless as evidence for Polish folk-belief.

Even so, it has bounced down through the echo-chambers of vampire literature ever since. The following year, a lawyer called Marigner built on the narrative — which he took at face value — with long philosophical musings on the nature of vampires. Inevitably, in 1746, it was republished in Calmet's book, which made it permanently available to vampire-aware readers.

While otherwise faithful to des Noyers, Calmet's version irons out the motif of demonic corpse-possession by calling this predator a vampire 'or a demon in its form.' This process of moulding to a more familiar template culminates in a recent version that presents the story as straightforward ethnographic reporting, omitting the demonic motif completely.

So far, this has just been a morality tale of plagiarism and uncritical copying. But in 1713, at Dąbrówka (now western Ukraine), some villagers were tried in the Uniate episcopal court for exhuming a woman's corpse and mutilating it in inventive ways. They admitted to the exhumation (because the dead woman had been walking around and attacking people), and to drinking the corpse's blood mixed with vodka. They denied cutting out the heart, mixing the blood into flour, and baking cakes with it, but the judges were sceptical and made them swear an oath.

This will sound very familiar to readers of early modern witch trials, where suspects were regularly bullied into admitting bizarre fantasies formulated by the persecutors. In this case, it seems clear that at least the idea of the blood-cakes was suggested by the judges; the same could be true of the blood-drinking, even though the accused were induced to confess that. It is distinctly possible, not to say likely, that an ordinary corpse-killing was embellished with luridly fi­ctitious detail by judges who knew des Noyers's report from twenty years earlier.

Killing the Dead provides the first in-depth, global account of one of the world’s most widespread yet misunderstood forms of mass hysteria—the vampire epidemic. In a spellbinding narrative, John Blair takes readers from ancient Mesopotamia to present-day Haiti to explore a macabre frontier of life and death where corpses are believed to wander or do harm from the grave, and where the vampire is a physical expression of society’s inexplicable terrors and anxieties.

John Blair is an emeritus fellow of The Queen’s College, Oxford, and emeritus professor of medieval history and archaeology at the University of Oxford. His many books include "Building Anglo-Saxon England" (Princeton University Press), "The Church in Anglo-Saxon Society, and The Anglo-Saxon Age: A Very Short Introduction" (Oxford University Press).

#6643. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6639. Pumpkin S’mores Cookies

Recipe by Lauren Habermehl, Pewaukee, Wisconsin

Preheat the oven to 350°F and line two sheet pans with parchment paper.

Melt the butter in a medium saucepan over medium heat. Cook, stirring often with a whisk, until the butter has melted, begins to foam, and turns a rich golden brown color. Remove the saucepan promptly and pour the butter into a bowl of a stand mixer. Cool the brown butter at room temperature for 10 to 15 minutes. (This is important! Editor’s Tip: Keep a close eye on the butter, as it can burn easily if you’re not careful. Browning butter typically takes 3 to 5 minutes and is ready when the butter has a warm, nutty aroma.

#6638. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6636. Paul Hollywood Once Had A Very Different Look & Bake Off Fans Know Exactly Who He Resembles

Turns out the man behind the Hollywood handshake has quite the origin story.

If you know Paul Hollywood from The Great British Bake Off, you know the routine: a steely blue-eyed stare, a brutally honest critique, and, if you're lucky, one of those coveted Hollywood handshakes. But the man who's been judging everybody else's baking since 2010 nearly ended up in an entirely different creative field—and he had a whole lot more hair while figuring it out.

In an Instagram video posted on October 25, Hollywood revealed how he went from aspiring artist to professional baker, a career change that apparently came down to a £500 haircut.

After leaving school at 16, Hollywood enrolled in art school, where he tried everything from pottery and photography to textiles, fine art, and sculpture. He eventually settled on the latter, and by all accounts, was having a pretty great time. Then his father, who owned several bakeries, came along with a different career proposal.

Hollywood wasn't exactly eager to leave art school behind as he was enjoying life there all while sporting a glorious head of long hair. So his dad sweetened the deal by offering him a hefty chunk of change to chop it all off and join the family business.

Apparently, that was enough to get the scissors moving. Hollywood shaved his head, traded sculpture for sourdough, and started learning the ropes.

He said he took to baking surprisingly quickly, even embracing the rather brutal hours. Hollywood recalled getting up at 1 or 2 a.m. six days a week, with Friday shifts sometimes starting at 11 p.m.

From there, he went on to work at major hotels across the U.K., eventually took his talents abroad, and found himself on television. As Hollywood put it, "The rest is history."

But the most entertaining part of this story arrived the following day, when Hollywood posted photographic evidence of the hair that’d been worth £500.

"Pictures mid long hair obviously with cat too !!" he captioned the throwback, which shows a much younger Hollywood holding a fluffy cat while sporting shoulder-length dark hair. It's quite a departure from the neatly cropped silver look we've come to know, and somehow, the cat isn't even the most talked-about part of the picture.

That's because fans immediately noticed a striking resemblance to someone else in the Bake Off tent: co-host Noel Fielding.

"Looking like Noel here Mr H!" one person commented. "Thought this was Noel for a second 😆," another admitted, while a third agreed, "this could easily be Noel."

Hollywood wasn't about to let the comparisons go unanswered, either. "Agree, I’m older so he was channeling me!" he joked in response.

Now I'd like Noel to dig up a photo of himself with short hair. It seems only fair.

#6635. 21 Easy Weeknight Dinners for November

As daylight dwindles and the November chill settles in, dinner calls for something cozy. Think chicken thighs nestled into caramelized onions, pasta slicked with brown butter, and hearty soups that practically demand a hunk of crusty bread. It’s time to lean into comfort food.

The good news? You don’t need to spend your whole Sunday cooking to make dinner feel special, so you’ll have plenty of time for that When Harry Met Sally rewatch. These 21 easy weeknight dinners deliver all the comfort without the commitment. There’s a three-ingredient pumpkin soup, gochujang chicken that gets a quick blast under the broiler, and a smoky one-pan pasta made with pantry staples. Plus a few Thanksgiving-adjacent flavors—sage, stuffing, squash—because the holiday is right around the corner.

Greek yogurt tenderizes the chicken quickly, but the real weeknight win is the broiler: just 15 minutes under high heat, and you’ve got dinner.

Juicy chicken meatballs and crisp-tender sesame green beans roast on opposite sides of the same sheet pan, streamlining both dinner prep and cleanup.

This speedy stir-fry recipe brings together thin strips of boneless pork shoulder and crisp-tender bok choy for a satisfying, weeknight-ready dinner.

Savory ground beef, fluffy scrambled eggs, and crisp vegetables turn a bowl of steamed rice into a satisfying Japanese dinner that’s ready in 35 minutes.

Give boxed stuffing mix a new lease on life with this clever, holiday-inspired crust. Mixed with Parmesan, lemon zest, parsley, and butter, it gives tender fish a golden, crispy topping. Genius.

Brushed with a sticky, sweet teriyaki sauce, then hurled under the broiler, this salmon develops a glossy, caramelized finish in a matter of minutes.

This easy sheet-pan dinner pairs tender cod with a savory chorizo topping. Big flavor, minimal effort, and only one pan to wash.

Canned chickpeas and frozen spinach make this richly spiced saag quick to prepare—and any leftovers taste even better the next day.

Inspired by satay, this saucy, lip-smacking tofu dish comes together in 30 minutes in just one skillet—so cleanup is a breeze.

Cheesy, creamy, and deeply comforting, these fondue-inspired beans bring a little alpine indulgence to an ordinary Tuesday. Serving them over crusty bread is a must.

Nutty brown butter, crunchy pecans, and hot Italian sausage make this an easy dinner bursting with fall flavors. One reader reports, “Made me feel like a 5-star chef.”

Buttery, garlicky shrimp scampi meets pasta in this weeknight-friendly dinner. A splash of white wine and a pinch of red pepper flakes make the sauce sing.

Canned butternut squash purée (find it by the canned pumpkin!) makes this cozy, cold-weather recipe come together in a snap. Vegetable broth and certified vegetarian parm keep it meat-free, but chicken broth works if that’s what you’ve got.

Four ingredients are all you need for these grown-up buttered noodles. Toasted almonds and parsley are totally optional, but add welcome texture and zing.

Pumpkin purée adds richness, body, and a gentle orange hue to this speedy ground beef chili, letting the flavors of the spices and aromatics shine.

Roasted squash, crispy bacon, and crunchy walnuts turn chopped salad into a proper fall dinner. Use pre-cut butternut squash to streamline prep.

This comforting chicken noodle soup is ideal for chilly evenings or sick days. Chicken breast, kabocha squash, and tiny ditalini cook right in the broth.

A vegetarian spin on the classic Reuben swaps in hearty kale for the meat but keeps the melty cheese and tangy sauerkraut. One reader reports, “I didn’t miss the pastrami one bit.”

Made almost entirely from pantry ingredients—S&B curry powder, red lentils, crushed tomatoes, and coconut milk—this cozy soup is, as one reviewer puts it, “way more delicious than it should be.”

When dinner needs to get on the table pronto, a tuna melt is hard to beat: pantry-friendly, cheesy, and comforting.

This fiery soup has a shockingly trim ingredient list: curry paste (we like Maesri), a can of pumpkin purée, and coconut milk. Perfect for busy November weeknights.

#6633. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

The original Bearista Glass Cold Cup returns to select Starbucks coffeehouses on Dec. 1, just in time for holiday gifting. The bear-shaped glass comes with a green beanie-shaped lid and striped straw, ready to hold your cold brew.
